docs.title: Slots and Inter-node Value Passing
docs.text: Every producing node in a Tryll workflow — Generate, GenerateAndSpeak, CannedResponse, Transform, and the instruction nodes — writes its output into a slot: a named piece of text on a shared, per-turn blackboard. Downstream nodes in the same turn, and Mustache templates anywhere in the graph, can read any slot that has been written so far. This page explains the model; see the node reference pages for each node's specific input/output_name/send/history_role behaviour.

docs.title: The blackboard
docs.text: Each turn has one blackboard (an Interaction). At the start of the turn the client's message is written into the reserved slot user_message. As the graph runs, every node that produces text writes it into a slot too — named by that node's output_name if set, otherwise the node's own name. Slot names must match [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]* and user_message is reserved (no node may claim it).

docs.title: Reading a slot: input
docs.text:
Nodes that consume text — Generate, GenerateAndSpeak, Retrieve, Speak, ClassifyIntent, ClassifyIntentLLM, and ToolCall — have an input parameter: the name of the slot to read. Leave it empty for the default, user_message, uniformly across every one of these nodes (including Speak, whose empty input used to auto-voice the latest assistant-role slot instead — that special-cased default was removed in favor of this uniform rule). Set it to any upstream node's name to consume that node's output instead — this is how you chain nodes: a Transform (or Generate) rewrites or composes text into its own slot, and the next node reads it via input.

flowchart LR
    rewrite["Transform<br>rewrite"] -->|input=rewrite| retrieve["Retrieve<br>retrieve"]
    retrieve --> generate["Generate<br>generate"]

ClassifyIntentLLM is a partial exception: input only re-selects the current turn's user-area message; the history_turns of past turns it replays for coreference always use the plain user_message slot, matching Generate's own history projection.

docs.title: Reading a slot in a template: {{slot.<name>}}
docs.text: Any Mustache template (on Generate, GenerateAndSpeak, or Transform) can reference a slot directly with {{slot.<name>}} — this is a look-up, distinct from input (which replaces the resolved user turn). Use {{slot.<name>}} to weave a slot's value into a larger composed message without displacing the conversational turn structure. {{user_message}} is always available as the raw client input regardless of input. See Use Mustache templates for the full tag reference ({{#instructions}}, {{knowledge_<source>}}, …).

docs.title: Controlling the wire: send
docs.text:
send: SendAnswer controls whether a node's text is streamed to the client as AnswerText frames:

Value Behaviour None Captured into the slot only — never sent. Use this for internal/scratch nodes (a query-rewrite step, a draft the user should never see). Whole One AnswerText frame, sent once the full text is ready. Streamed Per-token/delta AnswerText frames as text is generated.

Every AnswerText frame carries node_name, so a client that cares which node produced a chunk of text (e.g. attributing multiple NPC speakers in one turn) can distinguish them; clients that don't care can ignore the field.

docs.title: Controlling replay: history_role
docs.text:
history_role: HistoryRole controls whether a slot's text is replayed as a separate assistant message in the projected prompt — both on later turns and, for downstream nodes, within the same turn it was written (see Same-turn effects below):

Value Behaviour None Never replayed — a scratch value that only exists within the turn it was written, readable only via input/{{slot.<name>}}. Assistant Replayed as a separate assistant message, in the order it was produced, both to downstream nodes later in the same turn and on every later turn's projected prompt.

User and System are reserved for future use and not implemented yet.

docs.title: Same-turn effects
docs.text:
Within the same turn, send/history_role have two independent effects on downstream nodes — neither is gated by "did this go out on the wire":

  1. Every slot is directly readable, no matter its send/history_role. Any downstream node's input selector and any template's {{slot.<name>}} reference can see it. A Transform node with send=None can still feed a Retrieve or Generate node two steps later; nothing about "not on the wire" means "not available internally".
  2. history_role=Assistant slots additionally replay as assistant-role messages into every downstream node's projected prompt within the same turn — the same replay mechanism used for later-turn history, applied within-turn to upstream outputs. A "draft → refine" chain gets the draft in context for free: the refine node sees it both as {{slot.draft}} and as a natural assistant message immediately before its own prompt.

docs.title: Naming and renaming
docs.text: Slot names are just node names (or output_name overrides) — there's no separate GUID layer. Both the Unity and Unreal editors provide a rename commit-point for a node's name and for its output_name override: committing a new value there (Enter/focus-loss in Unity's delayed text fields, OnTextCommitted in Unreal's Details-panel customizations) automatically rewrites every exit field and StartNode referencing the old node name, every input selector naming the old effective slot, and every {{slot.<old_name>}} tag in every node's template/instruction text across the graph — as a single undoable transaction. The commit point also enforces the [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]* grammar, rejects the reserved user_message, and uniquifies against existing node/slot names. The input field itself renders as a dropdown of only the slots that are may-reachable upstream of that node ("User Message" plus one entry per upstream producer) — no free-text entry — so stale references are visually distinguishable and structurally harder to create in the first place.

docs.title: Slots vs. Variables
docs.text: Slots and Agent Variables look similar (both render via a Mustache {{namespace.<name>}} tag) but serve opposite purposes: a slot is per-turn and node-produced — it exists only because a node ran this turn, and disappears with the turn unless replayed as history. A variable is persistent and game-produced — declared once at CreateAgent, it survives across every turn until the game changes it, and no node ever writes one. Use a slot to pass a node's output to another node or template within (or across) a turn; use a variable to inject external game state (player level, mood, inventory) into a prompt or a Retrieve filter without a ChangeParam round-trip.

docs.title: STT and Voice Input
docs.text:
Voice input lets a player speak to an agent instead of typing. The client streams raw microphone audio to the server, a speech-to-text (STT) model transcribes it, and the transcript comes back as a stream of updates. The client can then send the final text to an agent as if the player had typed it.

This page explains the mental model: the utterance lifecycle, the two choices that shape how a turn ends, and the kinds of transcript update you receive. For the step-by-step API, see Use Voice Input; to bias recognition toward game-specific words, see Bias Voice Input with Hotwords.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    mic["Microphone<br>(client)"] -->|PCM frames| handle["VoiceInput handle"]
    handle -->|AudioBuffer| server["Server STT session<br>(Sherpa-ONNX)"]
    server -->|TranscriptUpdate| handle
    handle -.->|UtteranceFinal, then SendMessage| agent["Agent (optional)"]

You create a VoiceInput handle (bound to an STT model), open an utterance, stream 16-bit PCM audio as it's captured, and receive transcript updates. The server resamples your audio to the model's rate, runs it through the STT engine, and pushes updates back. A non-empty final transcript is text the client can send to an agent; the server does not start that turn.

Voice input needs an STT model on disk — download one in the Model Manager. Its catalog entry names its engine (Sherpa-ONNX), so the session needs no engine setting. STT runs on the CPU, so it costs system RAM but no VRAM; see Models and Inference Engines.

docs.title: The utterance lifecycle
docs.text:
An utterance is one Begin … End cycle on a handle — a single thing the player says.

  1. Begin — opens a recording window and starts mic capture. The server only transcribes. On a non-empty final, send the text to an agent yourself (the Unity and Unreal voice components do this when a target agent is set, and drop it when that agent already has a turn in flight).
  2. Stream audio — push PCM chunks as they arrive. Sending is fire-and-forget; chunks that arrive with no open utterance are dropped.
  3. Updates arrive — the server streams transcript updates as it recognises speech.
  4. End — the utterance closes (see who ends it), producing exactly one UtteranceFinal with the complete text. An utterance also closes automatically after max_utterance_ms (default 60 s).

Cancel discards an open utterance without producing a final transcript.

docs.title: Transcript updates
docs.text:
Every update carries a kind and the text so far. Treat a Partial as overwrite-in-place — it is always superseded by a later update.

Kind Meaning SpeechStart The recogniser detected the start of speech (empty text). Offline models only. Partial A revisable in-progress hypothesis ("cast" → "cast fire" → "cast fireball"). Streaming (online) models only. SegmentFinal A committed chunk while the utterance stays open. UtteranceFinal The last update for the cycle; carries the complete concatenated text. Exactly one per utterance.

docs.title: The two choices
docs.text: How a turn behaves comes down to two independent choices that combine into four cases.

docs.title: 1. Who ends the utterance — push-to-talk vs hands-free
docs.text:
• Push-to-talk (PTT) — you decide when the utterance ends by calling End (e.g. on key release). Set autoFinishOnSilence = false. Best when the player holds a button to talk.
  • Hands-free — the server closes the utterance when the player stops talking. Set autoFinishOnSilence = true (the default). Best for always-listening NPCs.

docs.title: 2. Which recogniser — offline vs online
docs.text:
The STT model's family decides how speech is segmented and whether you get partials. You don't set this directly — it comes from the model you pick.

Offline (e.g. Whisper, SenseVoice, Parakeet) Online / streaming (e.g. streaming Zipformer, Paraformer, T-One) Partials none yes (revisable, low latency) SpeechStart yes no Segmentation Silero VAD (voice-activity detection) slices speech from silence the recogniser's built-in endpointer Feel segment-lagged (decodes a chunk once it's complete) streaming (updates as you speak)

Offline models attend over a whole window at once, so Tryll wraps them with Silero VAD to cut the stream into speech segments. Online models decode incrementally and have their own endpointer — Tryll does not layer VAD on top of them.

docs.title: How the two combine
docs.text: PTT/hands-free × recogniser What closes the turn PTT + offline your End call (or the timeout) PTT + online your End call (partials stream meanwhile) Hands-free + offline the first VAD speech segment Hands-free + online the first non-empty endpointer result; brief pauses emit empty "heartbeat" segments that keep the turn armed so the player can keep talking

docs.title: Sending the transcript to an agent
docs.text: The server never starts a turn from speech. When a Unity or Unreal voice component has a target agent, the component sends the non-empty UtteranceFinal text to that agent with SendMessage, and drops it if the agent already has a turn in flight. Without a voice component, call SendMessage with the final text yourself. Either way the spoken words drive a normal turn (streamed AnswerText, and TTS if the graph has a Speak/GenerateAndSpeak node). Open the next utterance after the reply and any TTS playback finish, so the mic doesn't transcribe the agent's own voice.

docs.title: Choosing a model
docs.text:
STT models are declared in the catalog like any other, with model_type: "stt" and engine: "sherpa-onnx"; you reference one by name when creating the handle. Rough guidance:

  • Latency-sensitive / always-listening → a streaming model (partials give immediate feedback).
  • Best accuracy, short commands → an offline model (Whisper family, Parakeet).
  • Hotword biasing (NPC/spell names) is supported by transducer/CTC families (Parakeet, streaming Zipformer/Paraformer, T-One) — not by Whisper or SenseVoice.

Every offline model also loads a VAD model (default Silero VAD) as a dependency; VAD entries are download/config only and are not separately pinnable. See Model Management and, for on-disk sizes, Estimate Memory Footprint.

docs.title: Tool Calling
docs.text: "Tool calling" is the trick that turns a chat model into something that can act on the world — look up the weather, move a camera, trigger a quest. In Tryll, tool calling is detection-based: the server tells your client that a tool should be called and with what arguments, and your client decides whether to actually run it — the server never executes the tool itself. This page explains why that split exists, how small local models are coaxed into producing tool calls, and where the edges are.

docs.title: The shape of a tool call in Tryll
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    participant TC as ToolCall node
    participant M as Model

    C->>S: CreateAgent(graph with ToolCall node + tools[])
    C->>S: SendMessage("turn on the porch light")
    S->>TC: Execute
    TC->>M: Generate (non-streaming) with tool-schema prompt
    M-->>TC: "{"tool": "set_light", "args": {"name":"porch","on":true}}"
    TC-->>S: parsed call + ToolCallNotification (if disposition notifies)
    S-->>C: ToolCallNotification{tool_name, arguments_json}
    TC->>TC: record the call on the current turn
    TC-->>S: exit "tool_called"
    Note over S,C: pause + Resume(tool_results) when AwaitResult;<br/>else Acknowledge / RouteOnly close history without a result

Three things to notice:

  1. The model never talks to tools directly. It only produces text. The node parses that text for a tool-call pattern.
  2. The server never executes the tool. It fires a notification to the client and moves on. For model-visible results use disposition = AwaitResult and resume with tool_results; for side effects use Acknowledge / RouteOnly / other non-AwaitResult dispositions.
  3. A failed parse is not an error. If no tool pattern is found, the node takes the no_tool_called route. That is a perfectly normal control flow — branch the graph on it.

docs.title: Why detection-only?
docs.text:
Small local models in 2025 are not uniformly good at tool calls. Different model families were fine-tuned on different prompt shapes and different output grammars. Crucially, none of them know about your tools.

Running the tool server-side would force Tryll to:

  • sandbox arbitrary code,
  • make network / filesystem policy decisions for your app, and
  • embed a universal tool-dispatcher that can never match the specifics of a game engine or a desktop app.

Detection-only punts all of that back to the client, where the code to "turn on the porch light" already lives. The server's job is to reliably extract {tool_name, arguments} from the model — which is the hard part in small models anyway.

It also means tool calls compose naturally with the rest of Tryll. A graph can put a guardrail in front of a ToolCall node, a CannedResponse on the rejection path, and so on. Nothing about the graph structure is special because tools are in it.

docs.title: Prompting is driven by the model's own chat template
docs.text:
You do not pick a tool-call "format" in Tryll. Tool prompting and parsing flow through each model's own chat template (via llama.cpp's common/ engine): the model's GGUF decides where the tool schema goes in the prompt, how each tool definition is rendered, and what pattern its tool calls take. Tryll advertises the tools, the template renders them, the returned grammar constrains generation, and the same template's parser extracts {tool_name, arguments} from the output — the exact syntax the model was trained on (Qwen's <tool_call> XML, Granite's <|tool_call|> block, Llama-3's JSON, …).

This replaced an earlier hand-rolled system of four fixed formats (chatml / llama3 / mistral / generic) selected via a tool_call_format param. That param still exists on the ToolCall node for wire/config compatibility but is deprecated and ignored by the server — do not set it. If a converted GGUF's embedded template doesn't render tools even though the model was trained for them, a server admin can override it per-variant with chat_template_file (see Model Management), and CreateAgent fails fast when a template can't render tools at all (see Not every model can call tools).

docs.title: What the node actually does
docs.text:
On each turn the ToolCall node:

  1. Advertises the tool schema to the model through its own chat template (which decides where the schema goes and how each tool is rendered).
  2. Runs a non-streaming Generate against the node's model, with the template-provided grammar constraining generation. Temperature is typically low for tool calls (the default is to inherit sampling params; override them to 0 for determinism).
  3. Parses the output with the same template's parser to extract content, reasoning, and any tool calls — in whatever syntax that model was trained on.
  4. For each parsed call, records the call on the current turn. If disposition notifies, also sends a ToolCallNotification wire frame so your client can react.
  5. Exits via tool_called (one or more parsed) or no_tool_called.

One param worth calling out: mode. It replaces the two independent ideas of "what if no tool call comes back" and "should a call even be optional" with a single three-way choice:

mode When no tool is called Use when call_or_answer (default) The model's residual text is emitted as a normal AnswerText reply Your graph puts the ToolCall node in place of a Generate node — one node either calls a tool or answers detect_only Nothing is emitted; the turn just routes no_tool_called A separate Generate node takes over after no_tool_called require_call Not applicable — a call is mandatory See Forcing a tool call below

mode is mutable — see How to change agent parameters — so a node can flip between require_call (for a turn you know is a command) and detect_only/call_or_answer (for free chat) without recreating the agent.

docs.title: Forcing a tool call
docs.text:
Some models — notably ones fine-tuned on the Mistral tool-call format, including Mistral 7B (with the chat_template_file override) and the Ministral 3 models — often "know" the right tool and arguments but simply never emit the format's trigger token under normal generation. The underlying reason is that the tool-call grammar is lazy by default: it only starts constraining the model's output once the model has already committed to calling a tool on its own. If it never does, generation drifts into plain text and the turn silently routes no_tool_called.

mode = require_call switches the grammar to eager: it constrains output from the very first token and guarantees at least one call. This reliably fixes the "knows the answer, never emits the tag" failure — but it comes with real trade-offs, so use it deliberately:

  • The model cannot answer plain questions anymore. If a turn isn't actually a command, require_call still forces a tool call — usually with "unspecified"-style placeholder arguments. Only use require_call behind something that already knows the turn is a command (an intent/routing node, or client-side knowledge of the input channel), and switch back to detect_only / call_or_answer for anything else.
  • It can occasionally stall instead of failing fast. On some models, a turn the model is reluctant to act on can run all the way to max_tokens before giving up, rather than immediately emitting a placeholder call. Budget max_tokens accordingly for require_call nodes.
  • It does not fix a template that can't render tools at all — that is the fail-fast check below, a separate problem require_call cannot work around.
  • Multi-turn Mistral-family tool calling is supported under the default complete-pair history projection (Acknowledge / RouteOnly / AwaitResult — see below). An earlier dangling-call shape used to crash those templates on the second tool-calling turn; that gap is closed.

Node creation rejects mode = require_call combined with an empty tools list up front (forcing a call with nothing to call is meaningless).

docs.title: Tool-call history: complete pairs, never dangling
docs.text:
Once a ToolCall node detects a call, the turn typically has no AnswerText — only tool-call records (and, depending on policy, tool results). Tryll projects those into later prompts as a complete assistant(tool_calls) → tool(result) pair in the model's native syntax — never a half-pair dangling before the next user turn (that shape was off-distribution and crashed Mistral-family templates).

ToolCallParams.disposition chooses notify, pause, and history shape (schema default Acknowledge):

Disposition History Client result? RouteOnly Omit tool syntax; empty assistant closer on historical turns No Acknowledge Complete pair with acknowledge_text (empty ⇒ "ok") No Notify Omit No (event only) NotifyAndAcknowledge Synthetic ack No (event only) Pause / PauseAndAcknowledge Omit / synthetic ack No — pause for ChangeParams, not results AwaitResult Complete pair with your ResumeAgentRequest.tool_results Yes — pause required

Use AwaitResult when the model must condition on a real tool payload: pause after the call, run the tool client-side, resume with results keyed by call_id, then let a downstream Generate speak. Unity and Unreal deliver the call on the agent component (ToolCallNotification / OnToolCall, plus the call-id and detailed forms). The session events on TryllClient and UTryllSubsystem are the all-agents form and still lead with the agent id. RegisterTool can auto-resume, but its handlers only run for pausing dispositions (Pause, PauseAndAcknowledge, AwaitResult) — they never fire for Notify / NotifyAndAcknowledge, which have no pause to auto-resume from. Among the dispositions a handler does run for, the client only attaches tool_results when the batch is AwaitResult (see disposition on the tool_call event); Pause / PauseAndAcknowledge auto-resume without a result payload. For Notify / NotifyAndAcknowledge, react via the typed call-ID notification event (or the generic NodeEvent callback) instead of RegisterTool. C++/Python use ResumeWithToolResult(s) / resume(..., tool_results=) (prefer the *Async / resume_async forms from a reader-thread callback). See Define and handle tool calls.

Prose summaries ("I called operate_door…") are deliberately not offered — strong instruction-followers imitate that text instead of emitting a real call next turn.

docs.title: Not every model can call tools
docs.text:
Advertising tools only works if the model's chat template actually renders them — and several shipped GGUF conversions simply don't (their template ignores the tools variable entirely, so the model never even sees that a tool exists). Running a ToolCall node against one of those models used to fail silently: every turn routed no_tool_called with no diagnostic.

CreateAgent now rejects a ToolCall node up front when its model can't render tool definitions, with an error naming the model and suggesting a fix:

tool calling is not supported for model 'Gemma 3 4B Instruct (Q4_K_M)'
because its chat template does not render tool definitions. Set
'chat_template_file' on the model's variant in models.json to an
override template with tool support, or remove the tools from this node.

If the model genuinely supports tool calling but the converted GGUF's embedded template doesn't render it (a real gap — the model itself may still have been trained on a tool format), a server admin can point chat_template_file at a replacement Jinja template for that variant. See Model Management: variants entry fields.

To see the verdict before downloading a model, check the selected model's detail pane in the Unity/Unreal Model Manager: every language model in the catalog declares an advisory tool_call_support value (supported or unsupported) per variant. It is a hint for picking a model, not a guarantee — the fail-fast check above is what actually decides at agent creation.

docs.title: What makes tool calls reliable (or unreliable)
docs.text:
From most to least impactful:

  1. Pick a model whose chat template supports tools. This is the biggest lever — a model trained and templated for tool calls (Qwen 3.x, Granite 4.x, Llama-3.x, …) is far more reliable than one coaxed into it. CreateAgent rejects a model whose template can't render tools at all.
  2. Keep the tool list short. Small models get overwhelmed past 5–8 tools. If you have many, put a routing / guardrail node in front to select a subset.
  3. Write tool descriptions like prompts. The description is what the model sees. "Turn a named light on or off" beats "light controller function". Name the unfiltered state (any, unspecified) instead of hoping the model omits a slot — see Design a tool-call prompt.
  4. Validate on the client. A small model will hallucinate argument names eventually. Treat arguments_json as untrusted input.
  5. Use low temperature. Tool calls are a classification / structure task, not a creative one. temperature=0 is often the right answer.

docs.title: Edges and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Arguments arrive as the model wrote them. arguments_json is the model's argument object as JSON text. A number or boolean stays whatever JSON the model emitted — which may be 3, "3", or something else entirely. Parse it, check the types, and coerce in your client.
  • The model can invent tools. A ToolCall node will happily parse {"tool": "nuke_from_orbit"} if the model emits it. The client must check the tool name against the allow-list before acting.
  • Multiple calls per turn need parallel_tool_calls = true. Most templates cap generation at one call per turn unless this flag is set; with it on (and where the model's format supports it — verified on Qwen and Granite) a single turn like "open all the doors" can produce one call per door instead of a single vague one. The node records one entry per parsed call on the turn and fires one ToolCallNotification per call either way.
  • No streaming. Tool-call generation is non-streaming by design — the parser needs the full output. Do not expect AnswerText frames from a ToolCall node unless mode = call_or_answer and no tool was called.

docs.title: Tryll in Ten Minutes
docs.text: This page is the whole idea of Tryll in one sitting: what it is, why it runs where it runs, and the handful of building blocks everything else is made of. Read it before anything else in these docs — every tutorial, how-to guide, and concept page assumes the picture drawn here. Each section ends with a link to the page that goes deeper.

docs.title: What Tryll is
docs.text:
Tryll runs small language models — together with speech recognition, speech synthesis, and vector search — on the player's own PC, inside your Unity or Unreal game. It ships inside the Unity package and the Unreal plugin and starts itself; there is no service to host and nothing to call over the internet.

Running a model is the easy part. The hard part is getting a small model to behave like your character, in your world, following your rules. So Tryll is mostly a harness around the model: the scaffolding that decides what the model sees, what it is allowed to say, and what happens with its output. If you know how a coding agent wraps a large model in tools and loops, or what a LangGraph-style workflow is, this is the same idea — built for small local models inside a game.

docs.title: Why on the player's machine
docs.text:
It is a trade-off, and it is worth being clear about both sides.

What you gain:

  • No bill that grows with your success. A cloud model charges per token, so every extra player and every extra hour of play costs you money. On-device, the player's hardware does the work.
  • No credits to abuse. When a player talks your NPC into writing them a Java program, that is their GPU's time, not your invoice.
  • Privacy and reliability. Nothing the player says leaves the machine. It works offline, with no network round-trip and no outage that is not on the player's desk.

What it costs you:

  • You share the machine with your game. The model needs GPU memory and RAM that your renderer would also like to have.
  • Small models need structure. A 3–4 billion parameter model will not hold a huge lore dump in its head or improvise reliably from a vague prompt. It does well when each step it takes is small and well defined — which is exactly what the rest of this page is about.

→ What your machine needs · Estimate memory footprint

docs.title: The model is the small part: agents are workflows
docs.text:
An agent is one character, or one conversation. Its behaviour is not a prompt; it is a workflow graph of small steps called nodes, which the agent walks once every time the player says something. Some nodes call a model. Most do not.

Here is the simplest useful agent, the Safe Receptionist from the demo project. It has two jobs: answer the player, and refuse what it should not answer.

flowchart LR
    P([Player line]) --> G{guard<br>Regex Guardrail}
    G -- triggered --> D[deflect<br>Canned Response]
    G -- not triggered --> A[answer<br>Generate]
    D --> E([Reply])
    A --> E

The guard checks the line against a list of patterns. If one matches, a scripted reply goes back and no model runs at all. Only a clean line reaches answer, the one node that calls the language model. Real agents add more steps — retrieve some lore, classify the request, call a game function — but they are all built the same way.

This is the key design choice: the rules and the decisions stay in your game. The model supplies words and choices, inside boundaries you set. Whether the door opens, how much the sword costs, and when the killer's name may be revealed are for your game code to decide.

→ Workflows, graphs, and nodes · All node types

docs.title: The building blocks
docs.text:
Every Tryll feature is one of the following, placed as a node in the graph or as data the graph reads.

The character and the conversation. The system prompt defines the character: who they are, what world they live in, how they talk, plus a few example lines. It is always kept. As a conversation grows, the oldest turns are trimmed so the prompt stays within budget — the character never forgets who it is, but it does eventually forget what you said an hour ago. → Design an NPC prompt · Projection and token budgets

Knowledge. Do not paste all your lore into the prompt. Keep it as a knowledge base of short facts, and let a Retrieve node pick the few that are relevant to each line of dialogue (this is retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG). It can search by meaning, by exact keywords — useful for the made-up words in your setting — or both. Facts can carry metadata, so you can gate them: the detective only learns what the player has already uncovered. → Retrieval-augmented generation · Create a simple RAG assistant

Game state in. Agent variables let your game push live values — the player's level, the NPC's mood, the current quest stage — straight into prompts and knowledge filters, so the character reacts to what is actually happening. → Agent variables · Drive prompts and retrieval from game state

Decisions. A classifier node works out what the player means — a threat, a bribe, a question about the quest — and the graph branches on the answer. The same technique can sort a line by tone, which is how you move an NPC's attitude towards the player. → Build an intent-driven NPC · Classify intent without a knowledge base · Branch on a slot

Actions out. With a tool call, the model picks an action and its arguments — open the gate, follow the player, sell item 12. Your code runs it and hands back the result, and the model answers from what really happened. Tryll never runs game code itself. When you need output in an exact shape, a grammar makes anything else impossible to generate; when numbers matter, your code owns the number and the model only owns the wording. → Tool calling · Define and handle tool calls · Keep merchant prices deterministic

Staying in character. Pattern and intent guards, paired with scripted replies, catch jailbreaks and out-of-world questions ("what model are you?") before a model ever sees them — and can keep them out of the conversation history, so they never become context. → Use canned responses and guardrails · Build an immersion guard

Voice. The player can speak, push-to-talk or hands-free. The character can answer out loud: speech is synthesized sentence by sentence while the reply is still being written, so it starts talking almost at once. Voices can be cloned from a short sample or described in words, and lip sync drives your character's face from the same audio. → Voice output · Voice input · Add lip sync to a character

More than one agent. Agents are cheap next to models, so do not force one agent to do everything. Next to the character you can run a narrator, a note-taker that summarises what happened, or a judge that scores the player's argument. An agent can also be stateless — no memory between calls — which suits classification and other utility jobs. → Agents and sessions · Run many agents on a small GPU

docs.title: Models and memory
docs.text:
Models are files. You pick them from Tryll's catalog — or bring your own GGUF file — and download them in the editor's Model Manager. The models you register for production are packaged with your build, so a shipped game never downloads anything behind the player's back.

A model is loaded once and shared by every agent that uses it, so ten NPCs on the same model cost one model, plus a small working cache for each node that generates. A few numbers to calibrate against:

  • 8 GB of VRAM is the comfortable target for a game with a language model in it; 6 GB works if you stay around 3B models.
  • A 3–4B model takes roughly 2–3 GB. The tutorials use Gemma 3 4B, with Llama 3.2 3B as the smaller, quicker choice.
  • Speech recognition and the lighter voices run on the CPU and cost no VRAM. The most expressive voices are themselves 3B models and are budgeted like one.

Each model can be placed in VRAM or in system RAM, so you can keep the GPU for rendering when the game needs it.

→ Models and inference engines · Manage models in the editor · Choose where models run

docs.title: How you work with it
docs.text:
On a team, the work splits naturally. Programmers wire agents into the game: which tools exist, which variables the game pushes, what happens when the model asks to act. Designers shape the character: the prompt, the lore, the graph — and they can do most of that without a programmer, because Tryll lives inside the editor:

  • a graph editor to build workflows visually,
  • a Chat window to talk to an agent without entering Play mode,
  • the Dialog Lab to run the same dialog across many prompt, model, and parameter variants and compare the spread — so you test changes, or a model swap, on hundreds of runs instead of a few typed lines,
  • the Agent Log to see what each agent received and produced, and the Memory window to see what it all costs.

AI coding agents can help too: both plugins ship an AGENTS.md that briefs them on Tryll, and on Unreal they can author workflows directly through the editor's MCP server.

→ Test an agent in the editor · Compare dialog variants · Agentic coding with Tryll

docs.title: What Tryll is not
docs.text:
• Not a cloud API. Everything runs locally; there is no hosted fallback.
  • Not a model. Tryll runs open models you choose; it does not train or fine-tune them.
  • Not an image, 3D, or animation generator. Tryll covers text, speech, and retrieval — the workloads that run well on today's player hardware.
  • Not a code runner. The model can ask for an action; only your code performs it.
  • Windows only, for now. Tryll ships as Windows 10/11 x64 binaries.

docs.title: TTS and Voice Output
docs.text:
Tryll supports server-side text-to-speech synthesis. Sherpa-ONNX hosts Supertonic 3 and Pocket TTS. llama.cpp runs Orpheus and Maya1, whose audio codes a shared SNAC 24 kHz ONNX decoder turns into sound on the CPU. See TTS Models for which catalog names are public and which controls each family accepts. Two graph nodes produce speech:

  • GenerateAndSpeak fuses LLM inference with TTS synthesis, streaming PCM audio frames alongside the text reply — lowest latency for a generated spoken answer.
  • Speak is TTS-only: it voices the slot named by its input param with no LLM pass. The default is user_message, the player's own words, so set input to an upstream node's output (e.g. a CannedResponse).

Both stream the same PCM audio frames to the client and use the same playback components. Neither node holds a voice: both speak with the agent's one voice profile. They differ only in whether generation is involved.

docs.title: The streaming pipeline
docs.text:
When a GenerateAndSpeak node runs:

  1. Format announcement — the first speaking node of the turn sends one TtsAudioFormatFrame: sample rate, channels (1) and bits per sample (16). It is sent once per turn: a later speaking node in the same turn reuses it, because the agent has one voice.
  2. Token generation — the language model produces tokens, forwarded to the client as AnswerText deltas (identical to Generate).
  3. Sentence segmentation — tokens accumulate until a sentence ends and the text since the last cut is at least min_sentence_chars wide (a CJK or other 3–4-byte character counts as 2):
    • . ! ? or … followed by a space or by the end of the text so far. A . right after a digit waits for the next character, so "3.14" stays whole.
    • At once: CJK 。！？｡, Devanagari । ॥, Arabic ؟, Urdu ۔, Ethiopic ። and ‼. Closing quotes and brackets right after them (」』）”…) stay with the sentence.
    • With first_chunk_max_chars set, the first chunk may also end at , ; : followed by a space or at an em dash, or at the next space once it is that wide — never before 5 words or min_sentence_chars. This has no effect on text without spaces, such as CJK.
    • Text that runs 16 KiB with no sentence end is cut at the last space, so the buffer stays bounded; the server logs a warning.
  4. TTS synthesis — each chunk is synthesized to mono int16 PCM at the model's native sample rate and streamed as TtsAudioFrame messages. At most one chunk is synthesizing at a time: the next finished chunk waits for it, and the text stream pauses briefly while it waits.

This keeps time-to-first-audio low: the NPC starts speaking as soon as the first chunk is ready, while the language model is still generating the rest of the answer.

Client                          Server
  │                                │
  ├─ SendMessageRequest ──────────►│
  │◄── TtsAudioFormatFrame ────────┤  (node starts)
  │◄── AnswerText … ───────────────┤  (LLM tokens)
  │◄── TtsAudioFrame … ────────────┤  (first sentence)
  │◄── AnswerText … ───────────────┤  (LLM still running)
  │◄── TtsAudioFrame … ────────────┤  (next sentences)
  │◄── TurnComplete ───────────────┤  (after the last audio)

docs.title: Audio format
docs.text: All TTS audio is mono signed-16-bit PCM at the sample rate reported in the TtsAudioFormatFrame frame. The sample rate is model-specific: for example 44 100 Hz for Supertonic 3 and 24 000 Hz for Orpheus and Maya1. Always read it from the format frame. The Unity speaker converts the int16 samples to float32; the Unreal speaker queues the int16 PCM directly.

docs.title: End of stream
docs.text: TtsAudioFrame carries no is_final flag. The last frame arrives before TurnComplete. The audio queue on the client drains naturally — the playback component fills the audio buffer with silence on underrun until the queue is empty.

docs.title: Session configuration
docs.text: There is no TTS engine to declare. Download a voice (a TTS model) in the Model Manager and name it in the agent's voice profile (tts_model_name). The catalog chooses the engine for each voice — Sherpa-ONNX for Supertonic / Pocket, llama.cpp for Orpheus / Maya1. A session warm-up hint is optional; see Choose where models run.

docs.title: Voice configuration
docs.text:
An agent has one voice, a voice profile, passed when the agent is created. Every speaking node of the agent uses it, so one workflow can serve many characters with different voices. A graph that speaks must be given a voice: without one, agent creation fails with 3025 AgentVoiceRequired. An agent whose graph never speaks loads no TTS model, even if it has a voice.

The profile holds:

Field Description tts_model_name Catalog voice name. Required; there is no default model. speaker_id Built-in voice index, 0 to the model's speaker count − 1. Supertonic 3: 0–9. Orpheus: 0–7 (Tara … Zoe). Maya1: 0–1 (or override with voice_description). Single-speaker models (Pocket TTS) must stay 0. reference_voice Reference clip (storage-root-relative) for voice-cloning models (Pocket TTS, Qwen3-TTS Base). Empty = model default voice (Qwen3-TTS Base has none). See Clone a Voice. voice_description Maya1 only: natural-language identity (age, accent, pitch, timbre). speed Speech-rate multiplier, 0.1–3.0. Orpheus, Maya1 and Qwen3-TTS: only 1.0. lang Synthesis language on models that choose it per call (Supertonic 3: 31 languages). Empty = the session locale, then the catalog default. Rejected on fixed-language models. emit_visemes Send a lip-sync viseme track for every sentence the agent speaks. delivery_modes Named deliveries (angry, calm, …). See below.

The profile is validated once, when it is set. A field the loaded model cannot use fails with 3023 InvalidVoiceProfile rather than being ignored.

The nodes keep only their chunking settings, because chunking acts differently on streamed LLM text than on ready text:

Node parameter Description min_sentence_chars Minimum width of a chunk before a sentence end closes it (a CJK or other 3–4-byte character counts as 2). Default 12, two or three English words. Lower = shorter first-audio latency. first_chunk_max_chars First chunk only: also end it at a clause mark, and at the next space once it is this wide (never under 5 words or min_sentence_chars). 0 = off. 48 cut the model-side wait before the first audio by about 40% in our measurements. Listen to it with your voice first: a clause can end on a falling tone.

Both are mutable with ChangeAgentParam (see Change Agent Parameters at Runtime). The voice itself is not: replace it with SetAgentVoice, which is accepted only while the agent is idle.

docs.title: Delivery modes
docs.text:
A delivery mode is a named way of speaking that a voice defines, such as angry or whisper. Game code switches it with SetAgentDeliveryMode(mode, intensity) at any time, even mid-turn; the change applies from the next sentence. The built-in mode neutral is the plain voice.

What a mode can change depends on the model. Clone models switch to a different recording of the same character. Maya1 adds a delivery clause such as "angry tone at high intensity". Supertonic 3 and Orpheus have no emotion control, so a mode can only change speed (Supertonic) or must be empty. A profile can still define the same mode names on every voice, so game code that says angry works for every character. See Voice Profile for the per-model table and what intensity does.

Do not encode identity or delivery as a spoken [emotion] prefix — that syntax is not supported. Model-native <tag> tokens (for example Maya <laugh>) may appear in the text the synthesizer hears; unknown tags are stripped from the audio copy only and do not rewrite history.

If synthesis fails during a turn, the client gets an ErrorResponse with 4001 ("TTS synthesis failed") and the turn still completes; the text reply is not affected.

docs.title: Lip sync (visemes)
docs.text:
An agent whose voice has emit_visemes on also sends a viseme track from every speaking node, Speak and GenerateAndSpeak alike: the mouth shapes that go with the speech, and when each one starts. It uses the 15 standard Oculus visemes (sil for rest, PP for p/b/m, aa for an open vowel, …), which map onto a face rig's blendshapes.

The server builds the track for each sentence as soon as that sentence is synthesized, from two inputs:

  • the text — the words are turned into speech sounds with an English pronunciation dictionary, and each sound into a mouth shape;
  • the synthesized audio — silences become rests (anchored to the sentence's punctuation where possible), the shapes are spread over the spoken stretches in proportion to typical sound lengths, and louder speech opens the mouth further.

The track also keeps lip closures on screen long enough to read, merges shapes too short to see, and starts each shape slightly before its sound, as real lips do. It arrives as one TtsVisemeFrame per sentence, after that sentence's audio once its synthesis is done, so under normal buffering it reaches the client before that audio plays. A sentence that produced no audio sends no frame. Offsets are in samples from the start of the turn's audio (its one format announcement), and keep counting across every speaking node of the turn.

No extra model runs. What to expect:

  • Timing is estimated, not measured per sound. Pauses, starts and ends follow the real audio closely; the shapes inside a stretch of speech are placed by proportion.
  • English pronunciation. Text in other Latin-script languages gets approximate shapes from English spelling rules. Text in other scripts (Cyrillic, CJK, …) gets no shapes: the mouth stays at rest.
  • Voice-agnostic. The track works with every TTS voice, since it only needs the text and the audio.

See Add Lip Sync to a Character for setup.

docs.title: Client-side playback components
docs.text:
The Tryll Unity and Unreal packages ship a ready-made playback component that wires the TTS audio stream to the platform audio engine:

Platform Component Audio backend Unity TryllSpeaker (MonoBehaviour) Streaming AudioClip with pcmReaderCallback Unreal UTryllSpeakerComponent (UActorComponent) USoundWaveProcedural + hidden UAudioComponent

The Unreal speaker is always non-spatialized (2D). The Unity speaker plays through its AudioSource and leaves that source's spatial settings alone. For custom audio, such as your own spatializer, subscribe to the raw PCM: TryllSpeaker.OnTtsPcm (Unity) or UTryllSpeakerComponent::OnTtsPcm (Unreal). You can also replace the speaker entirely with TryllAgent.SetOnTtsAudioFormat / SetOnTtsAudio; each holds one callback, so setting it replaces the speaker's.

docs.title: Workflows, Graphs, and Nodes
docs.text: A Tryll agent is not a prompt. It is a graph of small, single-purpose steps that you wire together. Each user turn re-walks the graph; each step decides where to go next. This page explains why Tryll is built this way and how the pieces fit.

docs.title: The building blocks
docs.text:
A graph has two things:

  • A set of nodes, each with a name, a node type, and a set of typed params that include the node's configuration and its exit wiring. Each exit is a string field on the params object (e.g. default_exit, triggered_exit); an empty value means route to END. The full set of sixteen node types is: Generate, GenerateAndSpeak, Speak, Retrieve, ToolCall, CannedResponse, RegexGuardrail, Instruction, IntentToInstruction, ClassifyIntent, ClassifyIntentLLM, Transform, Pause, Branch, WriteToMemory, and Summarize. See Workflow Nodes for the full catalog.
  • A start node — the first node to run on every user turn.

Graphs are authored once, sent to the server with CreateAgentRequest, frozen at agent creation, and then re-walked for every turn the agent lives.

Here is the simplest useful graph — a guardrail in front of a generator, with a scripted refusal on the rejected path:

flowchart LR
    guard["RegexGuardrail<br>guard"]
    refuse["CannedResponse<br>refuse"]
    gen["Generate<br>answer"]
    guard -- "triggered" --> refuse
    guard -- "not_triggered" --> gen
    refuse -- "default" --> END
    gen -- "default" --> END

The same graph, in each client:

UnityUnrealC++Python 
var graph = new TryllGraphBuilder()
    .AddRegexGuardrail("guard", new TryllRegexGuardrailParams
    {
        StringStorage    = "jailbreak_patterns",
        TriggeredExit    = "refuse",  // → refuse node
        NotTriggeredExit = "answer",  // → answer node
    })
    .AddCannedResponse("refuse", new TryllCannedResponseParams
    {
        StringStorage = "refusal_lines",
        // DefaultExit is "" (END) by default
    })
    .AddGenerate("answer", new TryllGenerateParams())
    .SetStartNode("guard")
    .SetDefaultModelName("My Local Model")
    .Build();

auto* GuardParams  = NewObject<UTryllRegexGuardrailParams>();
GuardParams->StringStorage    = TEXT("jailbreak_patterns");
GuardParams->TriggeredExit    = TEXT("refuse");
GuardParams->NotTriggeredExit = TEXT("answer");

auto* RefuseParams = NewObject<UTryllCannedResponseParams>();
RefuseParams->StringStorage = TEXT("refusal_lines");
// RefuseParams->DefaultExit defaults to "" (END)

FTryllGraphDescription Graph = FTryllGraphBuilder()
    .AddNode(TEXT("guard"),  GuardParams)
    .AddNode(TEXT("refuse"), RefuseParams)
    .AddNode(TEXT("answer"), NewObject<UTryllGenerateParams>())
    .SetStartNode(TEXT("guard"))
    .SetDefaultModelName(TEXT("My Local Model"))
    .Build();

namespace TC = Tryll::Client;

namespace NP = ::Tryll::NodeParams;

NP::RegexGuardrailParamsT guardParams;
guardParams.string_storage     = "jailbreak_patterns";
guardParams.triggered_exit     = "refuse";
guardParams.not_triggered_exit = "answer";

NP::CannedResponseParamsT refuseParams;
refuseParams.string_storage = "refusal_lines";
// refuseParams.default_exit defaults to "" (END)

TC::GraphDescription graph;
graph.AddRegexGuardrail("guard",  std::move(guardParams))
     .AddCannedResponse("refuse", std::move(refuseParams))
     .AddGenerate("answer", NP::GenerateParamsT{})
     .SetStartNode("guard")
     .SetDefaultModelName("My Local Model");

from tryll_client import GraphDescription
from tryll_client.graph import (
    RegexGuardrailParams, CannedResponseParams, GenerateParams,
)

guard_params = RegexGuardrailParams(
    string_storage     = "jailbreak_patterns",
    triggered_exit     = "refuse",
    not_triggered_exit = "answer",
)
refuse_params = CannedResponseParams(
    string_storage = "refusal_lines",
    # default_exit defaults to "" (END)
)

graph = (
    GraphDescription()
    .add_node("guard",  guard_params)
    .add_node("refuse", refuse_params)
    .add_node("answer", GenerateParams())
    .set_start_node("guard")
    .set_default_model_name("My Local Model")
)

docs.title: Exit fields: how nodes "talk" to each other
docs.text:
Nodes do not call each other. They return a named exit, and the agent follows the matching edge. Every node type declares its possible exits as typed string fields on its params object — see the table in Workflow Nodes.

For example:

Node type Exit fields on params Generate default_exit Retrieve found_exit, not_found_exit ToolCall tool_called_exit, no_tool_called_exit CannedResponse default_exit RegexGuardrail triggered_exit, not_triggered_exit

An empty string means route to END; this is the field's default value. A non-empty string must name another node in the same graph — the server rejects graphs where an exit field names a node that doesn't exist (3003 GraphCompilationFailed).

Because exits are fields on the params object, exits that terminate the turn (route to END) can simply be left at their default — you only need to set the fields that route somewhere other than END.

docs.title: The per-turn loop
docs.text:
When a SendMessage arrives, the agent:

  1. Appends a new interaction to its dialog, starting with the user's message.
  2. Walks the graph from start_node, one node at a time. Each node:
  3. reads from the current interaction (and anything earlier nodes attached to it),
  4. does its work (retrieve from an index, run the model, match a pattern, pick a canned line, …),
  5. optionally attaches new components to the interaction, and
  6. returns its chosen exit.
  7. Follows the route for that exit to the next node.
  8. Stops when the route target is "END", when the step budget is exceeded, or when the turn is cancelled.

What each node attaches along the way is what makes the dialog itself useful state. A Retrieve node attaches retrieved knowledge to the current turn, and a downstream Generate node's projection picks that knowledge up and folds it into the prompt.

docs.title: Passing values between nodes: slots
docs.text: Producing nodes (Generate, GenerateAndSpeak, CannedResponse, Transform, Instruction/IntentToInstruction) don't just route — they each write their text into a named slot on the turn's shared blackboard (the slot name is the node's output_name, or its own name if unset). Downstream nodes select which slot they consume with an input param (empty = the reserved user_message slot), and Mustache templates reference slots as {{slot.<name>}}. Two more per-node knobs control delivery: send (a SendAnswer of None / Whole / Streamed) decides whether/how the slot is emitted to the client this turn, and history_role decides whether it replays as history on later turns. This is how you build things like a hidden query-rewrite step (send=None) or a multi-sender turn. See Slots and inter-node value passing.

docs.title: Why a graph instead of a prompt template
docs.text:
Three reasons:

1. Composition. "Retrieve, then generate" is different from "check for jailbreak first, then retrieve, then generate". Prompt templates push this branching into strings; a graph makes it executable and inspectable. Every node is typed and diagnostics-friendly.

2. Cost control. The graph lets you short-circuit expensive work. A guardrail that routes to a canned response never touches the model. A tool-call node with mode=DetectOnly does zero extra generation on a miss (the default, CallOrAnswer, instead emits the model's plain-text reply).

3. Reuse. Graphs are data. You can build them at runtime from C++, Python, or Unreal, ship them in a UTryllWorkflowAsset, or construct them dynamically from user configuration. The server does not know or care where the graph came from.

docs.title: Turns are serial; graphs are stateless between turns
docs.text:
An agent runs one turn at a time. If a second SendMessage arrives while the previous turn is still running, it is rejected with 3004 AgentBusy; the in-flight turn keeps running. Cancellation is explicit (CancelRequest, DestroyAgent, socket close), not pre-emption.

The graph itself carries no per-turn state. All state lives on the agent's dialog (the accumulated interactions) and in the per-node KV caches. This is why the same graph description can be replayed cleanly every turn — the work of "what has been said" is separate from the work of "what to do next".

docs.title: Edges and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Routing loops. Nothing stops you from routing node A → node A; every agent stops after 64 node steps in one turn, which breaks infinite loops by aborting the turn with an error. The budget is fixed; it is not a CreateAgent setting.
  • Exits you "know" will never fire still need a value. Leave them at the default empty string (routes to END). The server validates that no exit field names a missing node, but it does not enforce that every exit field is reachable.
  • Model sharing is cross-graph, not cross-node. Two Generate nodes in one graph that use the same model share the underlying weights (good) but have independent KV caches (necessary — they see different prompts). Budget token-count accordingly; see Projection and Token Budgets.
  • The start node runs every turn. If your start node is Generate, it will generate every turn, even if a later node would have short-circuited. Put guardrails and retrieval before the model, not after, if you want them to actually gate work.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
In about fifteen minutes you will install Tryll, download a model, and stream a reply from a language model running on your own machine. Pick the client that matches your project:

  • First inference in Unity Install the UPM package, add TryllAgentComponent to a GameObject, see streaming text in the Console. The server is bundled and launches itself.

  • First inference in Unreal ★ Hero tutorial. Install the plugin, add UTryllAgentComponent to a sample actor, see streaming text in the Output Log. The server is bundled and launches itself.

  • First inference in Python pip install tryll-client, a 20-line script, streamed tokens on stdout. You point it at a server yourself — see Run the Tryll Server.

  • First inference in C++ Build the client library with CMake and run the test-chat console demo.

Each tutorial starts by downloading the distribution and ends with a working agent — including acquiring the model, which Tryll never does behind your back.

docs.title: What your machine needs
docs.text:
Tryll runs the model on the player's hardware, so the hardware is part of the design. Check this before you start.

Operating system

  • Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit. Tryll ships as Windows x64 binaries — the server, the Unity package, the Unreal plugin, and the C++ client library. There is no Linux or macOS distribution.

GPU

  • 8 GB of VRAM or more is the comfortable target. That fits a quantised 7–8B model with a useful context window, and leaves room for speech synthesis and recognition running alongside it.
  • 6 GB works if you stay around 3B models — a good fit for focused NPC dialogue, intent classification, and routing.
  • More VRAM is mostly about freedom to experiment: larger models, longer contexts, and several agents resident at once. It is not required to ship something good.
  • Speech recognition and the lighter Sherpa-ONNX voices (Supertonic, Pocket TTS) run on the CPU and cost no VRAM. The 3B voices, Orpheus and Maya1, are llama.cpp models: they follow the same GPU placement as a language model, and only their SNAC audio decoder stays on the CPU.

Disk and RAM

  • 1.5–5 GB per language model, plus a working internet connection the first time you download one.
  • Budget roughly the same again in system RAM: a model file is memory-mapped and offloaded to the GPU, so it counts in both columns.

Work out the real numbers for a specific line-up with Estimate the RAM and VRAM your setup needs.

Engine and language versions

Path Needs Unity Unity 6 (6000.x) or later Unreal Unreal Engine 5.7, a C++ project (Blueprint-only projects cannot compile the plugin) Python Python 3.11 or newer C++ Visual Studio 2022, CMake

docs.title: What you will build
docs.text: Each tutorial ends at the same milestone: the user sends one message, the server runs it through a minimal graph (just a Generate node), and the client prints the streamed reply. Everything else — retrieval, tool calls, voice, guardrails — builds on top of this pattern.

docs.title: After the tutorial
docs.text:
You have a one-node graph. These are the shortest paths to something that feels like a game feature:

  • Author the graph visually instead of in code. Edit workflows in the Unity graph editor or in the Unreal graph editor
  • Iterate without entering Play mode. Test an agent in the editor
  • Write a character worth talking to. Design an NPC prompt
  • Ground answers in your own lore. Create a simple RAG assistant
  • Give the character a voice. Add voice output to an agent
  • Feed it live game state. Drive prompts and retrieval from game state

If you want the why before the how, start with Tryll in Ten Minutes.

docs.title: First Inference in C++
docs.text: Build the C++ client library from source, run the bundled test-chat demo, and see streamed tokens on stdout.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Visual Studio 2022 with the C++ workload, CMake 3.24+, and Git.
  • An internet connection the first time you run the demo. It downloads Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (Q4_K_M) from the server's models.json catalog if that model is not on disk yet.

No need to start the server manually

tryll_test_chat finds tryll_server.exe in the tryll\build tree and starts it automatically. If you prefer to manage the server yourself, launch the demo with --profile external-text.

docs.title: Step 1 — build the two projects
docs.text:
The server and the console demo are two separate CMake projects. Build the server first (its tree also produces the tryll_client static library), then build test-chat:

git clone <tryll-repo-url>

:: 1. Server + C++ client library — built from the tryll/ tree.
cd tryll
cmake --preset default
cmake --build --preset debug

:: 2. test-chat console demo — its own CMake project that links tryll/
::    with the server disabled.
cd ..\test-chat
cmake --preset default
cmake --build --preset debug

The default preset uses the Visual Studio 17 2022 generator with CUDA and Vulkan PREBUILT — no GPU SDK required. For a CPU-only build add -DTRYLL_VULKAN=OFF -DTRYLL_CUDA=OFF. The first build produces tryll_server.exe under tryll\build\server\Debug\; the second produces tryll_test_chat.exe under test-chat\build\Debug\.

One-shot build-and-run

test-chat\build_and_run_dbg.bat runs both builds in order and then launches the demo — handy while iterating.

docs.title: Step 2 — run the demo
docs.text:
test-chat\build\Debug\tryll_test_chat.exe --profile managed-text

Profiles live in test-chat\data\test-chat-config.json. The default profile, managed-voice, turns on speech output and push-to-talk voice input, so this tutorial picks managed-text: a typed chat on the demo workflow. Add --workflow rag or --workflow tools to start on a different workflow.

The demo looks for tryll_server.exe under tryll\build\server\ (the Debug, Release, then Production folder), starts it, waits for it to be ready, and then connects. Set TRYLL_SERVER_EXE or pass --server-exe <path> to use a different binary.

If you want to connect to a server you started yourself on 127.0.0.1:9100, use the external-text profile instead. Add --server-host and --server-port for another address:

test-chat\build\Debug\tryll_test_chat.exe --profile external-text

After the launch lines, the demo prints the session id and a table of the models the server lists, then the prompt:

[test-chat] Session <id> ready
[test-chat] Models returned by the server for this session's engine (…)
[test-chat] ListModels count: …
…
[test-chat] Workflow: demo. Type a message or /help. Press Ctrl+C or Ctrl+Z then Enter to quit.

You: hello
AI (generate): Hi! How can I help you today?
You:

Each token of the reply appears on stdout as it is produced, which is exactly what your own application will see through the SetOnAnswerText callback. The name in brackets is the node that produced the text. Type /help to list the demo's commands.

docs.title: Step 3 — write your own minimal client
docs.text:
For a smaller starting point than test-chat, use RunAndConnect to spawn the server and connect in a single call. The returned ConnectedSession owns both the child process and the TCP session; its destructor shuts them down in the correct order:

#include <filesystem>
#include <future>
#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>

#include <tryll/TryllClient.h>

int main()
{
    namespace TC = Tryll::Client;

    // Spawn the server and connect. Throws Tryll::Client::TryllError on failure.
    // Leaving opts.port at its default (9100) picks a free port.
    TC::ManagedServerOptions opts;
    opts.exe = std::filesystem::path{"tryll/build/server/Debug/tryll_server.exe"};

    auto session = Tryll::Client::TryllClient::RunAndConnect(opts);
    session.GetClient().CreateSession({});

    // Build the simplest possible graph: one Generate node.
    // default_exit defaults to "" = END, so no wiring needed.
    TC::GraphDescription graph;
    graph.AddGenerate("answer", ::Tryll::NodeParams::GenerateParamsT{})
         .SetStartNode("answer")
         .SetDefaultModelName("Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (Q4_K_M)");   // downloaded by test-chat

    auto agent = session.GetClient().CreateAgent(graph);

    // SendText is fire-and-forget, so we must block until the turn finishes;
    // otherwise the session (and the process) would tear down before the
    // streamed tokens arrive. Signal completion from OnTurnComplete.
    std::promise<void> turnDone;
    agent.SetOnAnswerText([](std::string_view /*nodeName*/, std::string_view text,
                             bool /*isDelta*/, bool /*isFinal*/)
    {
        std::cout << text << std::flush;   // streams by default (SendAnswer::Streamed)
    });
    agent.SetOnTurnComplete([&turnDone](::Tryll::TurnStatus, std::string_view, std::int32_t)
    {
        std::cout << "\n";
        turnDone.set_value();
    });

    agent.SendText("In one sentence: what is Tryll?");
    turnDone.get_future().wait();   // block until OnTurnComplete fires

    agent.Destroy();
    // session destructor: shuts down the client, then stops the server
}

ManagedServerOptions::port defaults to 9100, and that default means "pick a free port": the launcher allocates an unused port and starts the server on it. Only a different value is bound exactly as given. To connect a second client to the same server, use the port it really bound, session.GetServer().Port().

Already running a server?

If your server is managed separately (remote host, Docker, etc.) use Connect directly — no ManagedServerOptions needed. A server you start yourself listens on the port in its server-config.json (9100 in the shipped file):

auto client = Tryll::Client::TryllClient::Connect("127.0.0.1", 9100);
client.CreateSession({});
// …
client.Shutdown();

Link it against tryll_client and tryll_common (both already built by the preset):

target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE tryll_client tryll_common)

docs.title: What you built
docs.text:
• A C++ client that connects, creates the session, creates a one-node agent, and streams a reply to stdout.
  • The same surface as the bundled test-chat demo, which is a good reference when you are ready to add RAG, tool calls, or guardrails.

docs.text:

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• FindServerExe: could not locate tryll_server — the server exe was not found under tryll\build\server\Debug, Release, or Production in the repository the demo was built from. Build the server with cmake --build --preset debug in tryll\, set TRYLL_SERVER_EXE, or pass --server-exe <path> to point directly at the server binary. Use --profile external-text to skip auto-launch entirely and start the server yourself: see Run the Tryll Server.
  • connection refused with --profile external-text — the server is not running or is on a different port. Check the server log, and pass --server-port if it does not listen on 9100.
  • Linker errors about FlatBuffers — make sure you are linking the generated target that was built alongside tryll_client; the CMake preset handles this automatically.
  • Build picks Ninja accidentally — pass --preset default explicitly or add -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -A x64 to the configure command.

docs.title: First Inference in Python
docs.text: Install the Python client, connect to a running Tryll server, and stream a reply from a local language model — all in about twenty lines of code.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• The Tryll server is running on 127.0.0.1:9100. If not, see Run the Tryll Server.
  • At least one language model from the server's data/models.json is on disk, with status Downloaded, Local, or Loaded. You can check with any client, or bring your own — see Use Your Own Local Model.
  • Python 3.11 or newer.

docs.title: Step 1 — install the client
docs.text:
pip install tryll-client

That installs the tryll_client package and its one dependency, the flatbuffers runtime.

docs.title: Step 2 — write the script
docs.text:
Save this as first-inference.py:

from tryll_client import TryllClient
from tryll_client.graph import GraphDescription, GenerateParams

# Connect and create the session.
client = TryllClient.connect("127.0.0.1", 9100)
client.create_session()

# Pick a model — use the actual name from your server's models.json.
MODEL = "My Local Model"

# Build the simplest possible graph: one Generate node.
# default_exit defaults to "" = END, so no wiring needed.
graph = (
    GraphDescription()
    .add_node("answer", GenerateParams())
    .set_start_node("answer")
    .set_default_model_name(MODEL)
)

agent = client.create_agent(graph)

# Ask a question and print the full reply.
reply = agent.send_message("In one sentence: what is Tryll?")
print(reply)

agent.destroy()
client.shutdown()

docs.title: Step 3 — run it
docs.text:
python first-inference.py

Want the client to start the server for you?

Use TryllClient.run_and_connect — it spawns the server, waits for it to be ready, and returns a ConnectedSession that shuts everything down automatically:

from pathlib import Path
from tryll_client import TryllClient
from tryll_client.graph import GraphDescription, GenerateParams

with TryllClient.run_and_connect(
    exe=Path("path/to/tryll_server.exe"),
) as session:
    session.client.create_session()

    graph = (
        GraphDescription()
        .add_node("answer", GenerateParams())
        .set_start_node("answer")
        .set_default_model_name("My Local Model")
    )
    agent = session.client.create_agent(graph)

    reply = agent.send_message("In one sentence: what is Tryll?")
    print(reply)
# server is stopped automatically when the `with` block exits

run_and_connect takes a port argument, and its default of 9100 means "pick a free port": the launcher allocates an unused port for the server. Only a different value is bound exactly as given. A second client must use the port the launcher really bound, session.server.port. The fixed 9100 in Step 2 is the port a server you start yourself takes from its server-config.json.

For lower-level control, or if you need to manage the server lifetime independently, see Auto-launch the Server.

Expected output (your model's wording will vary):

Tryll is a local small-language-model inference server with C++, Python, and Unreal clients for building on-device AI agents.

send_message blocks until the server's TurnComplete arrives and returns the full reply as a single string — the simplest thing for a script. The server streams tokens as they're generated, and Python receives them too: register agent.set_on_answer_text(cb) — callback (node_name, text, is_delta, is_final) — before sending, or use the non-blocking agent.send_message_async(...). Every client (Python, C++, Unity, Unreal) exposes the same per-token streaming callback; see Stream Answers to a UI.

docs.title: What you built
docs.text:
• A minimal session with one agent.
  • A one-node graph: Generate → END.
  • A blocking send_message call that returns the full reply.

The graph is deliberately minimal; everything else in Tryll (retrieval, tool calls, guardrails) plugs into exactly this shape by inserting extra nodes before Generate.
