• How-to Guides — ready-made recipes: RAG, tool calls, streaming to UI, guardrails.
  • Concepts — the mental model. Start with Tryll in Ten Minutes.
  • Python Client API — surface map of tryll_client.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• ConnectionRefusedError — the server is not running on the expected host/port, or a firewall blocked it. Re-check Run the Tryll Server.
  • TryllError [3003] from create_agent — the graph does not compile, most often because the model name in your script does not match any entry in models.json (GraphCompilationFailed). List models with client.list_models().
  • Script hangs after send_message — the model is loading for the first time. Watch the server log; the next turn will be fast.

docs.title: First Inference in Unity
docs.text:
Unpack a Tryll release, drop the package into your Unity project (the server is bundled inside it), configure one project setting, download a model through the Model Manager, and watch a single Generate node print its answer to the Console during Play Mode — no chat UI required.

Working with an AI coding agent?

The Unity package ships an AGENTS.md at its root. Attach it to your agent's context (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Codex, …) before asking it to write Tryll code — it carries the graph/slot mental model and the ways Tryll differs from a cloud LLM SDK. Agents that fetch docs themselves can start from llms.txt.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: A scene with a TryllAgentComponent on a GameObject that, on Start, connects to a locally-spawned Tryll server and creates a one-node agent. You trigger the first inference by right-clicking the component in the Inspector (Context Menu → Ask Tryll), and the answer streams into the Unity Console.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Unity 6 (6000.x) or later, with a blank 3D project.
  • ~5 GB free disk space for the downloaded model and a working internet connection on first run.
  • Familiarity with creating GameObjects, adding components, and writing a short C# MonoBehaviour.

You do not need to build anything from source — the distribution ships pre-generated FlatBuffers bindings.

docs.title: Step 1 — Get the distribution
docs.text:
1. Download tryll-unity-<version>.7z from the releases page and extract it somewhere temporary (e.g. C:\Downloads\tryll\).

  2. Inside is the Unity package — the server is bundled inside it, so there is nothing else to install:

    UnityPlugin/                       <-- the UPM package (everything you need)
├── package.json
├── Runtime/
├── Editor/
└── .Server/Default/               <-- bundled server (rides inside the package)
    ├── tryll_server.exe
    ├── llama.dll, ggml*.dll, ggml-vulkan.dll
    └── data/
        ├── server-config.json
        ├── models.json
        ├── default-canned-responses.txt
        └── default-guardrail-patterns.txt

The archive ships no model weights — you download the models your graph references up front through the Model Manager (Step 4). CreateAgent fails fast if a referenced model is not already on disk; the server does not download it for you at agent-creation time. In Client Dev, downloaded weights land under <Project>/TryllStorage/models/.

docs.title: Step 2 — Install the Unity package
docs.text:
Copy the UnityPlugin/ folder into your project's Packages/ directory and name it com.tryll.client. Unity auto-discovers embedded packages there, so there is no manifest.json edit to make:

<YourProject>/
├── Assets/
├── TryllStorage/                    <-- default storage root (outside Assets/)
├── Packages/
│   ├── manifest.json
│   └── com.tryll.client/        <-- copy UnityPlugin/* here
│       ├── package.json
│       ├── Runtime/
│       ├── Editor/
│       └── .Server/Default/     <-- server rides inside the package
└── <YourProject>.sln

Unity imports the package on focus; Window → Package Manager → In Project lists Tryll Client, and you should see no compile errors.

Keep the package embedded here (a writable folder) rather than in a read-only cache. Model downloads and authored storage files live under <Project>/TryllStorage/, not inside the package.

Add this to .gitignore if you do not want models in source control (committing them is optional):

/TryllStorage/models/

Nothing else to copy

The server binary and its data/ ride inside the package's .Server/Default/ folder, so installing the package installs the server too — one folder to drop in, one to update on a new release.

docs.title: Step 3 — Configure Tryll Client in Project Settings
docs.text:
Open Edit → Project Settings → Tryll Client and set:

Setting Value Why Auto Launch Server true (default) TryllClient spawns the bundled server automatically. Uncheck to run a server yourself. Llama.cpp backend Vulkan (default) Portable GPU API. Set Auto to prefer CUDA on NVIDIA (also ships CUDA DLLs in a player build). Game Name e.g. my-game Short slug for telemetry and the project-name fallback. Storage Data Folder TryllStorage (default) Project folder outside Assets/. The editor launches the server with --storage-root here.

There is no server-path setting — the location is resolved from the package automatically, identically in the Editor and in packaged builds. Client Dev usage telemetry is always on in the editor; set TRYLL_SERVER_MODE=tryll-dev only for Tryll’s own CI. Player builds that still launch Client Dev are unreleasable until a Client Prod binary ships.

Settings are saved to Assets/Resources/TryllRuntimeSettings.asset (created on first access).

Models must be registered before use

CreateAgent fails fast if a referenced model is not already on disk — the server does not download it for you. Continue to Step 4 to download and register a model via the editor Model Manager before running the graph below.

docs.title: Step 4 — Download and register a model
docs.text:
Model name fields in the Inspector are dropdown lists populated from the models you have registered in this project. On a fresh installation those dropdowns are empty — you must open the Model Manager, download a model, and register it before it appears.

  1. Open Window → Tryll → Model Manager. The window launches the bundled server, connects, and lists every model the server knows about. Wait for the status indicator in the toolbar to show ● Ready.

  2. In the model list, find a language model to start with. Recommended: Gemma 3 4B Instruct (Q4_K_M) (~3 GB download). Smaller / quicker: Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (Q4_K_M) (~2 GB download).

  3. Click the model row to select it. In the Model properties panel on the right:

    • Status shows Absent — the files are not on disk yet.
    • Click Download. A progress bar appears and the toolbar shows active download count.

  4. Once the status changes to Downloaded, set the Build registration to Experimental (usable in the editor, excluded from packaged builds) or Production (shipped in builds).

    • For this tutorial, Experimental is fine.

  5. Close the Model Manager.

The Model Manager writes a TryllModelManifest asset to Assets/Resources/TryllModelManifest.asset. Any Model Name dropdown in the Inspector now lists the models you registered here.

Registration controls build inclusion

Experimental models are available during development but stripped by the build post-processor when you build a player. Production models are staged into the Server/ folder next to the player executable. A model that is downloaded but unregistered (status None) is invisible to the build system.

docs.title: Step 5 — Create a workflow asset and set up the scene
docs.text:
1. In the Project window, right-click → Create → Tryll → Workflow Asset. Name it DemoWorkflow.

    The Create → Tryll submenu (the same menu as Assets → Create → Tryll). 2. Select DemoWorkflow. In the Inspector, expand Graph: - Under Nodes, click + to add one entry. - Set Name = answer. - Click the Params type picker (shows <null> by default) and select Generate from the dropdown. The node's parameter fields expand below it — leave them all at their defaults; the Default Exit field stays empty, which routes the turn to END. - Set Start Node = answer. - Set Default Model Name using the dropdown — it now lists the models you registered in the Model Manager. Pick the one you downloaded in Step 4. 3. Create a new empty GameObject — call it TryllDemo. 4. Add a Tryll Agent Component (Add Component → Tryll → Tryll Agent Component). 5. Assign DemoWorkflow to the component's Workflow Asset field. 6. Un-check Auto Create On Connect — this tutorial wires the lifecycle explicitly so you control exactly when the agent is created. 7. Create a C# script TryllDemo.cs and attach it to the same GameObject:

using UnityEngine;
using Tryll.Client;

public class TryllDemo : MonoBehaviour
{
    private TryllAgentComponent _agent;

    void Start()
    {
        _agent = GetComponent<TryllAgentComponent>();

        _agent.OnAnswerText.AddListener((nodeName, text, isDelta, isFinal) =>
        {
            // Send = Streamed: every chunk is a delta, and the last one is an
            // empty terminator with isFinal = true.
            // Send = Whole: one chunk with isDelta = false and the full text.
            if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(text))
                Debug.Log($"[Tryll] {(isDelta ? "delta" : "reply")} from {nodeName}: {text}");
            if (isFinal)
                Debug.Log($"[Tryll] {nodeName} finished its answer");
        });

        _agent.OnTurnComplete.AddListener((status, debugInfo, tokens) =>
            Debug.Log($"[Tryll] turn complete — status={status} tokens={tokens}"));

        _agent.OnError.AddListener(error =>
            Debug.LogError($"[Tryll] error: {error}"));

        _agent.OnAgentCreated.AddListener(() =>
            Debug.Log("[Tryll] agent ready — right-click this component and choose 'Ask Tryll'"));

        var client = TryllClient.Instance;
        client.CreateSessionComplete += err =>
        {
            if (!err.IsOk) { Debug.LogError($"[Tryll] CreateSession failed: {err}"); return; }
            _agent.CreateAgent();
        };

        client.StartSession();
    }

    [ContextMenu("Ask Tryll")]
    void AskTryll()
    {
        if (!_agent.HasAgent)
        {
            Debug.LogWarning("[Tryll] agent not ready yet");
            return;
        }
        _agent.SendMessage("In one sentence: what is Tryll?");
    }
}

docs.title: Step 6 — Test without entering Play Mode
docs.text:
Before pressing Play, use the Chat Window to verify your setup is working:

  1. Open Window → Tryll → Chat.
  2. Confirm the Tryll Settings field shows your TryllRuntimeSettings asset (auto-found).
  3. Drag the TryllDemo GameObject's Tryll Agent Component into the Agent Component slot.
  4. Click Start — the window launches the server, connects, and creates the agent. The status label turns green: Ready.
  5. Type a message and press Enter. You should see a streamed reply.
  6. Click Stop when done.

See Test an Agent in the Editor for the full walkthrough including troubleshooting.

docs.title: Step 7 — Enter Play Mode
docs.text:
Press Play.

On the first run you'll see:

  1. A brief pause while the server starts and the client connects.
  2. The model loads from disk (a few seconds the first time it is used in a session) — this only works because you already downloaded and registered it in Step 4; CreateAgent fails fast otherwise.
  3. The Console prints: [Tryll] agent ready — right-click this component and choose 'Ask Tryll'.

Once the agent is ready:

  1. In the Hierarchy, select the TryllDemo GameObject.
  2. In the Inspector, right-click the TryllDemo script component header and choose Ask Tryll.
  3. Watch the Console — answer deltas stream in as [Tryll] delta from answer: … lines, then [Tryll] answer finished its answer and [Tryll] turn complete.

docs.title: Where to see what's happening
docs.text:
Open the Console window and filter by [Tryll]:

Prefix Source Useful for [TryllClient] TryllClient singleton Connection attempts, session config, agent lifecycle. [TryllAgent] TryllAgentComponent Agent created/destroyed, DownloadProgress, errors. [TryllServer] tryll_server.exe stdout (re-emitted by the client) [Listener] Listening on 127.0.0.1:<port> (in the editor, auto-launch binds loopback on the Server Port project setting, default 9100, and falls back to a free port only if that port is taken; player builds always pick a free port), model load lines, server errors.

Client Dev writes one log file per run under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Tryll\projects\<project-key>\logs\ (project key from the sanitized game name plus a hash of the project directory).

docs.title: What you built
docs.text:
• A session connected to a Tryll server the client spawned for you.
  • One agent with a one-node graph authored in the DemoWorkflow Workflow Asset (Generate node, driven by a model you downloaded and registered in the Model Manager).
  • Model output surfaced as OnAnswerText events, which stream token-by-token by default (Send = Streamed on the Generate node); set Send = Whole for a single full-reply frame instead of delta chunks.
  • A [ContextMenu] method as the simplest way to trigger a turn from the Inspector without any UI setup.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Test an Agent in the Editor — iterate on your workflow without entering Play Mode.
  • How-to Guides — RAG, tool calls, guardrails, model management.
  • Concepts — the mental model behind the graph abstraction.
  • Unity Client API Reference — complete class-level reference.
  • Manage models in the editor — download, register, and pin models with explicit progress.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Compile errors on import — check that the package's Runtime/Generated/ folder contains .cs files. If it's empty, the distribution was packaged without the FlatBuffers step; contact support or re-download.
  • [TryllServer] server not found — the package's .Server/Default/ folder is missing or empty. A release package ships it populated; if you cloned the repo instead, build the Tryll server so the committed .Server/Default symlink resolves to your build.
  • Model name dropdown is empty — open the Model Manager (Window → Tryll → Model Manager), download a model, and set its build registration to Experimental or Production. Unregistered models do not appear in Inspector dropdowns.
  • Stuck at connecting — the server crashed or didn't start in time. Check the Console for [TryllServer] lines and the Client Dev log under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Tryll\projects\<project-key>\logs\ as a fallback.
  • CreateSession fails — usually a server-side error reading models.json or initialising the inference engine. Check [TryllServer] Console output.
  • OnError fires during CreateAgent — read the error message. Common causes: Default Model Name is empty or doesn't match any entry in models.json (fails fast — download it via the Model Manager first), or a route targets a node that doesn't exist.
  • Right-clicking the script shows no Ask Tryll option — you must be in Play Mode with the agent already created. Check the Console for the agent ready log line first.
  • Nothing appears in the Console — confirm OnAnswerText is wired in Start() and that the script is attached to the same GameObject as TryllAgentComponent. With the default Send = Streamed on the Generate node, OnAnswerText fires once per chunk (isDelta = true), the last call is an empty terminator (text is empty, isFinal = true), and OnTurnComplete follows. Set Send = Whole to get a single full-reply frame (isDelta = false, isFinal = true).

docs.title: First Inference in Unreal
docs.text:
Unpack a Tryll release, drop the plugin into your Unreal project (the server is bundled inside it), set a few project settings, download a model through the Model Manager, and watch a single Generate node print its answer to the screen during PIE — no chat UI required.

Working with an AI coding agent?

The Unreal plugin ships an AGENTS.md at its root. Attach it to your agent's context (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Codex, …) before asking it to write Tryll code — it carries the graph/slot mental model and the ways Tryll differs from a cloud LLM SDK. Agents that fetch docs themselves can start from llms.txt.

docs.title: What you'll build
docs.text: A blank actor with a one-node workflow. You download a model up front in the Model Manager, then the plugin auto-launches a local Tryll server, connects, and creates the session for you; the agent component creates itself once the session is ready. The actor runs one inference turn with the prompt "In one sentence: what is Tryll?" and prints the answer to the viewport and the Output Log.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Unreal Engine 5.7 and a blank C++ project (Blueprint-only projects can't compile the plugin source).
  • ~5 GB free disk space for the downloaded model and a working internet connection on first run.
  • Familiarity with creating a Blueprint actor and binding events.

The Unreal plugin bundles the server and spawns it for you, so installing the plugin is the whole setup.

docs.title: Step 1 — Get the distribution
docs.text:
1. Download tryll-unreal-<version>.7z from the releases page and extract it somewhere temporary (e.g. C:\Downloads\tryll\).

  2. Inside is the UnrealPlugin/ folder — the server is bundled inside it, so this one folder is everything you install:

    UnrealPlugin/                     <-- everything you need for Unreal
├── TryllClient.uplugin
├── Generated/messages_generated.h
├── Source/
└── Binaries/ThirdParty/TryllServer/Default/  <-- bundled server
    ├── tryll_server.exe
    ├── llama.dll, ggml*.dll, ggml-vulkan.dll
    └── data/
        ├── server-config.json
        ├── models.json
        ├── default-canned-responses.txt
        └── default-guardrail-patterns.txt

The archive ships no model weights — you download the models your graph references up front through the Model Manager (Step 4). CreateAgent fails fast if a referenced model is not already on disk; the server does not download it for you at agent-creation time. In Client Dev, downloaded weights land under <Project>/TryllStorage/models/.

How the archive is built

ci/scripts/release.py builds the production server, then stages the Unreal plugin (FlatBuffers codegen + the server bundled into its Binaries/ThirdParty/TryllServer/Default/ folder) and zips it into a per-engine archive. The server's data/server-config.json is patched with production overrides and models.json is filtered to the shipping audience. The Unity package ships separately as tryll-unity-<version>.7z.

docs.title: Step 2 — Install the Unreal plugin
docs.text:
Copy the UnrealPlugin/ folder into your project as <YourProject>/Plugins/TryllClient/:

<YourProject>/
├── TryllStorage/                    <-- default storage root (outside Content/)
├── Plugins/
│   └── TryllClient/
│       ├── TryllClient.uplugin
│       ├── Generated/messages_generated.h
│       ├── Source/TryllClient/{Public,Private}/
│       └── Binaries/ThirdParty/TryllServer/Default/  <-- server rides along
└── <YourProject>.uproject

The bundled server ships inside the plugin, so installing the plugin places the server alongside it. The plugin resolves it at <Plugin>/Binaries/ThirdParty/TryllServer/<variant>/tryll_server.exe via the plugin directory, so the path is identical in the editor and in packaged builds (a shipped plugin has just the Default variant). Auto-launch passes --mode client-dev, --storage-root (default <Project>/TryllStorage/), and related project flags. Models download into TryllStorage/models/.

Then:

  1. Right-click <YourProject>.uproject → Generate Visual Studio project files.
  2. Open the solution and build in Development Editor.
  3. Launch the editor. Edit → Plugins → Project lists Tryll Client as enabled.

docs.title: Step 3 — Configure Tryll Client in Project Settings
docs.text:
Open Edit → Project Settings → Plugins → Tryll Client and set:

Setting Value Why Auto Launch Server true (default) Subsystem spawns the bundled server on Initialize. Uncheck to run a server yourself. Llama.cpp backend Vulkan (default) Portable GPU API. Set Auto to prefer CUDA on NVIDIA (also ships CUDA DLLs in a packaged build). Auto Connect true (default) Subsystem opens the session on Initialize (connect-retry covers server startup). Uncheck to call Connect yourself. Auto Create Session true (default) On connect, the subsystem creates the session from the models you registered — no Blueprint wiring needed. Uncheck to call Create Session yourself. Connect Max Attempts / Connect Retry Delay Seconds defaults Subsystem retries while the freshly-spawned server warms up. Game Name e.g. my-game Short slug for telemetry and the project-name fallback. Please fill it. Storage Data Folder TryllStorage (default) Project folder outside Content/. The plugin passes --storage-root.

Settings are persisted to Config/DefaultGame.ini under [/Script/TryllClient.TryllRuntimeSettings].

Project Settings → Plugins → Tryll Client with the defaults: auto-launch and auto-connect on, Vulkan backend, port 9100, and TryllStorage as the storage folder.

Client Dev usage telemetry is always on in the editor; set TRYLL_SERVER_MODE=tryll-dev only for Tryll’s own CI. Player builds that still launch Client Dev are unreleasable until a Client Prod binary ships.

The Model Manager is the primary way to get models

You download and register your model up front in the next step, so it is already on disk before the first turn. CreateAgent fails fast if the model is not already there — it does not download it for you — so shipped builds rely on the Model Manager's registration tiers. See Manage Models in the Editor.

docs.title: Step 4 — Download and register a model
docs.text:
Before your agent can run, it needs a model on disk. Download one with the Model Manager and register it to your project, then you can select it on the workflow in the next step.

  1. Open Window → Tryll → Tryll Model Manager. The window launches the bundled server, connects, and lists every model the server knows about. Wait for the toolbar status to read Ready · N models (green).
  2. In the list, pick a language model to start with:
    • Recommended: Gemma 3 4B Instruct (Q4_K_M) (~3 GB download).
    • Smaller / quicker: Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (Q4_K_M) (~2 GB download).
  3. Select the row. In the Model Properties panel on the right, the Status section shows State: Not downloaded. Click Download — a progress bar tracks the bytes and the toolbar shows the active download count.
  4. When the state turns to Downloaded, set Build registration (this project) to Experimental — that makes it available in the editor, which is all this tutorial needs. (Production additionally ships the files inside packaged builds; choose that when you're ready to ship.)
  5. Close the Model Manager.

Registrations live in your project, written to Config/DefaultGame.ini via the Tryll Model Manifest developer settings. Every model-name dropdown in the editor now lists what you registered here.

Registration controls where a model is available

The tier you pick decides a model's reach: Experimental keeps it in the editor for development; Production ships it inside packaged builds beside the server. Node dropdowns list your Experimental and Production models, each with a tier badge. See Manage Models in the Editor.

docs.title: Step 5 — Create a workflow asset and add the demo actor
docs.text:
1. In the Content Browser, right-click → Tryll → Workflow Asset. Name it DemoWorkflow.
  2. Open DemoWorkflow. In the Details panel configure the graph:
    • Under Nodes, add one entry and set Name = answer.
    • On that node's Params, pick Generate from the type picker — that makes it a Generate node and expands its parameter fields below. Leave them at their defaults; the Default Exit field stays empty, which routes the turn to END.
    • Set Start Node = answer.
    • Set Default Model Name to the model you registered in Step 4.
  3. Create a blank Blueprint actor — call it BP_TryllDemoActor.
  4. Add a Tryll Agent Component to it.
  5. Assign DemoWorkflow to the Workflow Asset slot on the component.
  6. Leave Auto Create On Connect ticked (the default). The component waits until the session is created before creating the agent, and queues itself if it spawns earlier — so it manages its own lifecycle.
  7. Drop BP_TryllDemoActor into the level.

docs.title: Step 6 — Wire the Blueprint
docs.text:
With Auto Launch Server, Auto Connect, and Auto Create Session on (Step 3), the subsystem launches the server, opens the connection, and creates the session from your settings — all by itself. The agent component then creates itself as soon as the session is ready. So the only thing left to wire is what to do when the agent answers.

Open BP_TryllDemoActor's Event Graph:

flowchart LR
    OAR[OnAgentReady] --> SM["Send Message<br>In one sentence: what is Tryll?"]
    OAT[OnAnswerText] --> P1["Print String: Text"]
    OTC[OnTurnComplete] --> P2["Print String: Done."]

Select the Tryll Agent Component in the Components panel, then add each event from the Events section at the bottom of the Details panel:

  1. On Agent Ready → Send Message with "In one sentence: what is Tryll?".
  2. On Answer Text (Node Name, Text, bIsFinal) → Print String — wire Text into In String, set Print to Screen = true, Print to Log = true, Duration = 10. The Generate node streams by default, so this fires once per chunk with Text holding only the new text. The last call is an empty terminator: Text is empty and bIsFinal is true. Node Name names the node that produced the chunk (answer here).
  3. On Turn Complete (Status, DebugInfo, TokensGenerated) → another Print String that prints "Done." (or Enum to String on Status).

That's the whole graph — no Connect, no Create Session, no Create Agent. Those are the subsystem's job now.

Want the whole reply as one line?

Streaming (Send = Streamed) is the Generate node's default. To get a single frame with the complete reply instead of per-chunk deltas, either bind On Answer Full (fires once after OnTurnComplete with the full accumulated text) or set the node's Send to Whole in Step 5.

Driving the session yourself

For full control — a loading screen, or deciding yourself when the session opens — untick Auto Connect / Auto Create Session and call Connect then Create Session (or Create Session From Settings) yourself. Engines are not a reason to do this: each model's engine comes from the model catalog, and Create Session only takes an optional warm-up hint. Create Agent still waits for the session to be ready, so the old connect-vs-create race can't happen either way.

docs.title: Step 7 — Test without entering PIE
docs.text:
Before pressing Play, use the Chat Window to verify the agent responds — no Blueprint wiring required:

  1. Open Window → Tryll → Tryll Chat.
  2. Select the actor that has your UTryllAgentComponent (with DemoWorkflow assigned on the component).
  3. Click Start — the panel launches the server, connects, and creates an editor agent from that component. The status label turns green: Ready.
  4. Type a message and press Enter. You should see a streamed reply.
  5. Click Stop when done.

See Test an Agent in the Editor for the full walkthrough including troubleshooting.

docs.title: Step 8 — Play
docs.text:
Press Play. On the first run you'll see:

  1. A few seconds while the server starts and the plugin connects.
  2. The model you downloaded in Step 4 loads from disk into memory — a few seconds the first time it's used in a session.

  3. The answer streams to the viewport and the Output Log, one chunk per OnAnswerText event, followed by your OnTurnComplete marker:

    LogBlueprintUserMessages: [BP_TryllDemoActor] Tryll is a local
LogBlueprintUserMessages: [BP_TryllDemoActor]  small-language-model
LogBlueprintUserMessages: [BP_TryllDemoActor]  inference server.
LogBlueprintUserMessages: [BP_TryllDemoActor] Done.

The Generate node streams by default (Send = Streamed), so each OnAnswerText chunk carries a delta. The last call is an empty terminator with bIsFinal = true (it prints an empty line), then your OnTurnComplete handler prints Done.. For a single full-reply frame instead, bind On Answer Full or set the node's Send to Whole (see the tip in Step 6).

Subsequent runs skip the download and load steps — the model stays in the server process, and TryllStorage/models/ survives across PIE sessions.

docs.title: Where to see what's happening
docs.text:
Open Window → Output Log and use the Categories filter:

Category Source Useful for LogTryllServer tryll_server.exe stdout (drained by the subsystem and re-emitted in Unreal) [Listener] Listening on 127.0.0.1:<port> (in the editor, auto-launch binds loopback on the Server Port project setting, default 9100, and falls back to a free port only if that port is taken; Standalone Game and packaged builds always pick a free port), ConnectionReady, model load lines, server-side errors. LogTryll Plugin (subsystem, agent component, connection thread) Connect attempts, CreateSession outcome, agent lifecycle, DownloadProgress. LogBlueprintUserMessages Print String calls The answer text, your "Done." marker.

The server's output funnels through the Unreal Output Log, so a single window shows everything.

Client Dev writes one log file per run under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Tryll\projects\<project-key>\logs\.

docs.title: What you built
docs.text:
• A session connected to a Tryll server that the plugin spawned for you.
  • One agent with a one-node graph.
  • Model output surfaced to Blueprint as OnAnswerText events, which stream token-by-token by default (Send = Streamed); set the node's Send to Whole, or bind On Answer Full, for a single full-reply frame.

Everything the plugin exposes in Blueprint — connection, session, agents, models, string storages, tool calls — is listed in the Blueprint Catalog.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Tryll server exe not found at '...' in LogTryll/Error — no variant folder under <Plugin>/Binaries/ThirdParty/TryllServer/ resolves. From a release archive the Default variant ships populated; from a source build, run cmake --build of the server so the committed Default symlink resolves to your build.
  • OnConnectionChanged(false) fires repeatedly — the server crashed or didn't start. Check LogTryllServer for the failure reason and %LOCALAPPDATA%\Tryll\projects\<project-key>\logs\ as a fallback.
  • OnCreateSessionComplete(false) — usually a server-side error reading models.json or initialising the inference engine. Check LogTryllServer.
  • Default Model Name dropdown is empty — register a model first. Open Window → Tryll → Tryll Model Manager, download one, and set its Build registration to Experimental or Production; it then appears in the dropdown.
  • OnError fires during CreateAgent — read ErrorMessage. Common causes: Default Model Name is empty or names a model that isn't yet on disk (fails fast — download it via the Model Manager first), or a route targets a node name that doesn't exist.
  • CreateAgent takes several seconds even after the model is downloaded — normal on the first agent using a given model in a session; the server is loading it from disk into RAM/VRAM. Subsequent agents on the same model are instant.
  • Nothing prints after Send Message — bind both On Answer Text and On Turn Complete. With the default Send = Streamed, OnAnswerText fires once per chunk (each Text is a delta), the last call is an empty terminator with bIsFinal = true, and OnTurnComplete follows. Set the node's Send to Whole to get a single full-reply frame with the whole text and bIsFinal = true.

docs.title: How-to Guides
docs.text:
Task recipes. Each page solves one concrete problem and shows a minimal working example in Unity, Unreal, C++, and Python where applicable. If you are new to Tryll, start with First inference; if you want the why, see Concepts.

Guides marked ★ are the ones to read first in their area.

docs.title: Setup and connection
docs.text:
• Run the Tryll Server — install or build from source, edit server-config.json, start, watch logs.
  • Auto-launch the Server — let the client spawn and manage the server process for you (Unity, Unreal, C++, Python).
  • Connect and Manage a Session — connect, create the session, reconnect, clean shutdown.

docs.title: Editor tools
docs.text:
• Test an Agent in the Editor ★ — iterate on a workflow in the Unity/Unreal Chat window without entering Play/PIE.
  • Edit Workflows in the Unity Graph Editor and in the Unreal Graph Editor — author a workflow visually: add nodes, wire exits, validate, save.
  • Manage Models in the Editor — browse, download, load/unload, and register models for builds from the GUI.
  • Choose Where Models Run — put each model in RAM or VRAM, and understand why placement is a hint rather than a guarantee.
  • Use the Agent Log — the per-agent send/receive narrative in the editor: what your game asked for, and what came back.
  • Inspect Server Memory — Unity and Unreal Memory windows: live RAM/VRAM for the whole server process (Refresh only).
  • Inspect and Edit Knowledge Stores — Unity and Unreal Knowledge windows: list, query, and edit experimental mutable stores, save and load game memory, and export or import one store.
  • Compare Dialog Variants in the Lab — run one scripted dialog across parameter variants and seeds, and read the spread instead of guessing from a single reply.
  • Test Tool Calls in Chat and the Dialog Lab — register a handler on the scene agent, talk to it in Chat, then script canned or live-tool Lab runs.
  • Agentic Coding With Tryll — have an AI coding agent build Tryll agents: AGENTS.md, the Unreal MCP tools, and how to write a prompt it can finish.

docs.title: Build an agent
docs.text:
• Build a Chat Agent with a Graph ★ — compose a Generate + guardrail graph. Start here when writing your first agent.
  • Design an NPC Prompt ★ — measurement-backed recipes for writing a role-play system_prompt: what actually improves character dialogue, what provably does not, and how model choice changes the answer.
  • Design an Intent-Classifier Prompt — the ClassifyIntentLLM template contract ({{intents_block}} required; {{letters}} optional), how to write and order the labels, and how to tune threshold/margin.
  • Use Mustache Templates — control exactly how instructions, slots, variables, and retrieved chunks land in the prompt.
  • Stream Answers to a UI — wire streaming tokens into your application's view layer.
  • Send Multiple Answers in One Turn — two speakers, or a thinking channel plus a reply, routed by AnswerText.node_name.

docs.title: Dialogue and turn control
docs.text:
• Change Agent Parameters at Runtime — mutate a node's params (prompt, sampling, threshold, …) between turns, and which params are structural and cannot change.
  • Seed and Edit Dialog History — append scripted user/assistant turns, write an opener, or retry by removing the last turn — all without running the graph.
  • Export and Import Dialog — capture a full-fidelity snapshot and restore it from a game-owned save file.
  • Save and Load Agent State — coordinate quiescent multi-agent snapshots, variables, game state, atomic slot writes, strict restore, and KV-cache warm-up.
  • Cancel a Turn — stop an in-flight turn (a chat "Stop" button, or a rollback), keeping or discarding the partial reply.
  • Pause and Resume a Turn — suspend a turn between nodes and resume it after acting client-side.
  • Manage an Agent's KV Cache — prefill, evict, and inspect language-model KV caches to trade memory against first-turn latency.
  • Run Many Agents on a Small GPU — size every LLM node's context window, then evict the agents nobody is talking to: the two levers that fit several NPC agents into limited VRAM.
  • Keep Long Conversations Coherent — add a Summarize node so ageing turns fold into a rolling summary instead of being trimmed out of the prompt.

docs.title: Knowledge and retrieval
docs.text:
• Create a Simple RAG Assistant ★ — the hero recipe: prepare a knowledge base, add a Retrieve node in front of Generate, see grounded answers.
  • Query Rewriting and HyDE for RAG — rewrite the user's message before retrieval, while still answering what they actually asked. Covers both registers: a keyword query when your chunks read like questions, and a hypothetical answer (HyDE) when they read like statements.
  • Build an Intent-Driven NPC — classify the player's intent against a labelled knowledge base and route to tone-specific replies.
  • Classify Intent Without a Knowledge Base — the same NPC using ClassifyIntentLLM: describe each intent in a sentence, no embedding model and no corpus to author.

docs.title: Game state and control flow
docs.text:
The mental model for this section is the per-turn slot blackboard and the per-agent variable store.

  • Drive Prompts and Retrieval from Game State ★ — inject live game state (level, mood, quests) into a prompt template and a Retrieve filter via agent variables, updated each turn with no ChangeParam round-trip.
  • Branch on a Slot — conditional routing with the Branch node, including reacting to a verdict the model produced earlier in the same turn.
  • Add a Hidden Reasoning or Draft Step — an internal draft or "thinking" pass the conversation never remembers, using send and history_role.
  • Substitute Agent Variables in LLM Output — have the model emit __PRICE__-style markers and replace them with live variable values before the answer, history, or TTS sees the text.
  • Filter LLM Output Artifacts — strip speaker prefixes and roleplay markup spans out of streamed output.
  • Keep Merchant Prices Deterministic ★ — worked example: game code owns the number, the model owns the wording, and the two never disagree.

docs.title: Structured output and tools
docs.text:
• Define and Handle Tool Calls ★ — declare tool definitions on a ToolCall node, route on tool_called / no_tool_called, handle the call client-side, and hand the real result back to the model.
  • Test Tool Calls in Chat and the Dialog Lab — exercise that workflow in the editors without Play/PIE.
  • Compare Tool-Call Models ★ — exact-accuracy on the Tryll-authored suites and the BFCL slice; pick a catalog model by the job (commands, log query, parallel calls), not by parameter count.
  • Design a Tool-Call Prompt ★ — measurement-backed schema and prompt recipes: name "unfiltered", put it first in the enum, and do not add parameters the model cannot fill.
  • Fix Tool-Call Text in Answers — the player sees <|tool_call>… instead of dialogue: find which node wrote it, and fix the prompt, the routing, or the tool node.
  • Constrain Output with a Grammar — force a Generate node to emit exactly a fixed shape (command, choice, JSON) with a GBNF grammar; flip between command turn and free chat at runtime.

docs.title: Guardrails and safety
docs.text:
• Use Canned Responses and Guardrails — short-circuit jailbreaks and off-topic prompts to scripted replies, before spending a model call.
  • Build an Immersion Guard — gate out-of-character and out-of-world player lines before they reach the NPC, and drop the rejected turn from history.

docs.title: Voice
docs.text:
• Add Voice Output to an Agent ★ — make an NPC speak with GenerateAndSpeak / Speak and a playback component.
  • Add Lip Sync to a Character — move a character's mouth with its voice using the server's viseme track.
  • Clone a Voice from an Audio Sample — point a voice profile at a short reference WAV to speak in that voice.
  • Design a Voice Clip with Qwen3-TTS — make a reference clip from a text description, without an actor.
  • Add Emotions to a Voice — one clip per mood as delivery modes, switched at runtime.
  • Use Voice Input — create a VoiceInput handle, stream PCM audio, receive transcripts, push-to-talk vs. hands-free.
  • Bias Voice Input with Hotwords — nudge the STT decoder toward game-specific proper nouns, spell names, and other lexicon items without retraining the model.
  • Add Lip Sync to a MetaHuman (Unreal) — make a MetaHuman's mouth follow an agent's TTS voice with the separate Tryll MetaHuman Lip Sync plugin, using Epic's neural model or the viseme track.

docs.title: Models and shipping
docs.text:
• Use Your Own Local Model — register a GGUF file that lives on disk without a Hugging Face download.
  • Use a LoRA Adapter — run an LLM node with a fine-tuned GGUF adapter, and tune how strongly it applies.
  • Pin and Unpin Models — keep a model warm (LoadModelRequest) or release it (UnloadModelRequest).
  • Verify Required Models Before Play — gate Play/PIE on every registered model being downloaded first, and fail the build when a workflow references a model that will not ship.
  • Estimate Memory Footprint — work out the RAM and VRAM a model line-up needs before you ship, so it fits your target hardware. Check the live numbers in Inspect Server Memory.
  • Ship Storage Folders for Builds — lay out canned-response / guardrail / RAG / hotword files so they travel with a packaged build and resolve against the process storage root.
  • Ship an Agent in Another Language — set one session language and have speech, speech recognition, content files and prompt directives all follow it; plus what the language setting deliberately does not do.
  • Localize Prompts with Your Localization System — tick Localized on a prompt, store a Text ID, and let Unity or Unreal ask your string table for the text before the agent is created.

Downloading and registering models from the editor GUI is covered in Manage Models in the Editor.

docs.title: Add a Hidden Reasoning or Draft Step
docs.text:
Sometimes a node should produce text the conversation never remembers — an internal draft, a plan, a scratch calculation, or a "thinking out loud" pass that precedes the real answer. Slots make this a two-knob decision that is independent of what the node actually generates:

  • send — does the text go out on the wire to the client?
  • history_role — is the text replayed as an assistant message on later turns?

Setting history_role = None is what makes a step "hidden" from the conversation: its output is still written to a slot and is fully usable this turn (via input or {{slot.<name>}}), but it never becomes part of the remembered transcript. send then independently decides whether the user sees it happening.

Prerequisites

  • A working Generate agent — see Build a chat agent with a graph.
  • Read Slots and inter-node value passing for the send / history_role / input model this recipe applies.

docs.title: Two variants, one pattern
docs.text:
Both variants are a think → answer chain: an upstream node reasons or drafts into its slot, and a downstream Generate reads that slot and writes the reply the user actually keeps.

Variant send history_role The user… Hidden draft None None never sees the step; it is pure scratch Visible thinking Streamed None sees it stream live, but it is never remembered

The only difference is send. history_role = None is identical in both: the step is scratch as far as the transcript is concerned.

flowchart LR
    think["Generate<br>think<br>(history_role=None)"] -->|input=think| answer["Generate<br>answer<br>(history_role=Assistant)"]

docs.title: Variant A — a hidden draft
docs.text:
The think node reasons privately; answer reads its slot and produces the reply. Nothing about the think step reaches the client.

PythonC++ 
from tryll_client.graph import GraphDescription
from tryll_client._generated.node_params import (
    GenerateParams, SendAnswer, HistoryRole, SamplingOverrides,
)

think = GenerateParams(
    system_prompt=(
        "Think step by step about how to answer the user's latest "
        "message. Write a short plan. Do NOT answer the user yet."
    ),
    send=SendAnswer.None_,          # never streamed to the client
    history_role=HistoryRole.None_, # never replayed on later turns
    sampling=SamplingOverrides(temperature=0.0),
    default_exit="answer",
)

answer = GenerateParams(
    system_prompt="You are a helpful assistant.",
    # Render the private plan above the user turn (default placement
    # BeforeUserAsSystem):
    template="Your plan:\n{{slot.think}}",
    # send / history_role keep their defaults (Streamed / Assistant).
    default_exit="",                # END
)

graph = (
    GraphDescription()
    .add_node("think", think)
    .add_node("answer", answer)
    .set_start_node("think")
    .set_default_model_name("My Local Model")
)

using namespace Tryll::NodeParams;

GenerateParamsT think;
think.system_prompt =
    "Think step by step about how to answer the user's latest "
    "message. Write a short plan. Do NOT answer the user yet.";
think.send         = Tryll::SendAnswer_None;    // never streamed
think.history_role = Tryll::HistoryRole_None;   // never replayed
think.default_exit = "answer";

GenerateParamsT answer;
answer.system_prompt = "You are a helpful assistant.";
answer.template_     = "Your plan:\n{{slot.think}}";
// send / history_role keep their defaults (Streamed / Assistant).

Tryll::Client::GraphDescription graph;
graph.AddGenerate("think",  std::move(think))
     .AddGenerate("answer", std::move(answer))
     .SetStartNode("think")
     .SetDefaultModelName("My Local Model");

Because think.send = None, the client receives AnswerText frames only from answer. Because think.history_role = None, next turn's projected prompt contains the previous answer but no trace of the plan.

docs.title: Variant B — visible thinking
docs.text:
Flip send to Streamed and the reasoning streams to the client live — useful for a "thinking…" panel — while history_role = None still keeps it out of the remembered conversation:

PythonC++ 
think = GenerateParams(
    system_prompt="Reason out loud about the user's message.",
    send=SendAnswer.Streamed,       # streamed live to the client
    history_role=HistoryRole.None_, # still never remembered
    default_exit="answer",
)

GenerateParamsT think;
think.system_prompt = "Reason out loud about the user's message.";
think.send          = Tryll::SendAnswer_Streamed;  // streamed live
think.history_role  = Tryll::HistoryRole_None;      // never remembered
think.default_exit  = "answer";

Now the client receives streamed frames from both think and answer. Every AnswerText frame carries the producing node's name, so the UI can route the two streams to different places — a dim "thinking" area versus the main reply bubble. See Send multiple answers in one turn for the client-side routing.

docs.title: Why the slot is still usable
docs.text:
Both variants set history_role = None, yet answer reads the step's output via {{slot.think}}. That works because same-turn slot reads are unconditional — send and history_role govern the wire and the remembered transcript, never whether a downstream node in the same turn can see the slot (see Slots and inter-node value passing). history_role = None only means "don't carry this into future turns."

Draft → refine gets the draft for free

If you set the upstream step to history_role = Assistant instead of None, its output also replays as an assistant message into the downstream node's prompt within the same turn — so a refine node sees the draft both as {{slot.<name>}} and as a natural preceding assistant turn. Use None when the step is pure scratch; use Assistant when you want the downstream model to treat it as a real prior turn.

docs.title: Add Emotions to a Voice with Delivery Modes
docs.text:
Make a character sound angry, afraid or joyful, and switch between moods while the game runs. A voice profile holds one voice and a list of delivery modes: named ways of speaking, such as angry or whisper. Game code switches the mode with SetAgentDeliveryMode, and the next sentence is spoken in the new mood.

With a cloning model (Qwen3-TTS Base or Pocket TTS), each mood is a reference clip of the same character speaking in that mood. This page shows how to make those clips, put them in a profile, and switch between them.

Prerequisites

  • Voice output working — see Add Voice Output to an Agent.
  • A cloning model, Qwen3-TTS 12Hz 1.7B Base (Q4_K_M) or Pocket TTS (int8), and a neutral reference clip for the character — see Clone a Voice from an Audio Sample.

docs.title: Why one clip per mood
docs.text:
Cloning copies the register and energy of the reference clip along with the voice. In our measurements, neutral text cloned from a shouted, angry clip came out raised and loud on both models. Cloned from a sad clip, it came out low and flat. Cloning models have no emotion parameter: setting a delivery mode's Instruction on them fails with 3023. So the clip is the mood:

  1. One clip per character per mood, for example voices/guard/neutral.wav, voices/guard/angry.wav, voices/guard/afraid.wav.
  2. The neutral clip in the profile's Reference Voice. That is the built-in neutral mode.
  3. One delivery mode per mood in the same profile, each with its own Reference Voice.
  4. SetAgentDeliveryMode("angry") at runtime. It needs no agent rebuild.

Every mood must sound like the same person. A clip from another speaker changes who is talking, not just how.

docs.title: 1. Plan the moods
docs.text:
• Pick the few moods your game uses. Each one is a clip to make and to check. Three to five per character is plenty for most NPCs.
  • Use the same mode names on every character. Then one call, such as SetAgentDeliveryMode("angry"), works on everyone. A mode with no fields set sounds like neutral, so a character without an angry clip can still define an empty angry mode.
  • Keep names short and lowercase, such as angry, afraid, joyful. Game code and the editor's dropdown use them as written.

docs.title: 2. Make one clip per mood
docs.text: There are two ways to get a set of clips that sound like one person.

docs.title: Record one actor
docs.text: This gives the best result. Record every mood with the same actor, in the same session, with the same microphone and room. Follow the clip rules in Clone a Voice → Record a reference clip. Ask for each mood in character, and keep the same distance to the microphone, even when the actor shouts or whispers.

docs.title: Design the moods with Qwen3-TTS
docs.text:
Without an actor, render each mood with Qwen3-TTS VoiceDesign. The steps for one clip are in Design a Voice Clip with Qwen3-TTS. For a set of moods:

  1. Split the description into identity and delivery. The identity (gender, age, pitch, timbre, accent) stays word for word in every mood. Only the delivery changes.
  2. Write a line in each mood. An angry line for the angry clip, a frightened line for the afraid one.
  3. Render several takes per mood and keep the ones that sound most like the neutral clip. Listen to them side by side. Drop a take that sounds like someone else, even if its mood is right.

For example, a palace guard:

Mood Voice description neutral A man in his forties with a deep, slightly hoarse voice and a light Northern English accent. He speaks calmly, at an even pace. angry A man in his forties with a deep, slightly hoarse voice and a light Northern English accent. He is furious and shouts, fast and sharp. afraid A man in his forties with a deep, slightly hoarse voice and a light Northern English accent. He is frightened; his voice shakes and he speaks quickly and quietly.

Each render is a new sample, so designed moods can drift slightly away from each other. Picking takes by ear keeps the drift small.

Put the clips together in one folder per character:

<storage root>/
  └─ voices/
      └─ guard/
          ├─ neutral.wav
          ├─ angry.wav
          └─ afraid.wav

docs.title: 3. Add the modes to the voice profile
docs.text:
UnityUnrealPython
  1. Select the character's Voice Profile asset (Create → Tryll → Voice Profile if it has none).
  2. Set Tts Model Name to the cloning model and Reference Voice to the neutral clip.
  3. Under Delivery Modes, add one element per mood. Set its Name (angry) and its Reference Voice (voices/guard/angry.wav, with the … button or typed). Leave Instruction empty.
  1. Open the character's Tryll Voice Profile data asset.
  2. Set the TTS model to the cloning model and Reference Voice to the neutral clip.
  3. Under Delivery Modes, add one element per mood with its Name and Reference Voice. Leave Instruction empty.
from tryll_client import DeliveryMode, VoiceProfile

guard = VoiceProfile(
    tts_model_name="Qwen3-TTS 12Hz 1.7B Base (Q4_K_M)",
    reference_voice="voices/guard/neutral.wav",
    delivery_modes=[
        DeliveryMode(name="angry",  reference_voice="voices/guard/angry.wav"),
        DeliveryMode(name="afraid", reference_voice="voices/guard/afraid.wav"),
    ])
agent = client.create_agent(graph, voice=guard)

A mode can also set Speed Scale, for example 1.15 to make afraid a little faster.

By default, the server prepares every clip in the profile when the agent is created, so the first sentence in a new mood has no extra delay. Set Prepare to Lazy to prepare each clip on its first use instead. A bad or missing clip path, in the profile or in any mode, fails agent creation with 3023, and the message names the field.

docs.title: 4. Switch the mood at runtime
docs.text:
UnityUnrealPythonC++ 
await agentComp.SetDeliveryModeAsync("angry");    // the guard loses his temper
await agentComp.SetDeliveryModeAsync("neutral");  // and calms down again

Call Set Delivery Mode on the Tryll Agent component with the mode name. It reports completion through its delegate.

agent.set_delivery_mode("angry")
agent.set_delivery_mode("neutral")

agent.SetDeliveryMode("angry", 1.0f);
  • It applies from the next sentence. The call is accepted at any time, even mid-turn. A sentence already sent to the TTS model keeps its mood.
  • neutral is built in. It always exists and means the profile's own Reference Voice.
  • Intensity does not blend clips. A clip is all or nothing. On Pocket TTS, intensity only scales the mode's Speed Scale; on Qwen3-TTS Base it does nothing.
  • An unknown name fails with 3024 UnknownDeliveryMode, and the current mode stays.

To try a mood without code, use the agent component's Voice Delivery override in the Inspector (Unity) or Details panel (Unreal). Its dropdown lists neutral and the profile's modes, and changing it on a live agent switches the mood at once.

docs.title: Decide when to switch
docs.text: Tryll does not detect the mood for you: only the API switches the mode, and the language model cannot. Your game owns the character's emotional state, the same way it owns health or quest progress, and calls SetAgentDeliveryMode when it changes. Pass the same mood into the prompt too, so that what the character says matches how it sounds. See Talking NPC → Emotions.

docs.title: Example: the Unity demo
docs.text:
The Unity demo's EmotionalVoiceCharacter is a complete example. Kira, a K-pop singer giving a magazine interview, speaks with one Qwen3-TTS voice and eight moods:

  • Voice profile: Assets/Voices/VoiceCharacterWithEmotions, on Qwen3-TTS 12Hz 1.7B Base (Q4_K_M).
  • Neutral clip: voice/young_female/female_young_calm.wav.
  • Delivery modes: angry, very_angry, fear, hysteria, joy, sad, flirty and terror, each with its own clip in TryllStorage/voice/young_female/.
  • Workflow: Assets/Workflows/EmotionalVoiceCharacter.

The clips were made with Qwen3-TTS VoiceDesign, with one description per mood. To hear it, open DemoScene, select the EmotionalVoiceCharacter object, pick a mood in the agent component's Voice Delivery dropdown, then enter Play mode and talk to Kira. Change the mood while she speaks to hear the switch at the next sentence.

docs.title: Other TTS models
docs.text:
How a mode expresses a mood depends on the model:

Model What a mood is Qwen3-TTS Base, Pocket TTS A reference clip per mood (this page) Maya1 A text Instruction, such as angry or whisper, with intensity Supertonic 3, Orpheus No emotion control: a mode can only change speed, or stay empty

The details for each model are in Voice Profile → Delivery modes.

docs.title: Add Lip Sync to a Character
docs.text:
Make a speaking character's mouth move with its voice. The server sends a viseme track (mouth shapes with timings) alongside the speech, and a lip sync component plays it on the character's face in step with the audio: TryllLipSync in Unity, Tryll Lip Sync in Unreal. Nothing is precomputed and no extra model runs.

For a MetaHuman, use Add Lip Sync to a MetaHuman with its Viseme solver instead.

For how the track is produced and what it can and cannot do, see Concept: TTS and Voice Output.

Prerequisites

  • A character that already speaks, with a voice profile and a GenerateAndSpeak or Speak node — see Add Voice Output to an Agent.
  • A face mesh with ARKit blendshapes (morph targets in Unreal): jawOpen, mouthClose, mouthFunnel, mouthPucker, mouthStretchLeft, …. Most avatar pipelines can export them. Unity needs the names to match exactly; Unreal ignores case.

docs.title: 1. Turn on visemes in the voice profile
docs.text:
Set emit_visemes on the agent's voice profile. It is off by default. A lip-synced character either has visemes or not, so the flag is on the voice, not on a node: with it on, every speaking node of the agent, GenerateAndSpeak and Speak alike, sends a viseme track.

UnityUnrealPython

Select the character's Voice Profile asset and tick Emit Visemes.

Open the character's Tryll Voice Profile asset and tick Emit Visemes.

VoiceProfile(
    tts_model_name='Supertonic 3 (int8)',
    emit_visemes=True,
)

To turn visemes on or off for a live agent, replace its voice with SetAgentVoice while the agent is idle.

docs.title: 2. Add TryllLipSync to the character (Unity)
docs.text:
1. Select the GameObject that has your TryllAgentComponent.
  2. Add Component → Tryll → Tryll Lip Sync. It needs a TryllSpeaker on the same GameObject — the speaker is both the audio and the clock the face follows — and adds one if it is missing.
  3. Drag that TryllSpeaker into the Speaker field of the TryllAgentComponent, so the agent plays its audio through the speaker the face follows.
  4. Set Face Root to the parent of the face meshes (for example the imported avatar's root). The component finds every SkinnedMeshRenderer under it. To bind specific meshes only, fill Renderers instead. If the face is spawned at runtime, call BindFace(avatarRoot) once it exists.
  5. Enter Play mode and make the character speak. The Console logs the blendshape weight scale it found on the mesh (1 for glTF imports, 100 for FBX imports — both are handled).

Only the mouth is driven

TryllLipSync writes only the blendshapes its viseme map uses (the mouth and jaw channels). Blinks, brows and expressions on the same mesh are left alone, so other animation can drive them. Channels you add to the Map become owned by lip sync.

docs.title: 2. Add Tryll Lip Sync to the character (Unreal)
docs.text:
1. Open the character's Blueprint. It needs a Tryll Speaker component next to its Tryll Agent, as in Add Voice Output to an Agent. The speaker is both the audio and the clock the face follows. With one speaker on the actor, the agent and the lip sync both find it by themselves.
  2. Add Component → Tryll Lip Sync.
  3. Press Play and make the character speak.

When the character starts, the component uses the Tryll Speaker on the same actor and looks through the actor's skeletal meshes for one with ARKit morph targets. If several have them, a mesh whose name contains Face wins. To choose yourself, set Speaker and Face Mesh. If the face is spawned at runtime, call Bind Face once it exists. Is Face Bound reports whether any ARKit morph target was found.

Only the mouth is driven

Tryll Lip Sync writes only the morph targets its pose table uses. The rest of the face is left to the character's animation. While a mouth morph target is non-zero it overrides the AnimBP's value for it, and at rest the AnimBP's value applies again.

docs.title: 3. Tune the look
docs.text:
All settings are on the component and can be changed in Play mode, except Map (read when the component wakes) and Compensate Output Latency (read at start).

Setting Default What it does Intensity 0.4 Scales every mouth pose. Raise it for a more pronounced mouth, lower it if speech looks exaggerated. 0 keeps the mouth at rest. Smoothing Per Second 16 How quickly the face moves toward each new shape. Lower is softer, higher is snappier. Closure Smoothing Per Second 60 Faster rate used for lip closures (p, b, m, f, v) so the lips actually meet on short sounds. Attack Decay Ms 50 Cross-fade between consecutive shapes. Max Hold Ms 400 Returns the face to rest if a turn is cancelled mid-sentence. Map built in The pose (ARKit channel weights) used for each of the 15 visemes. Leave it empty to use the built-in table; edit it to suit a rig.

Changing the smoothing does not shift sync: with Compensate Smoothing Lag on (the default), the component looks ahead by the delay the smoothing adds.

The Intensity is also available from code:

GetComponent<TryllLipSync>().Intensity = 0.6f;

In Unreal, the same settings are on the Tryll Lip Sync component, with the same defaults, and can be changed during Play except Poses. The differences:

  • The pose table is called Poses and is read at BeginPlay.
  • There is no Output Lead Trim Ms: Unreal needs no correction for a streaming-clip backlog. Both engines have Compensate Output Latency (on by default); see Check the sync.
  • From Blueprint, set the intensity with Set Intensity.

docs.title: 4. Check the sync
docs.text:
The mouth should neither trail nor lead the voice. If it consistently does:

  • Sync Offset Ms shifts the face against the audio. Positive values move the face earlier.
  • Output Lead Trim Ms (default 342) accounts for how far Unity's streaming audio buffer runs ahead of what is audible. It was measured on a typical Windows setup; a different audio device or DSP buffer size can change it. Adjust it if the offset you need is large. Unity only.
  • Compensate Output Latency (on by default, both engines) holds the face back by the audio engine's output buffer, read from the audio device's buffer settings, so the mouth lines up with the sound as heard. In Unreal, the Tryll Speaker's Get Output Latency Ms returns the value in use; in Unity, TryllLipSync.OutputLatencyMs.

docs.title: Use the track directly
docs.text:
If you drive a face some other way, subscribe to the raw events instead of using TryllLipSync. Each frame covers one synthesized sentence. Offsets are in samples from the start of the turn's audio (its one format announcement), and keep counting across every speaking node of the turn, at the sample rate from the audio format callback. Each shape lasts until the next event; sil is rest.

Unity (C#)Unreal (C++)PythonC++ 
agentComponent.Agent.OnTtsVisemes += (nodeName, events) =>
{
    foreach (var e in events)
        Debug.Log($"{e.SampleOffset}: {e.Viseme} ({e.Weight:F2})");
};

Speaker->OnTtsVisemes.AddLambda(
    [](const FString& NodeName, TArrayView<const FTryllVisemeEvent> Events)
{
    for (const FTryllVisemeEvent& E : Events)
    {
        UE_LOG(LogTemp, Log, TEXT("%lld: %s (%.2f)"), E.SampleOffset,
               *UEnum::GetValueAsString(E.Viseme), E.Weight);
    }
});

Speaker is the character's UTryllSpeakerComponent. The view is valid only during the callback.

def on_visemes(node_name, events):
    for e in events:
        print(e.sample_offset, e.viseme, e.weight)

agent.set_on_tts_visemes(on_visemes)

agent.SetOnTtsVisemes([](std::string_view nodeName,
                         std::span<const Tryll::Client::AgentProxy::VisemeEvent> events)
{
    for (const auto& e : events)
        std::printf("%u: %d (%.2f)\n", e.sampleOffset, int(e.viseme), e.weight);
});

weight (0–1) is how far the shape should open, from the loudness of that stretch of speech. Lip closures and rests always have weight 1.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Check The mouth never moves Emit Visemes is on in the agent's voice profile; TryllLipSync has the agent assigned (a Console warning says so if not); the agent's Speaker is the TryllSpeaker next to TryllLipSync; the face mesh has ARKit-named blendshapes. The mouth moves too much Lower Intensity. The mouth pops between shapes Lower Smoothing Per Second or raise Attack Decay Ms. Mouth lags or leads the voice Adjust Sync Offset Ms; for a large offset, re-check Output Lead Trim Ms (Unity) or that Compensate Output Latency is on (Unreal). Unreal: the mouth never moves The Output Log (LogTryll) says whether Tryll Lip Sync found no Tryll Speaker or no face mesh with ARKit morph targets. Also check Emit Visemes is on in the agent's voice profile. If the actor has several Tryll Speakers, both components pick the first one found; to use another, set it as Speaker on both — on the placed instance, or from Blueprint before the agent is created (the agent's Speaker cannot be set in the Blueprint class defaults).

docs.title: Add Lip Sync to a MetaHuman (Unreal)
docs.text:
Make a MetaHuman's mouth move in time with an agent's Tryll TTS voice. This uses the Tryll MetaHuman Lip Sync plugin (UnrealPlugin/TryllMetaHumanLipSync), a separate plugin installed alongside TryllClient. It has two solvers, and both feed the face through Live Link:

  • Neural (default) runs Epic's realtime speech-to-animation model on the CPU over the TTS audio. It drives the whole face.
  • Viseme plays the server's viseme track through Epic's ARKit mapping. It drives the mouth and jaw, and runs no model.

See Choose a solver.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Unreal Engine 5.7, Windows 64-bit.
  • The TryllClient plugin with voice output working — see Add Voice Output to an Agent.
  • A MetaHuman in your project. Both kinds work: characters assembled in the in-engine MetaHuman Creator and characters downloaded from Quixel Bridge.

docs.title: Enable and set up
docs.text:
1. Install the plugin into your project's Plugins/ folder and enable Tryll MetaHuman Lip Sync in Edit > Plugins. It is off by default.
  2. Open Project Settings > Plugins > Tryll MetaHuman Lip Sync and click Set Up. The status line changes to Set up.

Set Up copies Epic's speech-to-animation model from your engine installation into your project as Content/TryllMetaHumanLipSync/solar-1-2700_blend-0v65.uasset and configures it for CPU inference. Nothing is redistributed by Tryll. The asset is generated, so add it to .gitignore and run Set Up on each fresh clone.

Until Set Up has run, Play is blocked with a notification naming the step, and packaging a Win64 game target fails at build time with the same message. This applies with either solver. Dedicated server targets are not affected.

docs.title: Fresh clones and build machines
docs.text:
Run Set Up from the command line instead of the editor:

UnrealEditor-Cmd.exe <Project>.uproject -run=TryllMetaHumanLipSyncSetup
UnrealEditor-Cmd.exe <Project>.uproject -run=TryllMetaHumanLipSyncSetup -verify

Both exit with 0 when the project is set up and 1 otherwise. -verify checks without changing anything.

docs.title: Add lip sync to a character
docs.text:
Open the MetaHuman's Blueprint and add two components:

  1. Tryll Speaker, next to an agent component whose Voice Profile is set, as in Add Voice Output to an Agent.
  2. Tryll MetaHuman Lip Sync.

That's all. When the character starts, the component finds the speaker and the skeletal mesh named Face on the same actor, and the mouth follows the voice.

docs.title: Other layouts
docs.text: If the components are not on the MetaHuman itself, set Target MetaHuman to the character. If the owning actor has several Tryll Speakers, set Speaker to the one to follow. With nothing set, the component also looks in the owner's child actors for the face.

docs.title: Choose a solver
docs.text:
Set Solver on the component. It is read once when the character starts.

Neural Viseme Drives The whole face Mouth and jaw Input The TTS audio The server's viseme track Voice change None Turn on Emit Visemes in the agent's voice profile CPU per speaking character About 4 to 5 ms per 20 ms of audio No model runs Face timing Trails the audio by the lookahead plus one 20 ms block Follows the audio as it plays

docs.title: Use the Viseme solver
docs.text:
1. In the agent's Voice Profile asset, tick Emit Visemes. Without it no track arrives and the mouth stays still; the component logs a warning when the character starts. Every speaking node of the agent (Speak and Generate And Speak) then sends a track.
  2. Set Solver to Viseme.
  3. Check ARKit Mapping points at Epic's PA_MetaHuman_ARKit_Mapping pose asset. The default is /Game/MetaHumans/Common/Face/ARKit/PA_MetaHuman_ARKit_Mapping, where exported MetaHumans keep it. The MetaHuman Character plugin also ships one in its Face/ARKit folder.

For what the viseme track is and how to tune it, see Add Lip Sync to a Character. Its Unreal Tryll Lip Sync component uses the same viseme settings on faces with ARKit morph targets.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default Notes Target MetaHuman unset The character to animate. Unset means the owner, then its child actors. Speaker unset The Tryll Speaker to follow. Unset means the only one on the owner. Solver Neural Neural or Viseme. Read once when the character starts. Subject Name empty Live Link subject name. Empty derives TryllMetaHumanLipSync_<actor label>, suffixed only if that name is already in use.

Neural solver only:

Setting Default Notes Mood Neutral Emotional tone applied by the model. Mood Intensity 1.0 0 to 1. Lookahead 80 ms 80 to 240. Higher is smoother and adds the same amount of latency. Read once when the character starts.

Change mood while the game runs with Set Mood (SetMood(Mood, Intensity)).

Viseme solver only:

Setting Default Notes Viseme Settings > Intensity 1.0 Scales every mouth pose. 0 keeps the mouth at rest. Viseme Settings > Smoothing Per Second 16 How quickly the mouth moves toward each new shape. Lower is softer, higher is snappier. Viseme Settings > Closure Smoothing Per Second 60 Faster rate for lip closures (p, b, m, f, v), so the lips meet on short sounds. Viseme Settings > Attack Decay Ms 50 Cross-fade between consecutive shapes. Viseme Settings > Max Hold Ms 400 Returns the mouth to rest if a turn is cancelled mid-sentence. Viseme Settings > Sync Offset Ms 0 Shifts the mouth against the audio. Positive moves it earlier. Viseme Settings > Compensate Output Latency on Holds the mouth back by the audio engine's output buffer, so it lines up with the sound as heard. Viseme Settings > Compensate Smoothing Lag on Looks ahead by the delay the smoothing adds, so changing smoothing does not shift sync. Viseme Poses empty The pose for each viseme as ARKit channel weights. Empty uses the built-in table. Read once when the character starts. ARKit Mapping see above Epic's ARKit to MetaHuman pose asset.

Viseme Settings can be changed while the game runs.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Every message is logged under LogTryllMetaHumanLipSync with the owning actor's name. Get Lip Sync Status returns the same state from Blueprint, and On Lip Sync Status Changed fires when it changes.

Status Cause Fix SpeakerNotFound No Tryll Speaker on the owner. Add one, or set Speaker. SpeakerAmbiguous More than one Tryll Speaker on the owner. Set Speaker. FaceNotFound No skeletal mesh named Face on the owner, its child actors, or Target MetaHuman. Set Target MetaHuman to the character. LiveLinkUnavailable The Live Link plugin is disabled. Enable it. AnimBlueprintMissing The plugin's face AnimBP is missing from its content. Reinstall the plugin. ModelMissing Set Up has not run in this project. Run Set Up. ModelLoadFailed The model asset exists but ONNX Runtime rejected it. See the NNE log lines just above the message. InferenceFailed ONNX Runtime failed while the character was speaking. See the NNE log lines just above the message. ArkitMappingMissing Viseme solver: the ARKit Mapping asset could not be loaded. Point ARKit Mapping at PA_MetaHuman_ARKit_Mapping.

With the Viseme solver, a status of Bound and a mouth that never moves means no viseme track is arriving: turn on Emit Visemes in the agent's voice profile. The component warns about this at start when it can find the agent component on the same actor.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
With the Neural solver, each speaking character costs about 4 to 5 ms of CPU per 20 ms of audio, measured on a Ryzen 9 7900X. Characters that are not speaking cost nothing. The face trails the audio by the lookahead plus one 20 ms block.

The Viseme solver runs no model.

docs.title: What it does to the character
docs.text: The component sets the anim class on the Face mesh to the plugin's own face AnimBP, ABP_TryllMetaHumanLipSyncFace. It copies the neck and spine pose from the Body mesh, reads the Live Link subject, and provides a montage slot. With the Viseme solver, the AnimBP passes the Live Link ARKit curves through the ARKit Mapping pose asset, the same way Epic's ABP_MH_LiveLink handles ARKit input. Whatever face AnimBP the character had is not used while the component is on it. The MetaHuman's rig logic runs as normal in the mesh's post-process AnimBP, so no MetaHuman assets are referenced by the plugin, other than the ARKit Mapping you point it at.
