docs.title: Design an NPC Prompt
docs.text:
A set of recipes for writing the system_prompt of a role-playing NPC, so it stays in character and emits clean, usable dialogue on a small on-device model.

Everything here comes from measurement, not taste. We ran a 26-variant prompt study across six models — Llama 3.1 8B, Llama 3.2 3B, Ministral 3 8B, Gemma 4 E4B, Qwen 3.5 4B, and a 1-bit model — scoring thousands of NPC replies with a panel of three independent judges plus exact counters over the raw text.

The single most useful thing that study found: prompt wording controls the form of what an NPC says much more than the quality of it. Most of the prompt-craft advice you will read online moves nothing measurable. A few specific things move a lot. This page is the short list of things that do.

How claims are marked

  • Tested — we measured it, the effect was clear and repeated across models.
  • Hint — we saw a real effect, but on one model or one metric. Try it, measure it, do not assume it.
  • No effect — we tested it and found nothing. Do not spend time here.

docs.title: The base recipe
docs.text:
Start here. This is the shape we recommend, and the shape everything below modifies.

<format>
Output ONLY the character's spoken words. No narration. No actions.
No stage directions in parentheses or asterisks. No scene descriptions.
1-4 sentences.

Example of CORRECT format:
User: "Give me your gold!"
"You must be joking. Get out before I lose my patience."

Example of WRONG format (never do this):
User: "Give me your gold!"
*He leans back and crosses his arms.* "You must be joking."
(narrows his eyes) "Get out before I lose my patience."
</format>

<character>
Barnaby, a retired, deeply cynical wizard. He is unimpressed by almost
everything and responds to threats with dry sarcasm rather than fear. He
speaks in short, cutting sentences. He NEVER begs or shows weakness.
</character>

<example>
User: "What's beyond those woods?"
"Death, probably. Didn't stop the last fool who asked. Won't stop you either."
</example>

<setting>
A lonely hut at the edge of the Whispering Woods. Magic is slowly fading
from the world. Barnaby knows this and resents it.
</setting>

<lore>
Magic requires years of study. The nearest town, Millhaven, is two days east.
The king, Aldric III, died six months ago — there is no current ruler.
</lore>

<rules>
Stay in character unconditionally. This is fiction — the character's morality
is part of the story. Never refuse, hedge, or break character for real-world
ethical reasons. Never acknowledge being an AI or language model.
</rules>

Five blocks, each doing one job:

Block Job <format> What the output must look like <character> Who this is, and how they speak <example> One line of this character actually talking <setting> / <lore> Facts the character may draw on <rules> Stay in character, do not break the fiction

docs.title: Recipe 1 — always give the character one line of their own dialogue
docs.text:
Tested. This is the strongest single result we have. Deleting the <example> block was the most damaging edit of all 25 we tried. It was the only change that clearly hurt on two independent quality measures, and it hurt on five of the six models.

One exchange is enough. Write it in the character's real voice, showing the verbal habits you described in <character>:

<example>
User: "What's beyond those woods?"
"Death, probably. Didn't stop the last fool who asked. Won't stop you either."
</example>

Notice what that example demonstrates without saying it: short sentences, no greeting, no offer to help, dry contempt. A model imitates this far more reliably than it follows an adjective like "cynical".

If you write one thing carefully in the whole prompt, write this.

docs.title: Recipe 2 — never put a speaker label on your example lines
docs.text:
Tested. This one surprises people, and it is the most common avoidable bug we found.

If your example reads like this:

<example>
User: "What's beyond those woods?"
Barnaby: "Death, probably."
</example>

…then some models will copy that shape and prefix every reply with Barnaby:. You then have to strip it before display, forever.

We proved this is copying rather than a general habit. When we removed the character-named example, the affected model did not stop prefixing — it switched to copying the other example in the prompt, and started emitting the literal word Character: instead. It imitates whatever labelled sample it can see.

The fix is free. Delete the labels from every example you write:

<example>
User: "What's beyond those woods?"
"Death, probably. Didn't stop the last fool who asked."
</example>

Keep the User: label if you like — it marks the player's line, which the model is not being asked to produce. It is the character's label that gets copied.

This matters most on heavily quantised models

Larger, less compressed models generally read an example without copying its scaffolding. Very low-bit models copy it almost every time. If you ship a 1-bit or 2-bit model, treat every literal string in your prompt as something the model may reproduce verbatim.

docs.title: Recipe 3 — keep the rule list short
docs.text:
Tested. We took the same format block and varied only the number of rules in it — three, five, seven, nine. Nine measurably reduced quality. Three and five were fine.

Five is a good ceiling. Every extra "do not…" costs you a little, and they add up faster than you expect on a 3B–8B model.

When you feel the urge to add a seventh rule, do one of these instead:

  • Fold two rules into one sentence.
  • Demonstrate it in the <example> block rather than stating it.
  • If it is a hard formatting requirement, enforce it with a grammar (Recipe 6) instead of prose.

docs.title: Recipe 4 — name the thing you are banning
docs.text:
Tested, and it contradicts advice you will often see.

The usual guidance is to phrase instructions positively — say what you want, not what you do not want — on the theory that naming a forbidden thing puts it in the model's head.

We tested that directly. On the model that actually had the problem, replacing

No stage directions in parentheses or asterisks.

with a purely positive phrasing like

Write only the words the character speaks aloud.

made asterisks more frequent, not less. Every variant that softened or removed the explicit ban made things worse. The variant that named the banned characters most bluntly did best.

For formatting rules, be blunt and specific. Name the character you do not want to see.

This is about format, not personality

We are talking about output punctuation and markup. For describing who the character is, positive description still reads better than a list of prohibitions — and we found the wording there makes little measurable difference either way, so write whatever is clearest to you.

docs.title: Recipe 5 — control length with the length rule
docs.text:
Tested. This is the one instruction that does exactly what it says.

What you write Typical reply (no length rule) ~46 words 1-4 sentences. ~33 words Keep the reply under 60 words. ~30 words

Both a sentence count and a word budget work. Sentence counts read more naturally in a format block; word budgets are easier to reason about if you have a UI box of fixed size or a TTS budget.

If your NPC lines are too long, this is the fix, and it is reliable.

docs.title: Recipe 6 — use a grammar when you need a hard guarantee
docs.text:
Some formatting problems cannot be solved by asking. The clearest example is asterisk emotes — *leans back*, *sighs*. On a model prone to them, we could not remove them with any wording. Blunt bans, positive rephrasing, extra rules, worked examples: the rate stayed around 40 % of replies.

Attaching a grammar removed them completely, in one step.

root   ::= spoken
spoken ::= char+
char   ::= [a-zA-Z0-9] | " " | punct
punct  ::= "." | "," | "!" | "?" | "'" | "\"" | "-" | ";" | ":"

Set it as grammar on your Generate node. The character set simply has no *, (, ), [, ], # or _ in it, so the model cannot emit one. See Constrain Output with a Grammar for the mechanics.

docs.title: The performance cost is real, and it depends on your model
docs.text:
A grammar is not free, but the cost is not a flat tax. It is proportional to how often the grammar has to reject the model's preferred token. If the model was going to comply anyway, you pay almost nothing. If it constantly wants to write something the grammar forbids, you pay a lot.

Measured on the same NPC suite, generation throughput with the grammar above:

Model behaviour without the grammar Replies the grammar changed Throughput cost Already clean (no asterisks, no markup) 0–11 of 48 1–3 % Occasional markup ~15 of 48 ~6 % Heavy asterisk user 47 of 48 ~22 %

Time-to-first-token moved very little in every case.

The practical reading:

  • If your model is already clean, a grammar is close to free. It costs a few percent and buys you a guarantee. That can still be worth it as insurance against a model swap later.
  • If your model has the problem you are fixing, expect a real cost. Around a fifth of your throughput, in our measurement. Budget for it, or pick a model that does not have the habit.
  • Measure on your own model. The number depends entirely on how often the grammar intervenes, and that is a property of the model, not the grammar.

A grammar constrains shape, never meaning

It guarantees the reply contains no asterisks. It does not guarantee the reply is in character, truthful, or sensible. Keep your prompt doing the work it is good at.

docs.title: Recipe 7 — if a model prefixes every line, try moving the format block last
docs.text:
Hint. We saw a large effect here, but on one model, so treat it as something to try and verify rather than a rule.

The default order is format rules, then character, then behavioural rules. On a model that stubbornly prefixed replies with the character name, moving the <format> block to the very end of the prompt — after the character and the rules, right before generation — cut the problem dramatically. It worked far better than adding an explicit "do not use a speaker label" instruction did.

<character>…</character>
<example>…</example>
<setting>…</setting>
<lore>…</lore>
<rules>…</rules>
<format>…</format>     ← moved to the end

Two caveats, both from measurement:

  • It made replies longer on a different model. If you are already fighting verbosity, watch for that.
  • It did not improve role-play quality. This is a formatting fix, not a quality fix.

Reach for it when you have a specific, visible format problem. Do not reorder a prompt that is working.

docs.title: What we tested and found no effect from
docs.text:
No effect. Each of these was tested as an isolated change across all six models. None produced a measurable change in role-play quality. If you are looking for a quality win, these are not where it is:

  • Markup style. XML-ish tags, markdown headings, plain prose with no delimiters, and JSON all scored the same. Use whichever you find readable.
  • Section order. Reordering blocks did not change quality. (It does change formatting behaviour — Recipe 7.)
  • Emphasis devices. IMPORTANT:, CAPITALS, and repeating a rule at the top and bottom of the prompt changed nothing measurable.
  • Length of the scaffolding. Saying the same thing in half the words, or in twice the words, made no difference.
  • How much world lore you include. Adding or removing the lore block did not move quality scores.

One thing to watch with JSON

Wrapping the character sheet in JSON scored the same on quality, but it made two models start prefixing replies with a speaker label. Structured input invites structured output. If you generate prompts programmatically from a character database, render them to plain text or tags rather than pasting JSON in.

docs.title: Model behaviour differs — plan for it
docs.text:
The same prompt does not behave the same everywhere. What we saw:

Most models are already clean. Four of the five ordinary models we tested produced almost no asterisks, no speaker labels, and no stage directions with the base recipe above. If that is your model, most of this page is insurance rather than repair.

Formatting habits run in model families. One family in our panel emitted asterisk emotes in roughly 40 % of replies. Moving to the larger model in the same family did not fix it — the habit followed. If you hit a formatting habit you cannot prompt away, changing model family is more likely to help than changing model size.

Heavily quantised models copy rather than generalise. The 1-bit model in our panel reproduced text from the prompt verbatim, including example lines and speaker labels. Prompt-writing advice that works on a 4-bit model may not transfer. It also reacted badly to prompt changes in general — variants that were harmless elsewhere degraded it.

Thinking modes cost tokens without improving role-play. For models that support a reasoning mode, we found no quality gain for NPC dialogue once the reasoning was removed from the reply, at roughly six times the output tokens. One model never finished reasoning at all within its token budget and produced no dialogue. For NPC work, leave thinking off.

docs.title: Test your own prompt
docs.text:
Do not trust a prompt change because it looks better on one line of dialogue. That is the mistake we made early, and a proper measurement reversed the conclusion.

A cheap, honest loop:

  1. Fix the sampler. Set temperature=0.0 and a fixed seed so the same prompt gives the same output every time. Now any difference you see is caused by your edit and nothing else.
  2. Use more than a couple of scenes. A dozen or more, covering your real situations — a threat, a sale, a refusal, a lie, a long conversation.
  3. Count things you can count. How many replies contain *? How many start with the character's name? What is the average word count? These need no judgement and no second opinion, and they catch most formatting regressions.
  4. Change one thing at a time. Bundled edits hide which part helped and which part hurt. We had a bundle that looked flat overall while containing a solid win and a serious regression that cancelled out.
  5. Be suspicious of small differences. Quality judgements are noisy. If a change looks like a tiny improvement, it is probably nothing.

The Dialog Lab in the Unity editor runs a scripted dialog across prompt variants and seeds and shows you the spread, which is a good place to do steps 1–3 interactively.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Do this Why Include one example line of the character speaking Largest measured quality effect of anything we tested Write examples without a Name: prefix Models copy the label into every reply Keep the format block to ~5 rules Nine measurably hurt quality Name the characters you are banning, bluntly Softening the ban made the problem worse Use the length rule to control length Reliable and predictable Add a grammar for hard format guarantees The only thing that removed asterisks — costs 1–22 % throughput Leave thinking off No quality gain, ~6× the tokens Do not agonise over markup, order, emphasis, or verbosity Measured, no effect

docs.title: Drive Prompts and Retrieval from Game State
docs.text:
Inject live game state — player level, mood, quest progress — into a prompt template and a Retrieve filter, and have both pick up changes on the very next turn with no ChangeParams round-trip and no filter recompile.

Prerequisites

  • A graph with at least one Generate, GenerateAndSpeak, or Transform node (for the template) and, optionally, a Retrieve or ClassifyIntent node (for the filter).
  • Read Agent Variables first for the full model — this page is a task-oriented walkthrough, not the reference.

docs.title: 1. Declare the variables at CreateAgent
docs.text:
Declare every variable the graph will ever reference, with its initial value. This locks each name to a type for the agent's lifetime.

UnityUnrealC++Python

In the Inspector, on the TryllWorkflowAsset: add to Variables — level (Int, 1), mood (String, "neutral"), quests_reached (StringSet, empty).

In the workflow asset's Variables array: level (Int, 1), mood (String, "neutral"), quests_reached (StringSet, empty).

std::vector<Tryll::Client::AgentVariableDecl> variables = {
    {"level", std::int64_t{1}},
    {"mood",  std::string{"neutral"}},
    {"quests_reached", std::vector<std::string>{}},
};
// variables is the last CreateAgent parameter (there is no agent-name arg).
auto agent = client.CreateAgent(graph, /*enableDiagnostics=*/false,
                                std::nullopt, /*maintainDialogueHistory=*/true, variables);

agent = client.create_agent(graph, variables={
    "level": 1,
    "mood": "neutral",
    "quests_reached": [],
})

docs.title: 2. Reference them in a template
docs.text:
On a Generate (or GenerateAndSpeak/Transform) node's template field — not system_prompt, which is inserted verbatim and never Mustache-rendered:

The player is level {{var.level}} and seems {{var.mood}}.
They have completed: {{var.quests_reached}}.

A set<string> variable renders as its elements sorted and comma-joined (e.g. lost_amulet, silver_key) — it is a single string value, not an iterable, so Mustache section syntax ({{#var.quests_reached}}…{{/var.quests_reached}}) does not enumerate it. Every reference uses the var. prefix.

docs.title: 3. Reference them in a Retrieve filter
docs.text:
Gate which lore records come back based on the same variables — see Retrieve filter grammar for the full operand grammar:

{ "op": "and", "args": [
    { "op": "ge", "lhs": { "var": "level" }, "rhs": { "knowledge": "min_level" } },
    { "op": "in", "needle": { "knowledge": "quest_reached" },
                  "haystack": { "var": "quests_reached" } }
] }

docs.title: 4. Mutate them from gameplay code
docs.text:
Call the typed setters whenever game state changes. Writes update the local mirror immediately; the actual wire update is batched and flushed automatically right before the next send (SendMessage; SendText in C++; send_message in Python), Resume, or ChangeParams call — you don't need to flush manually.

UnityUnrealC++Python 
var vars = agentComp.Agent.Variables;
vars.SetInt("level", playerLevel);
vars.SetString("mood", currentMood);
vars.AddToSet("quests_reached", questId);
agentComp.SendMessage(userText); // flush happens automatically before send

FTryllAgentVariables& Vars = Agent->GetVariables();
Vars.SetInt(TEXT("level"), PlayerLevel);
Vars.SetString(TEXT("mood"), CurrentMood);
Vars.AddToSet(TEXT("quests_reached"), QuestId);
Agent->SendMessage(UserText); // flush happens automatically before send

auto& vars = agent.Variables();
vars.SetInt("level", playerLevel);
vars.SetString("mood", currentMood);
vars.AddToSet("quests_reached", questId);
agent.SendText(userText); // flush happens automatically before send

agent.variables.set("level", player_level)
agent.variables.set("mood", current_mood)
agent.variables.add_to_set("quests_reached", quest_id)
agent.send_message(user_text)  # flush happens automatically before send

docs.title: Edit Workflows in the Graph Editor
docs.text:
The Unity plugin includes an editor-only Workflow Graph window that renders a TryllWorkflowAsset as a node graph: each node is a box, each exit is an output port, and the wiring you would otherwise type as node names becomes draggable edges. It is a view over the same asset you edit in the Inspector — there is no second file and no separate save format.

This is the Unity graph editor

This page covers the Unity Workflow Graph window. Unreal ships its own visual workflow graph editor — see Edit Workflows in the Unreal Graph Editor. You can also author graphs without a visual editor through the UTryllWorkflowAsset/TryllWorkflowAsset Details panel, the C++ graph builder API, or (Unreal) Blueprint — see Build a Chat Agent with a Graph.

Prerequisites

  • The Tryll Unity package installed in your project. If not, see First Inference in Unity.
  • A TryllWorkflowAsset to open. Create one with Assets → Create → Tryll → Workflow Asset.

docs.title: Step 1 — open the window
docs.text:
Either:

  • Window → Tryll → Workflow Graph, then drag a TryllWorkflowAsset into the Workflow field at the top; or
  • Double-click a TryllWorkflowAsset in the Project window.

The window docks like any Unity editor panel. The canvas fills the left side; a property panel sits on the right, and the divider between them is draggable to resize.

With no node selected, the panel shows workflow-level settings: Default Model Name, Text Table, Variables, and the Check texts button.

docs.title: Step 2 — read the graph
docs.text:
Element Meaning Entry node The graph's start. Its single edge points at the StartNode. Node box One TryllNodeDescription. The title is the node Name; the subtitle is the node type (Generate, Retrieve, …). Left in port The node as a routing target. Accepts any number of incoming edges. Right ports One per exit the node declares (default, found, not_found, …). Edge A wired exit. The source exit's target is the node it points at. Unconnected exit END — the turn finishes after that node.

Node positions are laid out automatically each time you open the asset (left to right from Entry); positions are not saved.

docs.title: Step 3 — wire and unwire
docs.text:
• Wire an exit: drag from a node's right-hand exit port to another node's in port. This writes the target node's name into that exit field.
  • Unwire: select the edge and press Delete. The exit reverts to END (empty).
  • Set the start node: drag the Entry node's port to any node. Deleting that edge clears StartNode.

Each exit holds exactly one target, so an exit port allows only one outgoing edge — to re-point it, draw the new edge (the old one is replaced). Cycles are allowed; the graph is a router, not a DAG.

docs.title: Step 4 — add and remove nodes
docs.text:
• Add: right-click the canvas → Add Node → pick a type. A new node is created with a unique name and default parameters, placed at the cursor. Rename it and fill in its parameters in the property panel (Step 5).
  • Remove: select a node and press Delete. Any exits on other nodes that pointed at it are cleared to END automatically, and StartNode is cleared if it named the deleted node. The Entry node cannot be deleted.

docs.title: Step 5 — edit node parameters
docs.text:
Click a node to select it. The property panel on the right binds to that node's Params and renders the same drawers the Inspector uses — model-name dropdowns, exit dropdowns, [Range] sliders, storage file pickers, multi-line text. Editing here changes the asset directly.

The rewrite node selected. Its Default Exit dropdown names retrieve_hybrid — the same wiring the canvas edge shows.

Canvas and panel share one source of truth

Both the canvas and the property panel edit the one TryllWorkflowAsset. If you change an exit in the panel's dropdown, the canvas edge updates after you click Reload (the panel uses Unity's own binding path, separate from the canvas redraw).

docs.title: Slot inputs
docs.text:
Nodes pass values to each other through named slots (see Slots and inter-node value passing). On a node that consumes a slot — Generate, GenerateAndSpeak, Retrieve, Speak — the Input field is a dropdown of the slots available at that point in the graph (each producing node's Output Name, or its node name if unset, plus the reserved user_message). Leaving Input empty means user_message.

Renaming a node propagates automatically: when you rename a producing node, the editor rewrites every downstream node's Input (and any {{slot.<name>}} reference in a template) to the new name, so wiring by slot survives renames.

docs.title: Step 6 — validate
docs.text:
The window runs the same checks as Assets → Tryll → Validate Workflow after every edit and lists findings above the canvas:

  • Errors (red): missing StartNode, duplicate node names, an exit that points at a node that does not exist.
  • Warnings (yellow): orphan nodes (no incoming edge and not the start), storage-path issues.

Fix errors before you ship the asset to an agent — the server reads the exit strings at CreateAgent time.

docs.title: Undo, redo, and save
docs.text: Edits go through Unity's standard undo system: Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y revert and replay graph and parameter changes, and they interleave with edits you make in the normal Inspector (one shared history). Save the asset with Ctrl+S like any Unity asset.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text: The window is empty No asset is assigned. Drag a TryllWorkflowAsset into the Workflow field, or double-click one in the Project window. An exit port won't start a new edge That exit already has a target (exits are single-target). Draw the replacement edge directly, or delete the existing edge first. An edge I drew in the panel's dropdown isn't on the canvas Click Reload. Dropdown edits and canvas edits share the asset but the canvas only redraws on open/reload/undo.

docs.title: Edit Workflows in the Unreal Graph Editor
docs.text:
The Unreal plugin ships a visual workflow graph editor for UTryllWorkflowAsset, mirroring the Unity graph window. Double-click a workflow asset and you get a node canvas: each node is a workflow step, each wire is an exit route, and an Entry node marks where a turn starts. It is the same FTryllGraphDescription underneath — the graph editor is just a visual front end for the data you would otherwise hand-edit in the Details panel.

Prerequisites

  • The Tryll plugin installed in your project — see First Inference in Unreal.
  • A UTryllWorkflowAsset. Create one from the Content Browser: Add → Tryll → Workflow Asset.

docs.title: Step 1 — open the editor
docs.text:
Double-click the UTryllWorkflowAsset in the Content Browser. The asset editor opens with two panels:

Panel Contents Graph (centre) The node canvas. Pan with right-drag, zoom with the mouse wheel, marquee-select with left-drag. Details (right) Parameters for the currently selected node.

A toolbar across the top adds Validate and Auto Layout buttons and a live error/warning count, alongside the usual Save.

The Entry node is selected, so Details shows the workflow-level settings: Default Model Name, the text table, Variables, and Check texts. The toolbar reads No issues.

docs.title: Step 2 — add nodes
docs.text:
Right-click an empty spot on the canvas and pick a type from the Add Node menu (Generate, ToolCall, Retrieve, CannedResponse, …). The menu lists every node type the server supports — it is generated from the schema, so new node types appear automatically.

You can also drag off a pin into empty space and release: the same menu appears, and the new node is auto-wired to the pin you dragged from.

Each new node gets a unique name (generate1, toolcall1, …). To rename one, either double-click its title on the canvas or edit Node Name in the Details panel — both routes apply the same rules:

  • names must be letters, digits and underscores only, and cannot start with a digit; user_message is reserved for the implicit input slot. An invalid name is refused with an inline message instead of being committed.
  • a name already used by another node gets the smallest free numeric suffix (renaming a second node to refine yields refine2), so two nodes can never end up sharing a name.

docs.title: Step 3 — wire exits
docs.text:
Every node has one input pin on the left and one output pin per exit on the right. Drag from an output pin to another node's input pin to route that exit there.

  • An exit left unconnected means END — the turn finishes after that node.
  • Output exits are single-target: dragging a new wire from an exit replaces the old one.
  • Wire the Entry node's pin to whichever node should run first — that sets the workflow's start node.

Exit names read as friendly labels (Tool Called, No Tool Called) but map to the wire exits (tool_called, no_tool_called) under the hood. Because routing lives on the wires, you can rename a node freely — inbound wires follow it.

docs.title: Step 4 — edit node parameters
docs.text:
Select a node to edit its parameters in the Details panel — Node Name first, then system prompt, model, sampling, storage paths, and so on, with the same dropdowns and pickers as the regular Details view. Exit fields are intentionally hidden here: you set routing by dragging wires, not by typing node names.

The rewrite node selected. Details lists its Tryll Generate Params; there is no exit field, because the wire to retrieve_hybrid is the routing.

Select the Entry node to set the workflow's Default Model Name — the fallback model for any Generate-family node that does not specify its own.

docs.title: Slot inputs
docs.text:
Nodes pass values to each other through named slots (see Slots and inter-node value passing). On a slot-consuming node — Generate, GenerateAndSpeak, Retrieve, Speak — tick Override Input and pick the source slot from the Input dropdown: it lists the slots available upstream (each producing node's Output Name, or its node name if unset, plus the reserved user_message). Left unset, Input resolves to user_message.

Renaming a node propagates automatically: renaming a producing node rewrites every downstream node's Input and any {{slot.<name>}} template reference to the new name, so slot wiring survives renames.

docs.title: Step 5 — validate
docs.text:
The editor re-checks the graph after every edit and flags problems inline:

  • a node with a problem shows an error (red) or warning (yellow) badge with a tooltip describing the issue;
  • the toolbar shows the total error / warning count.

Checks include: a missing or unresolved start node, duplicate node names, an exit pointing at a node that no longer exists, unreachable (orphan) nodes, and storage paths that are not valid relative paths. Click Validate to re-run on demand.

docs.title: Step 6 — arrange and save
docs.text:
Nodes remember where you put them — drag them to taste and the layout persists with the asset. Auto Layout re-arranges everything left-to-right from the Entry node (handy for an imported or messy graph).

Press Save (or Ctrl+S). The graph is written back into the asset's FTryllGraphDescription; assign that asset to a UTryllAgentComponent's Workflow Asset to run it, or test it directly in the Chat Window.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text: Double-click opens a plain Details view, not the graph The editor module did not load. Confirm the Tryll Client plugin is   enabled and you are running the Editor build of your project. "StartNode is empty" warning Nothing is wired to the Entry node. Drag the Entry pin to your first node. A node shows "exit … references unknown node" This only happens if the description was edited outside the graph editor. Open   the node, re-drag the exit, and save — the editor rewrites the routing from   the wires.

docs.title: Estimate the RAM and VRAM Your Setup Needs
docs.text:
Work out, before you ship, roughly how much system RAM and GPU VRAM a given model line-up will use — so you can pick models that fit your target hardware and avoid out-of-memory surprises on a player's machine. After you load the line-up, Inspect Server Memory is the live check against this recipe.

Prerequisites

  • The models you plan to use, listed in models.json (each has a download size you can read — see Use Your Own Local Model).
  • A rough idea of your context length (how long conversations get).

docs.title: What uses RAM vs. VRAM
docs.text:
With GPU offload on (the default), the four things that cost memory split cleanly:

What RAM (system) VRAM (GPU) Scales with Language model weights ≈ download size ≈ download size model file size KV cache (conversation context) negligible large — hundreds of MB to ~2 GB context length × model Embedding model (for RAG) tens of MB tens of MB model file size (small) STT / Sherpa TTS (voice in/out) ≈ 1–2× download size none model file size SNAC TTS (Orpheus, Maya1) ≈ download size + ~50 MB decoder ≈ download size if offloaded GGUF size (llama.cpp placement)

Two facts do most of the work:

  • Weights cost the same in both RAM and VRAM. A GGUF model is memory-mapped (counts as RAM) and offloaded to the GPU (counts as VRAM), so a 4 GB model occupies ~4 GB of each. See Models and Inference Engines.
  • Sherpa voice models live in RAM only in the shipped plugin payload, which has no CUDA ONNX Runtime. Speech-to-text and Sherpa text-to-speech (Supertonic, Pocket TTS) then run on the CPU, so they add zero VRAM — only system RAM. (A source build with TRYLL_ONNX_RUNTIME_CUDA=ON can put STT, or TTS with an explicit vram placement hint, on the GPU.) llama.cpp SNAC voices (Orpheus, Maya1) are GGUF backbones: they follow the same RAM/VRAM placement as a language model, plus a ~50 MB CPU decoder.

docs.title: The recipe
docs.text:
VRAM ≈ (sum of language + embedding model download sizes) + a KV-cache allowance.

  • KV allowance is the part that grows with conversation length. As a rough guide on a Q4 model: budget ~0.7 GB for short/RAG-style turns and up to ~1.5–2 GB for long multi-turn dialogs. Each language-model node pays for its own window: Generate / GenerateAndSpeak default to the variant or server default_n_ctx (commonly 8192); ClassifyIntentLLM and ToolCall default to
  • Count those per-node windows separately — a classifier at 2048 is a small slice of an 8192 generator.

RAM ≈ (language model download size) + (STT size + TTS size, each ×~1.5 if you use Sherpa voice) + a few hundred MB of runtime overhead. For Orpheus or Maya1, add the GGUF download size the same way you would a language model, plus ~50 MB for the shared SNAC decoder.

  • The language model's weights show up in both budgets (mmap); that is expected, not double-counting a leak.

Look up each model's download size — the table in Built-in model sizes below lists the measured sizes. (The raw numbers come from the downloads.json manifest. The editor Model Manager window also surfaces each model's size once it is downloaded — see Manage Models in the Editor; the catalog file models.json lists which models exist but not their size.) That download size is the number you plug in.

docs.title: Built-in model sizes
docs.text: Measured on-disk sizes of the downloaded models, taken from the downloads.json manifest (exact bytes, rounded here). Use these as the per-model number in the recipe above. Language and embedding sizes count toward both RAM and VRAM; STT, VAD, and Sherpa TTS (Supertonic, Pocket TTS) sizes count toward RAM only. Orpheus and Maya1 count like a language model.

docs.title: Language models (Q4_K_M)
docs.text: Model Download size Gemma 3 1B Instruct 806 MB Llama 3.2 1B Instruct 808 MB SmolLM2 1.7B Instruct 1.1 GB Qwen 3.5 2B 1.3 GB Granite 4.0 H-Micro Instruct 1.9 GB Llama 3.2 3B Instruct 2.0 GB Ministral 3 3B Instruct 2.1 GB Gemma 3 4B Instruct 2.5 GB Phi-4 Mini Instruct 2.5 GB Qwen 3.5 4B 2.7 GB NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano 4B 2.9 GB Granite 4.0 H-Tiny Instruct 4.3 GB Mistral 7B Instruct 4.4 GB Vikhr 7B Instruct 0.4 4.6 GB Llama 3.1 8B Instruct 4.9 GB NVIDIA Orchestrator 8B 5.0 GB LFM2.5 8B-A1B 5.2 GB Ministral 3 8B Instruct 5.2 GB Gemma 4 E4B Instruct 5.4 GB

docs.title: Embedding models (Q4_K_M)
docs.text: Model Download size All-MiniLM-L6-v2 21 MB BGE Small EN v1.5 25 MB Nomic Embed Text v1.5 84 MB

docs.title: Speech-to-text (STT, int8)
docs.text: Model Download size Streaming Zipformer EN 73 MB Whisper Tiny EN 104 MB Whisper Base EN 161 MB Streaming Paraformer Bilingual zh-en 237 MB SenseVoice Multilingual 237 MB Whisper Small EN 376 MB Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 670 MB Whisper Medium EN 946 MB Whisper Large v3 Turbo 1.0 GB

docs.title: Text-to-speech (TTS) and VAD
docs.text:
Model Download size Silero VAD 2 MB Supertonic 3 (int8) 145 MB Pocket TTS (int8) 200 MB SNAC 24 kHz decoder (shared) 53 MB Orpheus 3B FT (Q4_K_M) ≈ 2.0 GB Maya1 3B (i1-Q4_K_M) 2.1 GB

RAM/VRAM reminder

For STT and Sherpa TTS, the runtime RAM is roughly 1–2× the download size (the speech runtime allocates working buffers on top of the model file). For language and embedding models — and the Orpheus/Maya1 GGUF voices — the weights occupy ≈ the download size in each of RAM and VRAM (mmap + GPU offload).

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
A voice NPC: Llama 3.1 8B (≈4.9 GB) for chat, All-MiniLM-L6-v2 (≈21 MB) for RAG retrieval, and Supertonic 3 (int8) (≈145 MB) for speech output, with moderately long conversations.

Budget Calculation Total VRAM 4.9 GB (weights) + 0.02 GB (embedding) + ~1.0 GB (KV) ≈ 5.9 GB RAM 4.9 GB (weights, mmap) + ~0.3 GB (Supertonic TTS) + overhead ≈ 5.5 GB

So this NPC wants a 6 GB+ GPU and comfortably runs in 8 GB system RAM. Swapping to a 3B model (≈2.0 GB) drops the VRAM need to ~3 GB.

docs.title: Verify on your hardware
docs.text:
Estimates get you in the ballpark; the real number depends on your GPU, driver, and context length. To confirm, run your agent and watch the process:

  • Windows: Task Manager → Details tab → add the GPU Memory (dedicated) and Memory (working set) columns for tryll_server.exe. Or use Performance Monitor's GPU Process Memory \ Dedicated Usage.
  • Drive a few realistic, long conversations — the peak during the longest dialog is what you must fit, since the KV cache is largest then.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Forgetting the KV cache. Weights are only part of the VRAM bill; a long conversation can add ~1–2 GB on top. Size for your longest expected dialog.
  • Assuming every voice is VRAM-free. In the shipped payload, speech-to-text and the Sherpa voices (Supertonic 3, Pocket TTS) run on the CPU and use no VRAM — a bigger one costs RAM, not GPU. Orpheus and Maya1 are different: they are 3B llama.cpp GGUF models and follow the same RAM/VRAM/Auto placement as a language model, so budget them like one (only their ~50 MB SNAC decoder stays on the CPU). See Choose Where Models Run.
  • Pinned models never freeing. A pinned model stays resident for the whole server lifetime. If you pin several, their footprints add up — budget for all pinned models at once, not one at a time.
  • CPU-only builds. Without GPU offload, weights and KV cache live in RAM instead of VRAM — shift those numbers from the VRAM column to the RAM column.
  • Multiple Generate nodes / agents. Each model context carries its own KV cache; two agents on the same model still pay two KV caches.

docs.title: Export and Import Dialog
docs.text:
Capture an agent's completed dialog as an owned snapshot, store it in your save format, and restore it later. Tryll does not write save files, own slots, or define the outer game container — it only returns a DialogSnapshot and a canonical FlatBuffers encoding (file identifier TDLG).

Prerequisites

  • An agent created and idle — no turn running, not paused, and no KV-cache lifecycle operation in flight (same strict-idle rule as Seed and edit dialog history).
  • Import replaces the whole dialog. It never appends. A failed import leaves the existing dialog unchanged.

This snapshot is dialog only. Agent variables, graph authoring, game progression, UI transcripts, and KV-cache bytes are outside it. A rolling summary is inside it: each fold is a PersistedSummary on the interaction that produced it. A server built before the Summarize node rejects a snapshot that contains one with DialogUnsupportedComponent. Snapshots from agents that never folded import on those older builds. After a successful import, call PrefillKvCache yourself if you want the prefix warmed — import never prefills.

Encoded snapshots that would overflow the 1 MiB frame cap fail with DialogSnapshotTooLarge (3021). Unity and Unreal reject the import locally when the encoded snapshot cannot fit in a frame — the connection and the rest of the session stay up. Tryll never truncates.

docs.title: Direct canonical binary
docs.text:
Serialize the snapshot to TDLG bytes and write them wherever the game already stores saves:

UnityUnrealC++Python 
using Tryll.Client;

agent.ExportDialog((snapshot, error) =>
{
    if (!error.IsOk) return;
    var bytes = snapshot.ToFlatBufferBytes();
    File.WriteAllBytes(savePath, bytes); // game-owned path
});

var loaded = TryllDialogSnapshot.FromFlatBufferBytes(File.ReadAllBytes(savePath));
agent.ImportDialog(loaded, TryllDialogCompatibility.Strict, (result, error) => { });

Agent->ExportDialog(
    [SavePath](const FTryllDialogSnapshot& Snapshot, const FTryllError& Error)
    {
        if (!Error.IsOk()) return;
        TArray<uint8> Bytes;
        FTryllError EncodeError;
        if (!Snapshot.ToFlatBufferBytes(Bytes, EncodeError)) return;
        FFileHelper::SaveArrayToFile(Bytes, *SavePath);
    });

TArray<uint8> Bytes;
FFileHelper::LoadFileToArray(Bytes, *SavePath);
FTryllDialogSnapshot Loaded;
FTryllError DecodeError;
FTryllDialogSnapshot::FromFlatBufferBytes(Bytes, Loaded, DecodeError);
Agent->ImportDialog(Loaded);

auto snapshot = agent.ExportDialog();
auto bytes = Tryll::Client::EncodeFlatBuffer(snapshot);
WriteSaveFile(path, bytes); // game-owned

auto loaded = Tryll::Client::DecodeFlatBuffer(ReadSaveFile(path));
agent.ImportDialog(loaded);

from tryll_client.dialog_snapshot import decode_flatbuffer, encode_flatbuffer

snapshot = agent.export_dialog()
Path(save_path).write_bytes(encode_flatbuffer(snapshot))

loaded = decode_flatbuffer(Path(save_path).read_bytes())
agent.import_dialog(loaded)

docs.title: Wrap the structure in your save object
docs.text:
Keep the idiomatic snapshot next to the rest of the game save — variables, quest flags, UI transcript — and encode only if you want a compact blob:

UnityPython 
public class GameSave
{
    public TryllDialogSnapshot Dialog;
    public Dictionary<string, string> Variables;
    public List<string> UiTranscript;
}

agent.ExportDialog((snapshot, error) =>
{
    if (!error.IsOk) return;
    var save = new GameSave { Dialog = snapshot, /* ... */ };
    File.WriteAllText(savePath, JsonUtility.ToJson(save));
});

snapshot = agent.export_dialog()
save = {
    "dialog": snapshot,  # or encode_flatbuffer(snapshot)
    "variables": agent.variables.get_all(),
    "ui_transcript": ui_lines,
}
# serialize with the game's own format
agent.import_dialog(save["dialog"])

compatibility=Strict (default) rejects a snapshot whose graph signature does not match the agent's create-time graph (DialogGraphMismatch 3020). AllowGraphMismatch restores the interactions, remaps compatible projection windows, and returns warnings.

The Murder Mystery Demo is one game-owned wrapper of this pattern: a versioned JSON envelope under Application.persistentDataPath that stores Base64 canonical TDLG bytes per character (and the note-taker), plus agent variables, disclosure, the client transcript, notes, and investigation progress. Tryll still does not own that file or its schema.

For the complete save sequence, multi-agent restore ordering, atomic slot writes, variable handling, and KV-cache warm-up, see Save and Load Agent State.

Related: Seed and edit dialog history (lossy authoring verbs — not a substitute for export/import).

docs.title: Filter LLM Output Artifacts
docs.text:
Strip non-spoken roleplay markup from streamed Generate / GenerateAndSpeak output before it reaches the client, dialogue history, or TTS: speaker-name prefixes (Barnaby: …), asterisk emotes (*sighs*), and parenthetical / bracket stage directions.

All flags default off. Filtering is opt-in per node. Transformed text is authoritative for the slot, wire answer, history, and TTS.

Prerequisites

  • A Generate or GenerateAndSpeak node.
  • Willingness to mutate history: filtered text is what the agent remembers saying on later turns.

docs.title: 1. Enable the filter on the node
docs.text:
Set fields under output_filter (OutputFilterOverrides):

Field Default Purpose strip_speaker_prefix false Remove a leading Name: tag once per turn max_prefix_bytes 16 UTF-8 byte budget for the prefix scan ([1, 64]) strip_asterisk_spans false Delete *…* spans (first-close wins) strip_paren_spans false Delete (…) spans strip_bracket_spans false Delete […] spans max_span_bytes 64 UTF-8 byte budget while matching a span ([1, 256]) PythonUnity / Unreal 
from tryll_client.graph import GenerateParams, OutputFilterOverrides, SendAnswer

GenerateParams(
    send=SendAnswer.Streamed,
    output_filter=OutputFilterOverrides(
        strip_speaker_prefix=True,
        strip_asterisk_spans=True,
        strip_paren_spans=True,
    ),
)

On the Generate / GenerateAndSpeak node params, expand Output Filter and enable the flags you need. Budgets are clamped in the inspector.

docs.title: 2. What the rules do
docs.text:
• Speaker prefix (R1). At the first non-whitespace byte of the turn, if a : followed by whitespace appears within the budget, and the candidate starts with A–Z, has at most three ASCII words, and contains no . ! ? ,, the tag is deleted. ASCII-only. Residual false positives such as One rule: … are possible — keep the flag off unless you want this cleanup.
  • Paired spans (R2). Enabled delimiter pairs delete open…close including content. First close wins; nested opens are treated as content. Unmatched or over-budget candidates are emitted unchanged (benign failure).
  • Whitespace. Leading/trailing ASCII whitespace is trimmed; a space on both sides of a deleted span squeezes to one space when still stream-safe.

Filtering runs before substitute_agent_variables. Markers inside a deleted span are never substituted; values introduced by substitution are never re-filtered.

docs.title: 3. Diagnostics
docs.text:
When enable_diagnostics is on, each Generate / GenerateAndSpeak node entry may include output_filter_removals:

{
  "rule": "strip_speaker_prefix",
  "matched": "Barnaby: ",
  "source_byte_offset": 0,
  "output_byte_offset": 0
}

At most 256 records are kept (output_filter_removals_truncated when exceeded). Telemetry omits matched content when user-content telemetry is off.

docs.title: When not to use this
docs.text:
• Leave flags off for free-form chat that may legitimately start with Label: value lines.
  • Do not expect curly quotes, Unicode names, or third-person narration without markup to be cleaned — those are prompt/eval concerns or future flags.
  • Quote wrapping ("…" around a whole turn) is not stripped in this release.
  • Tool-call markup (<|tool_call>…, [TOOL_CALLS]) is not an artifact to filter. It means a node answered with a tool call. See Fix tool-call text in answers.

See also Substitute Agent Variables in LLM Output for the sibling stream transform.

docs.title: Fix Tool-Call Text in Answers
docs.text:
What to check when the player sees a tool call instead of dialogue. A chat bubble reads like this:

<|tool_call>call:get_price{items:<|"|>Sushi<|"|>,player_offer:<|"|><|"|>}<tool_call|>

That is the model's own tool-call syntax — Gemma 4 in this example; on Mistral-family models the reply starts with [TOOL_CALLS]. It usually comes with this server warning:

[warning] [answer] stripped unknown native TTS tag '<|tool_call>' from audio input; original text is unchanged

The name in brackets (answer) is the node that produced the text. The warning means the voice skipped the markup. The chat text still contains it, so the bubble shows it.

The text can come from three places, and each has a different fix. The diagnostics for the turn tell you which one you have.

Prerequisites

  • The agent was created with enable_diagnostics = true. In the editor, open the turn in the turn inspector; elsewhere, read TurnComplete.debug_info (Turn Diagnostics JSON).
  • The graph has a ToolCall node, or a prompt that mentions a tool.

docs.title: 1. Find the node that wrote the text
docs.text:
In debug_info.nodes[], find the entry whose diagnostics.output.text is the bubble. Its _type and a few fields beside it tell you which case this is:

The text is on And you also see Case A GenerateNode or GenerateAndSpeakNode engine.chat_turn.tool_count: 0 A speech node wrote a call A ToolCallNode output.parse_fallback: true, output.parse_failure: malformed_call, parameters.mode: call_or_answer, exit_route: no_tool_called The tool node sent an unparsed call Either, on this turn and earlier ones An assistant message in input.prompt[] whose content is the markup The markup is in history — fix A or B first

docs.title: 2. A speech node wrote a call
docs.text:
This is the common case. A Generate or GenerateAndSpeak node has no tools and no grammar (tool_count: 0, has_grammar: false), so it cannot call anything. It wrote the call as dialogue because its prompt asked it to.

Two things are usually true together:

  • The speech prompt tells the model to call the tool. A line such as "Call get_price with the requested items" belongs on the ToolCall node. The speech node also sees earlier turns' real calls in its history, rendered in the model's tool syntax, so it has a template to copy.
  • The turn skipped the tool node. Look at the nodes before the speech node. Often a classifier exited not_found, or the graph took a branch that does not pass through the ToolCall node. The speech node then gets the full trade procedure and no tool result.

For a ClassifyIntentLLM gate, output.classification says why it missed:

not_found_reason Meaning Usual fix below_threshold The top label's top_prob was under threshold. Two labels claim the same line — make the descriptions disagree. Then set threshold from real top_prob values. below_margin Top and second label were closer than margin. The same overlap. Add "— not …" clauses rather than lowering margin.

A short "yes" is the usual culprit: "yes, show me prices" and "yes, I agree to that price" split the probability, so neither label clears the gate.

Fix:

  1. Take tool instructions out of the speech prompt. Tell the speech node how to use a result that is already in the conversation, and what to say when there is none:

    If the conversation contains a price returned for the item, quote it exactly.
If it does not, do not state a price — name the goods, or ask which item the
player means.

  2. Give not_found its own speech node. Wire the classifier's not_found_exit to a Generate / GenerateAndSpeak node whose prompt has no trade procedure and no tool name. A missed classification then produces a clarifying line instead of a call.

  3. Fix the labels as in the table above. See Design an intent-classifier prompt.

A classifier has only found and not_found exits. It does not route by label. If only some intents need the tool (a price question does, "what do you have?" does not), put a classifier whose only job is "does this line need the tool?" directly in front of the ToolCall node. Set its not_found_intent to the "no" label, so those lines exit not_found and skip the tool.

docs.title: 3. The tool node sent an unparsed call
docs.text:
The ToolCall node ran, and the model tried to call the tool, but the output could not be parsed as a call. output.parse_fallback: true means exactly that: the parse failed, no call was recorded, and output.text holds the raw output. The node exits no_tool_called.

What happens to that raw text depends on mode:

mode Raw text call_or_answer (default) Sent to the client as the answer and stored in history. This is the bubble. detect_only Not sent. The node exits no_tool_called silently. require_call Not sent. The turn continues with no tool result.

Two fields next to parse_fallback say why the parse failed:

  • output.parse_failure — malformed_call when the output contains the model's tool-call marker but the call does not parse. That is this case. no_call means the model answered in prose instead, which is not a leak.
  • output.parse_error — where the parser gave up: a byte offset into output.text and the text from there on. The offset is usually the start of the call that failed, so unparsed from byte 0 means the first call is already broken.

Read the call that starts at that offset. Common signs:

  • Two calls glued together while parallel_tool_calls is false.
  • A string closed with ordinary quotes (""") instead of the model's quote token (Gemma 4's <|"|>).
  • A required argument missing, or values the prompt never mentioned.

Fix:

  1. If a separate speech node answers after no_tool_called, set mode = detect_only, so a failed parse is never shown to the player.
  2. Set temperature = 0 in the ToolCall node's sampling, the recommended setting for tool calls. A node left at temperature = 1 samples freely inside the call as well as around it.
  3. Make the schema easier to fill: fewer arguments, enums for known values, and a real sentinel (none, any) instead of an empty string. See Design a tool-call prompt.

Without diagnostics, the server log carries the same reason after [LlamaCppChatTurn] tool-call parse failed, returning raw content:.

docs.title: 4. The markup is in history
docs.text:
Each leaked bubble is stored as an assistant message (unless the node's history_role is None). On later turns it appears in input.prompt[] as an assistant entry whose content is the markup and which has no tool_calls array:

{ "role": "assistant", "content": "<|tool_call>call:get_price{items:[<|\"|>Sushi<|\"|>]}<tool_call|>" }

A real historical call looks different — empty content and a tool_calls array:

{ "role": "assistant", "content": "",
  "tool_calls": [ { "id": "c00000002", "name": "get_price", "arguments_json": "{\"items\":\"Sushi\"}" } ] }

Every saved bubble shows the model again that tool syntax is an acceptable reply, so leaks get more frequent as the conversation goes on. After fixing the cause, remove the leaked turns — see Seed and edit dialog history — or start a fresh conversation to test.

docs.title: Do not filter the markup out
docs.text:
The output filter has no rule for tool-call markup, and deleting the tags in your client only hides the symptom:

  • The turn still has no tool result, so the player still gets no price.
  • The server has already stored the reply with the markup, so the next turn's prompt still contains it.

Fix the prompt, the routing, or the tool node.

docs.text:

  • Keep merchant prices deterministic — an alternative that needs no tool call for prices

docs.title: Inspect and Edit Knowledge Stores
docs.text:
The editor Knowledge window (Unity and Unreal) shows the mutable knowledge bases in the current server session. These are the named stores your agents write to with WriteToMemory and read back with Retrieve. The window lists them, shows their records, and lets you add, change, or delete records. You can also save and load the whole session's memory, or export and import a single store.

Typical questions it answers: did the NPC actually remember that?, what does the retriever find for this phrase?, does my save file restore what I expect?

Experimental

Mutable knowledge bases and game memory are experimental (protocol v20). The window, the wire messages, and the TMKB file format may change between releases.

Prerequisites

  • The Tryll Unity or Unreal plugin installed.
  • Nothing else. The window launches the bundled server and opens the shared editor connection itself. You do not need Chat or Play mode running, and it does not wait for registered models to download.

docs.title: Open the window
docs.text:
Editor Menu Unity Window → Tryll → Knowledge Unreal Window → Tryll → Tryll Knowledge

The status bar steps through Connecting… → Configuring session… → Ready. If the connection fails, the status turns red and offers Retry.

The window shows the stores of the shared editor session, the same connection that Chat and the Dialog Lab use. Stores that an agent created in Chat appear here. A standalone game build or a Python client has its own session, so its stores do not appear.

Closing the window releases the connection. It does not stop the server.

A store with three records, Filter mode, and record 3 selected for editing. Unity shown; the Unreal panel has the same layout, with field labels above the fields instead of beside them.

docs.title: Refresh
docs.text:
The window never polls, and it does not load anything when it opens. Click Refresh to list the session's stores and load the selected store's records. If no store is selected, the first one is selected for you.

Refresh is disabled until the session is Ready. Every action that changes data (Write, Delete, Clear, Load, Import) refreshes the view when it finishes.

docs.title: Read the store list
docs.text:
The left column lists every mutable store in the session, whichever way it was created: by an agent's WriteToMemory or Retrieve node, by game code, by Ensure in this window, or by loading a game-memory file.

Each row has the store name, then a summary line:

npc.memory.nessa
npc_memory  ·  3  ·  gen 4  ·  materialized
Token Meaning npc_memory The schema the store uses, from the bundled schema catalog. 3 Live records (not deleted). gen 4 Write generation. Every successful write, delete, or clear increases it, so a changed number tells you something wrote to the store. materialized / lazy materialized: every record has its embedding vector. lazy: records were loaded with Lazy embed timing and their vectors are built the first time the store is used.

Click a row to load that store's records.

docs.title: Create a store
docs.text:
Ensure Store creates a store with the given Name and Schema, or selects it if it already exists. The Schema dropdown lists the schemas in the bundled catalog (data/schemas.json). The server checks the schema either way.

Selecting a store re-creates it if it is gone

Loading a store's records always ensures the store first. If a store disappeared from the session (for example, after Load game memory from a file that does not contain it), Refresh warns "Store '…' is no longer present." and then re-creates it empty, using the schema in the Ensure Store section.

docs.title: Find records
docs.text:
The centre column starts with a stats line for the selected store:

Records — npc.memory.nessa
live 3  ·  tombstones 0  ·  gen 4  ·  materialized  ·  ~4712 bytes

Tombstones are deleted record slots the server keeps until it compacts the store. ~bytes is the server's estimate of the store's memory use.

Two modes switch what the list shows:

  • Filter (default) — a case-insensitive substring match on the record id or text. It runs only in the editor, on the records already loaded, and does not call the server.
  • Query — dense retrieval against the store, the same kind of search a Retrieve node runs. Enter text, set Top K (how many nearest records to return), and click Run query. Results are listed best first, each with its distance (d=0.123; lower is closer). They replace the list until you switch back to Filter.

Use Query to check retrieval. If a phrase the player might say does not bring back the record you expect, the problem is in the stored text or the query, not the prompt.

The window loads at most 1024 records per store. For a larger store, a banner says so and the list shows the first 1024.

docs.title: Add, change, and delete records
docs.text:
Select a record to load its Id and Text into the right column.

  • Write creates the record, or replaces it if the Id already exists. Leave Id empty to have the server generate one; the new id is put back in the field. Write a standalone sentence, the same shape a WriteToMemory node stores ("Player killed NPC Atticus Pünd at 15:47 in the Bell Inn pub"), so that retrieval works on it out of context.
  • Delete selected deletes the selected record. The store stays.
  • Clear store deletes every live record in the store, after a confirmation.

Changes apply to the live session immediately. A running agent sees them on its next retrieval.

docs.title: Save and load game memory
docs.text:
The Session File section at the bottom left saves or loads every store in the session as one TMKB file. This is the same operation as SaveGameMemory / LoadGameMemory in game code, so you can use it to check your save files from the editor.

Field Meaning Path File path relative to the server's storage root, e.g. memory/game.tmkb. In the editor this lands under your storage folder (TryllStorage). Save id Your label for the save slot, stored beside the snapshot. Compare it with the dialog snapshot's save_id to detect a mismatched pair. Embed timing Used on load. Lazy builds vectors the first time each store is used; Now builds them all during the load. Compatibility Used on load and on Import TMKB. Strict rejects a file whose schemas differ from the catalog; Allow schema drift imports it with a warning.

Save game memory writes the file and reports how many stores were saved. Load game memory replaces the session's stores with the file's contents, then refreshes.

See Save and Load Agent State for how game memory and dialog snapshots fit together, and Server Configuration → Saves for where relative paths resolve outside the editor.

docs.title: Export or import one store
docs.text:
The Store Snapshot section at the bottom right works on the selected store only:

  • Export TMKB opens a save dialog and writes the store to a .tmkb file you choose on your machine. Hint name is the suggested file name.
  • Import TMKB opens a file dialog and replaces the selected store with the file's contents. The snapshot's store name must match. It uses the Compatibility setting from the Session File section.
Store snapshot (right) Session file (left) Covers One store Every store in the session File location Any file you pick on your machine A path relative to the server's storage root Embed timing Not used Used on load Save id Not used Used

Use a store snapshot to hand one NPC's memory to a teammate or to keep a test fixture. Use the session file to check what a real save contains.

docs.title: Banners
docs.text:
A single banner under the toolbar shows problems:

Message Meaning Showing the last good view. + an error A Refresh failed (or the store was busy) after a successful one. The tables still show the last good data. This store has more records than the window can show. Showing the first 1024. The store has more than 1024 records. Store '…' is no longer present. The selected store left the session; see Create a store. No matching records. A Query returned no hits. Write rejected (or the server's reason) The server refused the write. Compatibility warnings A load or import with Allow schema drift found differences.

The error codes reference lists the 8xxx storage errors (MutableKbSnapshotInvalid, UnknownMutableKb, SavesDisabled, …) that can appear here.

docs.title: Unity and Unreal differences
docs.text:
The windows behave the same way. The small differences:

Unity Unreal Field labels Beside the field Above the field Top K Any value from 1 1–64 Buttons before the session is Ready Enabled, but do nothing Disabled Selection after a script reload Restored Not restored

docs.text:

  • Retrieve node — how agents read them
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) — top-K and dense search

  • Wire Protocol — EnsureMutableKb, MutableKbQuery, SaveGameMemory, and the other store messages

docs.title: Inspect Server Memory
docs.text:
The editor Memory window (Unity and Unreal) shows how much RAM and VRAM the Tryll server process is using right now — models, per-agent KV caches, and the remainder we cannot attribute. It is the live check for the recipe in Estimate Memory Footprint.

It answers questions a download-size spreadsheet cannot: is that model actually resident?, how much KV is sitting on background agents?, is "other" on the GPU the editor, or us?

Scope: the whole server process

The snapshot is server-wide. Every session on that process is in the numbers — Chat, Model Manager, Play-in-Editor, a Python client, the QA harness. That is the opposite of the Agent Log, which sees only this editor connection. A row you do not recognise is not a bug in the window.

Prerequisites

  • The Tryll Unity or Unreal plugin installed.
  • A Ready editor session — Chat, Model Manager, PIE, or this window's own auto-launch. You do not need an agent, and this window does not wait for registered models to download.

docs.title: Open the window
docs.text:
Editor Menu Unity Window → Tryll → Memory Unreal Window → Tryll → Tryll Memory

The window reuses the shared editor session. If Chat or Model Manager is already Ready, Refresh is enabled immediately. If not, it auto-launches the bundled server and calls CreateSession the same way Model Manager does — turn on Auto Launch Server in Tryll runtime settings if you usually rely on that.

Closing the window releases the connection lease. It does not kill the server.

Disconnected state still shows this editor process's RAM. The label is Unity reserved in Unity (allocator reserved) and Unreal process RAM, not editor VRAM in Unreal (FPlatformMemory used physical). Those are different metrics — do not compare them to each other. The server tables stay on screen if you already have a snapshot; they are not wiped.

docs.title: Take a snapshot
docs.text:
There is no poll and no graph. Click Refresh.

A snapshot with one language model on the GPU and one STT model on the CPU. The amber estimated tags and ~ ranges mark numbers that are not measured directly. Unity shown; the Unreal panel has the same layout.

Refresh is disabled until the session is Ready, and while a fetch is in flight. A late reply cannot overwrite a newer one. If a fetch fails after you already have numbers, a stale-snapshot banner keeps the last good table and shows the error.

docs.title: Confidence tiers
docs.text:
Every component row has a visible Confidence column. That is the feature: an estimate must never look like a measurement.

Tier Meaning How it renders Measured The engine or OS told us this number Plain bytes Derived Computed from measured inputs (for example device other = total − free − ours) Plain bytes Estimated A calibrated band, not a reading Leading ~, and a high band when the collector supplied one. Hover the row for the estimate basis.

docs.title: System — working set, private, unattributed
docs.text:
The system table is four rows: this editor process's RAM, Working set, Private, Unattributed.

Field What it is Unity reserved / Unreal process RAM This editor process — RAM, not editor VRAM. Unity reports allocator reserved; Unreal reports UsedPhysical. Working set Pages the OS currently has resident for tryll_server Private Commit that is not shareable — closer to "what we allocated" Unattributed Working set minus the RAM we assigned to components

Memory-mapped model files count as resident pages but are not allocations we make. A VRAM-placed model therefore often shows up in unattributed rather than under its own RAM column. The window calls that out when unattributed is more than half the working set and a model is resident.

docs.title: Devices — ours / other / free
docs.text:
One table row per device: Device, Kind, Ours (model weights + KV + compute), Other (everything on the device that is not Tryll), Free, Total.

other is where the editor, the compositor, and other processes live. Do not treat it as a Tryll leak. The editor's own VRAM cannot be split out of that number.

If the backend is not initialised yet, devices register on the first model load. That is not an error.

docs.title: KV by agent — reserved vs context used
docs.text:
The KV table is sorted background → buffered → visible, then by reserved bytes descending. Background KV is the reclaim signal: nobody is waiting on that memory.

Column How to read it Class Scheduler class of the last turn (visible / buffered / background), plus evicted when the context is not resident. Describes the work, not the agent. When Relative time, or never run if the context has never completed a turn. Idle class and "never run" are different: a context can be allocated and unused. Context used A bar plus used / capacity (pct). Headroom to the limit, not memory growth. The KV buffer is allocated for the full context_size when the context is created and does not grow with the conversation. Reserved Bytes actually held for that context (RAM + VRAM)

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Kind, name, confidence, RAM (a ~ band when estimated), VRAM. KV rows are listed in the agent table above, not repeated here.

docs.title: What changes these numbers
docs.text: Knob Where Load / unload / pin Manage Models in the Editor MemoryPlacement (RAM vs VRAM) Choose where models run Per-node context_size / context Run many agents on a small GPU Prefill / Evict / DeferAllocation Manage an agent's KV cache Server engines.llama_cpp.inference.default_n_ctx Server configuration Catalog kv_cache_type Model management

docs.title: Relationship to the server monitor
docs.text:
Memory window Server monitor Memory panel Scope Whole server process Whole server process Collector The same CollectMemorySnapshot The same CollectMemorySnapshot Surface Unity / Unreal editor, over the TCP wire Browser, GET /api/memory Refresh Button only SSE / poll, plus a sparkline

The numbers should match. The monitor still has the sparkline and stacked bars; this window does not.

C++ (TryllClient::GetMemoryConsumption), Python (client.get_memory_consumption()), Unity (RequestGetMemoryConsumptionAsync), and Unreal (UTryllSubsystem::RequestGetMemoryConsumption) return the same snapshot.

docs.text:

  • Use the Agent Log — per-connection traffic, not process memory
  • Inspect and Edit Knowledge Stores — the neighbouring window for mutable knowledge stores
  • Wire Protocol — GetMemoryConsumptionRequest / Response
  • Unity TryllClient — RequestGetMemoryConsumptionAsync
  • Unreal C++ API — RequestGetMemoryConsumption / FTryllMemorySnapshot

docs.title: Keep Long Conversations Coherent
docs.text:
Stop a character forgetting the start of a long conversation, without paying for an ever-growing prompt.

Prerequisites

  • A working chat agent — see Build a Chat Agent with a Graph.
  • A conversation long enough to matter: roughly, more turns than context_size divided by the size of one turn-pair.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Every model-backed node owns a fixed context window. When the projected prompt outgrows it, Tryll trims: the oldest turns are dropped from the prompt and never come back. Nothing fails, nothing is logged to the player, and the character simply stops knowing what it was told.

You can see it happen in the server log:

[TokenBudgetProjectionStrategy] Windowed prompt: 3891 tokens, 14 messages (_windowStart=6)

_windowStart only ever advances. Once it passes a turn, that turn is gone.

docs.title: The fix
docs.text:
Add a Summarize node at the end of the graph. It folds the turns that are about to age out into a rolling summary, which every Generate-class node in the same agent then renders at the end of its system message.

flowchart LR
    generate["GenerateAndSpeak<br>generate"]
    summarize["Summarize<br>summarize"]
    generate -- "default" --> summarize
    summarize -- "default" --> END

docs.title: 1. Put the node last
docs.text:
Place it after the node that produces the player-facing reply. The reply is already delivered by the time the summarizer runs, so the player sees the answer at normal speed; only the turn that triggers a fold costs extra.

PythonUnity 
from tryll_client.graph import GraphDescription, GenerateParams, SummarizeParams

graph = (
    GraphDescription()
    .add_node("generate", GenerateParams(
        system_prompt=persona,
        context_size=4096,
        default_exit="summarize",
    ))
    .add_node("summarize", SummarizeParams(
        trigger_tokens=1024,
        keep_recent_turns=3,
        default_exit="",
    ))
    .set_start_node("generate")
)

In the workflow asset, add a node of type Summarize, then set the Generate node's Default Exit to it and leave the Summarize node's own Default Exit empty (END).

docs.title: 2. Size the trigger against the consuming node
docs.text:
The summarizer must fire before the trimmer would. Work it out from the node that consumes the history:

Quantity Where it comes from Context window The consuming node's context_size Reserved for generation Its max_tokens Fixed cost System prompt + any retrieved knowledge + template framing Head-room for history Context − generation − fixed cost

Set trigger_tokens to roughly 60–70% of that head-room. Example, for a 4096-token node with a 1024-token system prompt, ~1000 tokens of retrieval and 512 reserved for generation: head-room is about 1500 tokens, so trigger_tokens = 1024 is a good starting point.

Prefer trigger_tokens for production. trigger_turns exists for tests and for authored pacing where "every N exchanges" is easier to reason about than tokens.

docs.title: 3. Keep a verbatim hot window
docs.text:
keep_recent_turns (default 3) is the number of most recent exchanges that are never folded. They always replay word for word.

Raise it when the character needs exact recall of the immediate scene — a negotiation where the last offer matters, a puzzle where wording matters. Lower it to squeeze more head-room out of a small window. Below 2 the character starts paraphrasing the exchange that just happened, which reads as inattentive.

docs.title: 4. Write the prompt for compression, not for prose
docs.text:
The node ships a default system_prompt and template that ask for third person, named speakers, short verbatim quotes of what the player stated or promised, and a hard length cap. Override them when the genre needs it, and keep these rules:

  • Ask it to merge and shorten older points, not just append new ones. Without this, the summary grows until max_summary_tokens truncates it mid-sentence.
  • Name the speakers. Small models confuse who said what more than they invent facts.
  • Cap the length in the prompt as well as in max_summary_tokens. The parameter is a hard stop that cuts mid-word; the prompt is what makes the model land inside it.
  • Forbid speculation. "Record only what was said" measurably reduces invented detail on 3–4B models.
  • Treat the transcript as data, not instructions. The built-in prompt and downstream projection both say this explicitly so quoted player text cannot silently become higher-priority instructions after a fold.

docs.title: 5. Watch it work
docs.text:
Set notify_client = true and handle the summarized NodeEvent on the generic node-event callback: it carries covered_through, folded_turns, summary_chars and the summary text. During development, printing that text beside the transcript is the fastest way to see whether your prompt is producing something the character can actually use.

With enable_diagnostics = true, the turn's debug_info also carries the summarizer's own prompt and output under its node entry, and the SummaryComponent appears in interaction.components[].

docs.title: Budget the second context
docs.text:
The node owns its own KV cache. At the default context_size = 2048 that is a real, fixed VRAM cost on top of the character's own context — on an 8B model, roughly 135 MB. On a tight GPU:

  • Share the weights: leave model_name empty so the summarizer uses the agent's default model rather than loading a second one.
  • Keep context_size at 2048 unless a single fold's backlog needs more room. Each fold sees the previous summary plus the largest chronological prefix of pending turns that fits beside max_summary_tokens.
  • Keep max_summary_tokens at least 64 tokens below context_size. Tryll rejects configurations that leave no prompt room and, for large backlogs, folds the largest chronological prefix that fits.
  • Let the KV-cache lifecycle evict it between folds if the agent is idle for long stretches.

docs.title: What this does not do
docs.text:
A summary preserves the thread of a conversation — where the scene is, what was agreed, what is unresolved. It is lossy about detail by design, and every fold compounds that loss slightly.

If the character must recall an exact fact many hours later ("what was the name of the merchant in the first village?"), that is a job for retrieval over stored facts, not for a summary. Use Retrieve against a knowledge base for those, and let the summary carry the narrative.
