docs.title: Keep Merchant Prices Deterministic
docs.text:
Let game code calculate a merchant's price while the language model decides how to say it in character. The model emits __PRICE__; Tryll replaces that marker with the authoritative value before the text reaches the client, dialogue history, or TTS.

This pattern is called Placeholder Post-Processing (PPP) in recent game-trading research. It separates pricing policy from language generation: the game is the cashier, and the model is the merchant's voice.

What this guide guarantees

Output substitution guarantees that a recognised marker is replaced with the value supplied by the game. It does not validate inventory, approve a discount, or commit a transaction. Keep those decisions in deterministic game logic.

Prerequisites

  • Read Agent Variables.
  • Follow Substitute Agent Variables in LLM Output for the complete substitution contract and validation rules.
  • Use a Generate or GenerateAndSpeak node.

docs.title: The pattern
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    input["Player request"]
    policy["Game pricing policy<br>inventory, quantity, discounts"]
    variable["Agent variable<br>price = 18"]
    model["Generate / GenerateAndSpeak<br>"For you, __PRICE__ gold.""]
    output["Authoritative output<br>"For you, 18 gold.""]

    input --> policy
    policy --> variable
    variable --> model
    model --> output

The model never needs to copy, round, or calculate the amount. It only chooses where the marker belongs in a natural sentence.

docs.title: 1. Calculate the quote in game code
docs.text:
Put every rule that can change the transaction in one authoritative pricing function: item cost, quantity, reputation, bundle discounts, reservation price, tax, and currency conversion.

For example:

def calculate_quote(*, unit_price: int, quantity: int,
                    reputation_discount: float, minimum_total: int) -> int:
    subtotal = unit_price * quantity
    discounted = round(subtotal * (1.0 - reputation_discount))
    return max(minimum_total, discounted)

Treat the result as transaction state, not presentation text. Store it with the item ID and quantity so the eventual purchase can be revalidated against the same quote.

Do not ask the model to multiply quantities, apply discounts, enforce a price floor, or recover the authoritative amount from conversation history.

docs.title: 2. Declare price as substitutable
docs.text:
Declare the variable when creating the agent and opt it into output substitution. This permission belongs to the declaration and cannot be enabled by a component override later.

Unity / UnrealPythonC++

On the workflow asset, add a scalar variable named price, then enable Allow Output Substitution. Use Int for whole currency units or String when the game supplies a localized spoken form.

from tryll_client.variables import VariableDecl

agent = client.create_agent(
    graph,
    variables={
        "price": VariableDecl(
            0,
            allow_output_substitution=True,
        ),
    },
)

std::vector<Tryll::Client::AgentVariableDecl> variables = {
    {"price", std::int64_t{0}, /*allowOutputSubstitution=*/true},
};

auto agent = client.CreateAgent(
    graph,
    /*enableDiagnostics=*/false,
    std::nullopt,
    /*maintainDialogueHistory=*/true,
    variables);

Use separate variables when one line contains independently authoritative values, such as __UNIT_PRICE__, __QUANTITY__, and __TOTAL__. Each one must be declared and explicitly allowed.

docs.title: 3. Configure the merchant response
docs.text:
Enable substitute_agent_variables on the Generate or GenerateAndSpeak node. Then tell the model exactly when and how to emit the marker:

You are Branna, a guarded but witty weapons merchant.

When stating the current total price, write exactly __PRICE__ where the amount
belongs. Do not calculate, spell out, round, or replace the marker yourself.
Do not state any other total price. Keep the reply to one sentence.

__PRICE__ matching is ASCII case-insensitive, but using one canonical spelling in prompts makes failures easier to diagnose.

For a fixed set of merchant barks, a GBNF grammar can require the marker literally. For open-ended negotiation, keep the grammar broad enough that it does not remove the language variation you wanted from the model.

With GenerateAndSpeak, substitution happens in the streamed server pipeline before synthesis. The player hears the replacement value, not the marker, without waiting for the complete generated line.

docs.title: 4. Set the quote before generation
docs.text:
Update the local variable mirror immediately before sending the player turn. The client flushes the pending write before SendMessage, so the same turn sees the new value.

UnityUnrealC++Python 
long quote = CalculateQuote(item, quantity, player.Reputation);
agentComp.Agent.Variables.SetInt("price", quote);
agentComp.SendMessage(playerText);

const int64 Quote = CalculateQuote(Item, Quantity, PlayerReputation);
Agent->GetVariables().SetInt(TEXT("price"), Quote);
Agent->SendMessage(PlayerText);

const std::int64_t quote = CalculateQuote(item, quantity, reputation);
agent.Variables().SetInt("price", quote);
agent.SendText(playerText);

quote = calculate_quote(
    unit_price=item.unit_price,
    quantity=quantity,
    reputation_discount=discount,
    minimum_total=item.minimum_total,
)
agent.variables.set("price", quote)
reply = agent.send_message(player_text)

This path works when gameplay already knows the relevant item and quantity—for example, the player selected an item in shop UI before speaking.

docs.title: If the player's words determine the quote
docs.text:
When the game must first extract an item, quantity, or offer from the same utterance, use this graph:

flowchart LR
    detect["ToolCall<br>extract item / quantity / offer<br>disposition=Pause"]
    game["Game validates input<br>and calculates quote"]
    update["Set price variable"]
    speak["Resume → GenerateAndSpeak<br>with __PRICE__"]

    detect --> game
    game --> update
    update --> speak

While the turn is paused, update price and then call Resume. Pending variable writes flush before resume, so the downstream generation uses the newly calculated value in the same turn. See Pause and Resume a Turn and Define and Handle Tool Calls.

Never trust the extracted arguments without validation. Check the tool name, item ID, quantity bounds, current inventory, and allowed state transition before calculating the quote.

docs.title: 5. Commit from game state, not narrated text
docs.text:
A correct spoken price is not transaction authorization. The model can still make an unsupported claim such as “I will include a free dagger.”

For a robust merchant:

  1. Keep inventory, currency, quote, and negotiation state in the game.
  2. Require an explicit confirmation step before purchase.
  3. Recheck the item, quantity, current funds, inventory, and quoted amount.
  4. Execute the transfer exactly once through game code or a validated tool call.
  5. Treat the generated sentence as presentation only.

Do not parse the substituted answer to discover the price again. You already have the authoritative value that produced it.

docs.title: 6. Make spoken prices unambiguous
docs.text:
An integer such as 18 is usually sufficient for fantasy currency:

"For you, __PRICE__ gold pieces."

For localized currency, ranges, decimals, or values whose pronunciation matters, declare a substitutable string and let the game provide the final spoken form:

price_spoken = "eighteen gold pieces"

Then make the marker own the complete phrase:

"For you, __PRICE_SPOKEN__."

This prevents duplicated units and avoids depending on a TTS normalizer to infer the intended currency or locale. Substitutable strings are limited to 2048 UTF-8 bytes.

docs.title: Verify the result
docs.text:
Test at least these cases:

  • Change the quote between turns and confirm the next response uses the new value.
  • Use a mixed-case marker such as __PrIcE__ and confirm it still resolves.
  • Confirm the wire text, dialogue history, and generated speech all contain the replacement rather than the marker.
  • Cancel during a partially generated marker and confirm no half-marker reaches the client or TTS.
  • Attempt a below-floor price and verify game policy rejects it before updating the variable.
  • Attempt to confirm a stale quote after inventory or player funds change and verify the transaction is revalidated.

With agent diagnostics enabled, inspect variable_replacements on the Generate or GenerateAndSpeak node to confirm the matched marker, replacement, and UTF-8 byte offsets.

docs.title: Why this pattern
docs.text:
The design follows a recurring result in negotiation and game-NPC research: separate deterministic strategy and state from neural language generation.

  • Decoupling Strategy and Generation in Negotiation Dialogues (He et al., 2018) established the manager/generator split: a controlled strategy chooses a move such as propose(price=50), and a language model renders it.
  • State-Inference-Based Prompting for Natural Language Trading with Game NPCs (2025) uses placeholder-based price calculation and reports 99.7% calculation precision across its 100-dialogue evaluation.
  • Aligning Large Language Models with Procedural Rules: Autoregressive State-Tracking Prompting for In-Game Trading (2025) names the technique Placeholder Post-Processing and reports 99.3% calculation precision across 300 trading dialogues. In that evaluation, the scaffold also reduced response time from 21.2 seconds to 2.4 seconds when moving from the compared larger model to the smaller model.
  • Leveraging LLMs for Active Merchant NPCs (MART, 2024) documents the pricing, arithmetic, giveaway, and hallucinated-inventory problems that deterministic policy and validated actions must address.

These are results from the papers' own models, datasets, and experimental settings—not performance guarantees for a Tryll workflow. Their reusable engineering lesson is the boundary: let the model produce expressive language, but do not let it own a value that has one correct answer.

docs.title: Localize Prompts with Your Localization System
docs.text: Store a prompt as a Text ID in the localization system you already ship, and have Unity or Unreal resolve it to plain text before the agent is created. The server still receives a string. There is no Tryll string table.

docs.title: 1. Tick Localized and set the table
docs.text:
On a workflow asset, set Text Table to the table that holds your prompts. On each prompt field (system prompt, template, instruction, acknowledge text, TTS delivery instruction, and a ClassifyIntent entry's prompt), tick Localize text. The box is then a Text ID, for example tobin.system. The inline text stays in the asset; only the resolved string is sent.

Leave the box unticked when that field should stay inline. A Summarize template that already says Write in {{language}} is a good candidate to leave inline: the session language fills the key, and the template itself does not need a translation.

Give prompt authors their own table, and keep it out of machine translation. A prompt is instructions to a model, not UI copy. Tryll does not enforce that split.

docs.title: 2. Point the project at a text provider
docs.text: The provider answers GetText(table, id) and reports the game's current language. When one is set, that language is the session language unless you pass a locale into CreateSession. An empty string passed in still means no session language.

docs.title: Unity
docs.text:
Assign a TryllTextProviderAsset under Project Settings → Tryll Client → Text Provider. The same asset is used in the editor preview and in Play.

  • Unity Localization (com.unity.localization), when that package is installed: create a Unity Localization Text Provider. Tryll reads the raw table entry. Turn Smart String formatting off for prompt entries. {} placeholders and Mustache {{ }} must not be nested in the same string; a Smart String would format the braces before the server sees the Mustache tags.
  • JSON Text Provider, for a demo or a prototype: one JSON TextAsset per language, each a flat object { "id": "text" }. Lookup tries the current locale, then the language subtag (de-DE then de), then the first other file that has the key. That last step uses another language, so it logs a warning once per key. A file that is not valid JSON logs an error with the line and column, and the inspector shows the same reason. Call SetLocale("de") to switch at runtime; the asset's Locale field is the start language and does not change in Play mode.
  • Your own class: implement ITryllTextProvider. A code-only provider works in Play. The inspector preview also needs ITryllTextProviderEditor (ListLocales, ListIds, GetTextForPreview, OpenInEditor). Without that, the field says it has no editor support.

A provider set on TryllClient.TextProvider from code wins over the settings asset. Setting that property to null turns resolution off even when the settings asset has a provider.

Raise LocaleChanged on the main thread. Tryll sends requests from that event.

I2 Localization, in about ten lines:

public sealed class I2TryllTextProvider : TryllTextProviderAsset
{
    public override string CurrentLocale => I2.Loc.LocalizationManager.CurrentLanguageCode;

    public override Task<string> GetTextAsync(string table, string id)
    {
        string text = I2.Loc.LocalizationManager.GetTranslation(id);
        return Task.FromResult(string.IsNullOrEmpty(text) ? null : text);
    }

    void OnEnable() => I2.Loc.LocalizationManager.OnLocalizeEvent += RaiseLocaleChanged;
    void OnDisable() => I2.Loc.LocalizationManager.OnLocalizeEvent -= RaiseLocaleChanged;
}

Shared snippets ({{text.some_id}} inside a prompt) are the provider's job in this version. Resolve them before you return the string.

docs.title: Unreal
docs.text:
Project Settings → Tryll Client → Text Provider is None by default, so the Tryll Locale field sets the session language, as before. Pick UTryllStringTableTextProvider to resolve Text IDs from Unreal String Tables. It reads FText::FromStringTable and follows the game culture. While it is set, that culture is the session language and wins over the Locale field.

Pick the workflow's Text Table with the String Table asset picker. The asset reference makes the cooker package the table, and Tryll loads it before the first lookup, so a table that nothing else uses still works in a packaged game. A custom UTryllTextProvider subclass may ignore the table and use only the key. Implement GetText and GetCurrentLocale, and call UTryllSubsystem::NotifyTextLocaleChanged when the language changes. Override SupportsEditorPreview when the details panel should show a preview.

Test a runtime language switch with Play → Standalone Game, not in the viewport. Play in Editor shares one culture with the editor, so SetCurrentCulture switches the editor's own language too, and the editor loads no game translations unless Localization.ForceLoadGameLocalizationInEditor is set.

docs.title: C++, Python, and Java
docs.text:
Those clients have no provider seam. Resolve the string in your game and assign it:

params->SystemPrompt = Loc.Get(TEXT("bartender.system"));

p.system_prompt = loc.get("bartender.system")

docs.title: 3. Check the texts before you play
docs.text:
Under a ticked field the inspector shows a key list (typing a new key is allowed), Open, and a language switcher.

  • Found — the first lines of the entry, with {{ }} marked.
  • Missing in this language — red. A fallback from another language is shown and marked as fallback. Language fallback is the provider's job; Tryll does not invent one at send time.
  • Missing in some languages — yellow. Check texts is the full matrix across every language the provider lists.
  • Empty ID — red, "Enter a Text ID".
  • No editor provider — grey. The runtime provider has no preview API.

Check texts on the workflow runs every Text ID against every language the provider lists. A missing cell is red.

Creation fails on the client before anything is sent when a ticked field has an empty ID, no provider is set, the provider returns no text, or the provider throws. The error names the asset, node, field, table, and ID (InvalidParamValue, 3007). There is no silent fallback to the inline string.

ChangeParams follows the same rules. Params with a ticked field are resolved first, so you can change a Text ID at runtime. With an asynchronous provider, the change can reach the server a frame later.

A Dialog Lab override on a ticked field is the text under test: it wins, and the field is unticked for that run.

Resolved text is plain text. The server's existing checks still apply: Mustache, {{intents_block}}, and the rest.

docs.title: 4. Change language on a live agent
docs.text:
When the provider raises its language-changed event, Tryll sets the session locale and re-resolves ticked fields that are not structural, then sends ChangeAgentParam for each live agent. A turn that is still running returns AgentBusy (3004); the update is sent when the turn ends, before your turn-complete handler runs. AgentBusy here is expected and is not reported as an error.

  • Your runtime changes stay. The update starts from the agent's current params, so values you set with ChangeParams are kept. Only nodes whose text changed are sent.
  • One agent is all or nothing. If any Text ID of an agent is missing in the new language, nothing is sent to that agent, and it keeps its previous prompts in full. Unity raises TryllClient.LocalizedTextFailed; Unreal broadcasts OnLocalizedTextFailed on the Tryll subsystem. The session language has already changed, so recreate the agent or switch back. In Unreal, a server that rejects an update raises the same event.
  • Wait for the update before work that must see it (Unreal). The Tryll subsystem broadcasts OnLocalizedTextApplied. It fires once per agent, when the server has acknowledged every prompt that changed, or right away when none changed. A busy agent gets it after its turn ends. If the language changes again before the acknowledgements arrive, only the latest change fires it. Start a KV prefill, a conversation reset, or your own ChangeParams from this event, not from the language change itself: those run against the old prompts if they reach the server first.
  • An agent created during the switch is updated as soon as its creation completes.
  • An explicit session language wins. If you passed a locale to CreateSession, a later provider change does not touch the session language. Prompts still follow the provider.
Reaches a live agent Needs the agent recreated Voice language and the {{language}} keys, via the session locale A ticked ClassifyIntent entry prompt (the intents list is structural) Ticked non-structural prompt fields, from the next turn Files already bound (a knowledge base, canned lines) A voice input that is already open — close it and open it again

There is no restart API. Recreating an agent to pick up structural text or files that are already bound is the same save-and-restore you already use for dialog state: export the dialog, destroy the agent, create it again, and import. See Save and Load Agent State.

docs.title: Manage an Agent's KV Cache
docs.text: Use an agent's KV-cache lifecycle controls to move language-model context memory out of a gameplay-critical moment. These controls affect per-agent LLM contexts, not shared model weights.

docs.title: Choose creation behavior
docs.text:
CreateAgent accepts AgentKvCacheInitialization:

Value Meaning AllocateOnly (default) Allocate eligible contexts without an explicit prefix prefill. Prefill Allocate and prefill eligible contexts before creation completes. DeferAllocation Create context shells only; allocate when you prefill or send the first message.

Use Prefill when creating an agent during a loading screen. Use DeferAllocation when you need an agent's graph and dialogue state now but do not need its LLM contexts until later.

docs.title: Prefill during a loading screen
docs.text:
Call PrefillKvCache after creating an idle agent to make every eligible LLM node current with its reusable prefix.

auto result = agent.PrefillKvCache();
if (result.applicable && result.prefixStatus == AgentKvCachePrefixStatus::Current) {
    // The agent's reusable LLM prefix is ready.
}

The Python equivalent is agent.prefill_kv_cache(). Unity and Unreal expose PrefillKvCache on both the raw agent and their agent components. The component APIs report completion through their KV-cache result callbacks/events; they do not provide a status UI.

docs.title: Evict an inactive agent
docs.text:
To release the raw contexts of an idle agent while retaining its graph, dialogue, parameters, and identity, call EvictKvCache.

auto result = agent.EvictKvCache();
// Repeating this is safe. If it was already evicted,
// result.contextsEvicted is zero.

Eviction is idempotent. GetKvCacheStatus returns the authoritative aggregate state:

  • applicable and eligibleNodeCount identify whether the graph has eligible LLM nodes.
  • residency is Evicted or Resident.
  • prefixStatus is NotCurrent or Current.
  • prefill results add contextsCreated, tokensDecoded, and tokensReused; eviction results add contextsEvicted.

docs.title: Send after eviction
docs.text:
There is no restore API and no option to reject a send from an evicted agent. Before every SendMessage, Tryll automatically recreates any evicted eligible contexts and restores their reusable prefix before it creates the interaction. The first response after eviction can therefore have a higher time to first token. Prefill explicitly when that cost belongs in a loading screen instead.

Cache operations are idle-only. A turn in progress, a paused turn, or another cache operation conflicts with AgentBusy. A failed explicit lifecycle operation returns KvCacheOperationFailed or KvCacheManagementUnsupported, depending on the cause.

docs.title: Use diagnostics safely
docs.text: Create the agent with enable_diagnostics to receive optional debug_info in cache-operation results. It can include per-node operational detail for troubleshooting. It never includes prompt or token content, and per-node data is not part of the normal public result contract.

docs.title: What eviction does not affect
docs.text: KV-cache operations apply only to Generate, the LLM half of GenerateAndSpeak, ToolCall, and ClassifyIntentLLM. They do not unload language-model weights and do not affect embeddings, Speak, or any STT/TTS model (Sherpa-ONNX voices and the llama.cpp voices Orpheus and Maya1). Manage shared model weights separately through Model Management.

docs.title: Several agents at once
docs.text: This page covers the operations on one agent. Driving them across a whole cast — which agent stays warm, when to prefill, and how to avoid paying for agents the player merely scrolled past — is a policy question with its own page, and both clients ship a component for it: Run many agents on a small GPU.

docs.title: Manage Models in the Editor
docs.text:
Both the Unity and Unreal plugins include an editor-only Model Manager window for working with the server's model catalog without writing any wire code: browse every model the server knows about, download and load them, free disk space, and mark which models ship in your packaged build.

It is a graphical front end over the model-management wire protocol (ListModels, DownloadModel, LoadModel / UnloadModel, DeleteModel). The catalog itself is defined server-side in models.json.

Prerequisites

  • The Tryll plugin installed (see First Inference in Unity / Unreal).
  • A TryllRuntimeSettings asset (Unity) or configured plugin settings (Unreal). The window launches the bundled server automatically, the same way the Chat Window does.

docs.title: Step 1 — open the window
docs.text:
UnityUnreal

Window → Tryll → Model Manager

The window opens with the title Tryll Models and connects to the server automatically.

Window → Tryll → Tryll Model Manager

Opens as a dockable tab (Tryll Model Manager) and connects on open.

The layout is the same in both engines: a filters column on the left, the model list in the middle, and a properties + actions panel on the right.

Model Manager with a downloaded language model selected. The pills in the list show build registration (PROD, EXP, or not registered); the dot colour is the model status from the legend at the bottom. Unity shown; the Unreal panel has the same layout plus a search box and an Audience filter.

docs.title: Step 2 — find a model
docs.text:
Use the left column to narrow the list:

Filter Values Search Match by model name or HuggingFace repo. Model type Language, Embedding, STT, TTS, VAD. Engine llama-cpp, sherpa-onnx, onnx-runtime. Status Absent, Downloaded, Local, Loaded, Downloading. Registration Production, Experimental, Not registered.

The left column also totals how many models are registered for the build and the on-disk / shipped size, so you can see your build's model footprint at a glance. Select a row to populate the properties panel on the right.

docs.title: Step 3 — download, load, unload, delete
docs.text:
Select a model, then use the action buttons in the properties panel:

Action Effect Wire call Download Fetch the model's files from HuggingFace; a progress bar tracks bytes. DownloadModel Load Pin a language / embedding / STT / TTS model into server memory so the first turn has no load latency. VAD cannot be pinned (catalog/download only). LoadModel Unload Unpin a loaded managed model (freed once no agent still uses it). UnloadModel Delete files Remove the downloaded files from disk. DeleteModel

A toolbar Download all action fetches every still-absent model in the current filtered list. See Model Management → Lifecycle for the load/unload rules (you usually do not need to Load manually — an agent loads its model on demand at CreateAgent).

docs.title: Step 4 — register models for your build
docs.text:
Each model can be tagged with a build registration tier, in the properties panel:

Tier Meaning Production Shipped in your packaged build. Experimental Available in the editor; stripped from packaged builds. Not registered Not part of the build at all.

Registrations are stored in your project, not on the server:

UnityUnreal

Persisted to a TryllModelManifest asset that the Model Manager writes at Assets/Resources/TryllModelManifest.asset. It must stay in a Resources folder so a player build can load it.

Persisted to DefaultGame.ini via the Tryll Model Manifest developer settings.

docs.title: Step 5 — pick registered models on nodes
docs.text:
Model-name fields elsewhere in the editor read this manifest. A Generate node's model, GenerateAndSpeak's TTS model, and the Voice Input component's STT model all show a dropdown filtered to registered models of the right kind, with a tier badge next to each. A name you set that is not registered still displays — it is never silently dropped — but it will not ship unless you register it Production.

This is the editor side of the (tryll_model) schema attribute; see Model Management → Build registration.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text: The list is empty / "Connecting…" never resolves The server did not start or did not bind port 9100. Check the Unity Console or Unreal Output Log for [Tryll Server] lines, as in the Chat Window troubleshooting. A model shows Absent and Download is disabled The catalog entry has no huggingface_repo, so it cannot be fetched over the wire — it must be supplied on disk. See Use Your Own Local Model. A registered model is missing from a build Only Production models ship. Experimental and unregistered models are excluded from packaged builds by design.

docs.title: Pause and Resume a Turn
docs.text:
Suspend a turn between nodes — react to a tool call, or any graph checkpoint, by mutating node parameters before the turn continues, without waiting for the turn to end and starting a new one.

Prerequisites

  • An agent created and ready to receive messages — see Build a Chat Agent with a Graph.
  • A graph with a pause trigger: either a Pause node, or a ToolCall node whose disposition is one of Pause, PauseAndAcknowledge, or AwaitResult.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Two things can pause a turn:

  • Pause node — a no-op checkpoint. The executor always pauses right after it exits.
  • ToolCall with a pausing disposition (Pause, PauseAndAcknowledge, AwaitResult) — pauses only when the node exits tool_called (a tool call was detected). No pause on no_tool_called, and no pause at all for the non-pausing dispositions (RouteOnly, Acknowledge, Notify, NotifyAndAcknowledge). See ToolCall node reference for the full ToolCallDisposition matrix.

While paused:

  • The turn stays open — SendMessage still returns 3004 AgentBusy.
  • ChangeParams / change_params becomes allowed — the one thing a normal in-flight turn forbids. This is the reason to pause: inspect a tool call, then mutate a downstream node's params before it runs.
  • A pause can time out. On a Pause node, pause_timeout_ms 0 (the default) waits forever. With a timeout set, timeout_exit continues the graph when it expires; an empty timeout_exit ends the turn with TurnStatus.PauseTimedOut. On a ToolCall, pause_timeout_ms 0 inherits the server's workflow.tool_call_pause_timeout_ms, which is 2000 ms in the shipped server-config.json. There is no timeout exit on ToolCall, so an expired tool-call pause ends the turn with PauseTimedOut.
  • Cancel aborts a pause at any time. It is the only way out of a pause that has no deadline, so give the player a way to cancel (or run your own watchdog if this agent is unattended).

Resume it with resume_node:

resume_node Effect Empty (default) Continue via the paused node's wired exit route. A node name Jump directly to that node, skipping the wired exit. Fails with 3005 UnknownNode if it doesn't exist in the graph — the turn stays paused, so a bad name is safe to retry.

When the pause follows a ToolCall with disposition = AwaitResult, also pass a complete tool_results batch (one {call_id, result} per pending call). Echo the call_id from the tool_call event (ToolCallNotificationWithId / set_on_tool_call_with_id / …). An invalid batch returns 3016 InvalidToolResults and leaves the turn paused for retry. An empty/omitted tool_results on a plain Pause node or a Pause/PauseAndAcknowledge ToolCall is a plain continue; the same empty batch on a pending AwaitResult batch is itself rejected with 3016 (the server does not silently treat "no results" as "no tool was called").

Client Plain resume Tool-result resume Unity / Unreal Resume() ResumeWithToolResult(s) or RegisterTool (auto-resume; retains the batch across a failed attempt — see HasPausedToolBatch / RetryPausedToolBatch) C++ Resume / ResumeAsync ResumeWithToolResult(s) / *Async Python resume() (never from a reader-thread callback) / resume_async() resume_async(tool_results=[ToolResult(...), ...]) from a callback, or blocking resume(tool_results=...) off the reader thread

docs.title: Examples
Jumping instead of continuing
docs.text:
Pass a node name to route the game's own decision, bypassing the graph's wired exit entirely — useful when the pause is a generic checkpoint (a Pause node) and the game, not the graph author, decides what happens next:

UnityC++Python 
// Player declined the trade — skip "confirm" and go straight to "decline".
agentComp.Resume("decline");

agent.Resume("decline");

agent.resume("decline")

docs.title: Combining with a ToolCall loop
docs.text:
For a single-round "call → result → answer" graph, set disposition = AwaitResult, pause after the call, resume with results, then let a downstream Generate speak:

flowchart LR
    tc["ToolCall<br>detect<br>(disposition=AwaitResult)"]
    gen["Generate<br>answer"]
    tc -. "tool_called (paused)<br>ResumeWithToolResult(s)" .-> gen
    tc -- "no_tool_called" --> gen

This single-pass shape (one call → one result → one downstream answer) is the only pattern currently validated end-to-end (see scenarios.tools.tool_result_v1). Repeated result-bearing jumps back into the same ToolCall node (an agentic multi-round loop) are not supported: correlation IDs (c%08x) restart at c00000000 on every ToolCallNode::Execute(), so a second pass in the same interaction can collide with the first, and there is no regression test for it. Model a bounded number of rounds as separate ToolCall nodes in the graph instead of looping through one, until unique per-interaction exchange IDs and a two-pause regression test exist.

Side-effect tools that do not need a client result can use the default disposition = Acknowledge (or RouteOnly) and skip tool_results entirely — see Define and handle tool calls.

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text: Code Name Cause 3012 AgentNotPaused Resume was called but the agent is idle, or actively running (not paused). 3005 UnknownNode The resume_node you passed does not name a node in the graph. The turn stays paused. 3016 InvalidToolResults tool_results is incomplete, has unknown/duplicate ids, was sent on a non-tool pause, or exceeds size limits. The turn stays paused.

docs.title: Pin and Unpin Models
docs.text:
Keep a model warm in memory or explicitly release it. Useful when you want the first turn to be fast, or when memory pressure forces you to pick which model lives.

Prerequisites

  • A connected session, with CreateSession already called.
  • A model listed in models.json with status Local or Downloaded — see Use Your Own Local Model.

docs.title: When to pin
docs.text:
Situation Pin? Single chat model used all session long Yes — avoids the first-turn load delay. Many agents with different models, short-lived No — let OnDemand eviction recycle memory as agents close. Embedding model for RAG Yes — embeddings run every turn; you do not want it evicted. Model used only once during startup (e.g. a warm-up probe) No — let it fall out when you destroy the probing agent.

The two retention policies apply to language, embedding, STT, and TTS (not VAD — VAD is download-only and rejected by LoadModel):

  • Pinned — set by LoadModelRequest / Blueprint Request Load Model. Only unloaded when you send UnloadModelRequest and no active contexts still reference the model.
  • OnDemand — the default. Set implicitly when you create an agent (or voice input / TTS / embedding use) and the model is not already loaded. The server frees unused OnDemand models after DestroyAgent, and again immediately before the next validated model load (across all four caches).

docs.title: Steps — pin a model
Steps — unpin a model
Verify it worked
docs.text:
Check status with ListModels:

  • Status = Loaded → model is in memory (pinned or on-demand with active users).
  • Status = Local or Downloaded → model is on disk but not in memory.

Server-side log lines:

[Session 1] LoadModel requested: 'My Local Model'
[ModelManager] Pinned 'My Local Model'
[Session 1] UnloadModel requested: 'My Local Model'
[ModelManager] Unloaded 'My Local Model'
[Session 1] Model 'My Local Model' unloaded immediately

If the last line reads unload deferred (active contexts) instead, agents still hold the model. It stays resident until their contexts are destroyed.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Pinning and never unpinning. Pinned models survive session tear-downs (they are global). A long-lived server can accumulate pins if clients forget to unload. Pair every LoadModelRequest with a matching UnloadModelRequest on shutdown.
  • Expecting pin to change load cost of subsequent sessions. Correct — pinning is global. A second client connecting will find the model already Loaded.
  • Trying to pin an Absent model. Pin requires the model to be at least Local / Downloaded. If it is Absent, call DownloadModel first.
  • Trying to pin a VAD model. VAD entries are catalog/download metadata only. LoadModel returns ModelResolutionFailed. Download the VAD bundle explicitly first — offline STT only resolves and loads VAD files that are already on disk (otherwise it falls back to flush-only mode).

docs.title: Query Rewriting and HyDE for RAG
docs.text:
A plain Retrieve → Generate pipeline searches your knowledge base with the user's raw message. That works for a single, well-formed question, but real conversations are messier: typos, sentence fragments, and pronouns that only make sense against earlier turns ("what about that fish?", "can it live with goldfish?"). Retrieval on the raw text alone will often miss.

This how-to adds a rewriting step: a dedicated Generate node folds the conversation so far into fresh search text, and Retrieve searches with that instead of the raw message — while the answering Generate node still responds to the user's original message, so the reply reads naturally. Because rewriting needs to resolve pronouns and fix grammar, it uses the LLM; a model-free Transform node is the alternative when a purely deterministic (template-based) rewrite is enough (see the note at the end of Step 3).

The graph is the same either way. What changes — and what this page is mostly about — is what you ask the node to write.

Prerequisites

  • A working Retrieve → Generate RAG graph — see Create a simple RAG assistant if you don't have one yet.
  • Read Slots and inter-node value passing for the input / {{slot.<name>}} mental model this how-to relies on.

docs.title: Choose a register first: query, or hypothetical answer
docs.text:
Embedding search compares your search text against your stored chunks. It works best when the two are written in the same register — so the shape of your knowledge base decides what the rewrite node should emit.

Your chunks read like… Ask the node for Known as questions, FAQ entries, player utterances a search query — keywords, pronouns resolved query rewriting statements, encyclopedia prose, lore, wiki text a hypothetical answer — a passage in the chunks' own voice HyDE

Most knowledge bases are the second kind. If your chunks read like

Betta fish are native to the shallow rice paddies and slow-moving streams of Southeast Asia…

then you are storing answers, and embedding a question to find them is a mismatch — the well-known query/document asymmetry (it is why several embedding models ship a separate "query" prefix). Writing a hypothetical answer and embedding that puts both sides in the same register. The technique is called HyDE — Hypothetical Document Embeddings.

It does not matter that the hypothetical answer is partly wrong. It is never shown to anyone; it only has to look like the chunk you want to find, so that it lands near it in embedding space.

On the aquarium demo knowledge base, HyDE resolved pronoun-only follow-ups more reliably than a query rewrite of the same graph, and both beat no rewriting at all. Numbers and method are in docs/research/workflow/rewrite-node-hyde-vs-query-measurement.md.

You do not have to guess

This is measurable without an LLM judge. Label a handful of turns with the chunk IDs a correct retrieval must return, then compare Recall@1 across prompt variants — see Compare dialog variants. Do include a no-rewrite control: rewriting is not always an improvement, and without the control you cannot tell.

docs.title: Step 1 — add a rewriting node
docs.text:
A rewrite step is just a Generate node whose only job is to produce search text. It should:

  • Never appear on the wire — set send = None.
  • Never be replayed as history — set history_role = None. It's a scratch artifact for this turn only.
  • See the conversation so far — this is automatic: every Generate node projects the full turn history by default. (This is also what makes the node drift; see the drift note.)

Pick one of the two prompts below, per the table above.

docs.title: Option A — rewrite into a search query
Option B — write a hypothetical answer (HyDE)
docs.text:
PythonC++ 
rewrite = GenerateParams(
    system_prompt=(
        "You generate a hypothetical reference passage for a knowledge-base "
        "lookup. You are NOT talking to the user and your output is never "
        "shown to anyone — it is embedded and used to search.\n\n"
        "The conversation history is CONTEXT ONLY: use it to work out which "
        "subject the latest message refers to. Never reply to it.\n\n"
        "Write the one or two sentences an encyclopedia would contain if it "
        "answered the latest message.\n\n"
        "Rules:\n"
        "- Plain declarative statements, the way an encyclopedia reads. No "
        "greetings, no \"you should\", no questions, no bullet points.\n"
        "- Always name the subject explicitly, even when the user only said "
        "\"it\", \"they\" or \"that one\".\n"
        "- Include concrete detail of the kind the entry would carry, even if "
        "you must guess. A plausible guess retrieves well; vagueness does not.\n"
        "- Be brief. One or two SHORT sentences, 40 words maximum.\n\n"
        "### Example\n"
        "Earlier turns were about: zebra danio\n"
        "Latest message: wat temperatur they need\n"
        "Passage: Zebra danios are hardy fish that do well in water from "
        "64 to 77 F (18 to 25 C).\n\n"
        "Now write the passage for the latest message. Output the passage "
        "and nothing else."
    ),
    send=SendAnswer.None_,
    history_role=HistoryRole.None_,
    sampling=SamplingOverrides(temperature=0.0, max_tokens=96),
    default_exit="retrieve",
)

GenerateParamsT rewrite;
rewrite.system_prompt =
    "You generate a hypothetical reference passage for a knowledge-base "
    "lookup. Your output is never shown to anyone - it is embedded and "
    "used to search. The conversation history is CONTEXT ONLY: use it to "
    "work out which subject the latest message refers to; never reply to "
    "it. Write the one or two SHORT sentences (40 words maximum) an "
    "encyclopedia would contain if it answered the latest message. Always "
    "name the subject explicitly. Output the passage and nothing else.";
rewrite.send = Tryll::SendAnswer_None;
rewrite.history_role = Tryll::HistoryRole_None;
rewrite.default_exit = "retrieve";

Keep the passage short — brevity is a retrieval setting, not a style choice

Two lines do most of the work in that prompt: the worked example, and "Be brief. One or two SHORT sentences, 40 words maximum." Dropping the brevity rule made a 3B model roughly a third more verbose and measurably worse at retrieval — long passages dilute the signal, and they can run into max_tokens and truncate mid-sentence. Keep max_tokens generous enough that the passage always finishes (96 is comfortable for two short sentences), and keep the instruction telling the model not to fill it.

Use the worked example on a subject that is not in your knowledge base. If the example passage is a near-duplicate of a real chunk, a model that parrots the example will retrieve the example's chunk instead of answering the user.

docs.title: Step 2 — point Retrieve at the rewritten slot
docs.text:
Set Retrieve.input to the rewrite node's name so it searches with the rewritten text instead of user_message:

PythonC++ 
from tryll_client._generated.node_params import RetrieveParams

retrieve = RetrieveParams(
    embedded_string_storage="my-kb.json",
    input="rewrite",          # <- read the Transform/Generate node's slot
    top_k=3,
    threshold=0.5,
    found_exit="generate",
    not_found_exit="canned_response",
)

RetrieveParamsT retrieve;
retrieve.embedded_string_storage = "my-kb.json";
retrieve.input = "rewrite";
retrieve.top_k = 3;
retrieve.threshold = 0.5f;
retrieve.found_exit = "generate";
retrieve.not_found_exit = "canned_response";

Re-check your threshold after switching register

threshold is a maximum cosine distance, and a HyDE passage is longer and differently worded than a keyword query, so the absolute distances it produces are not the ones you tuned the gate against. If you rely on not_found_exit to refuse out-of-scope questions, re-check that it still fires after changing the prompt.

docs.title: Step 3 — leave Generate reading the original message
docs.text:
Don't set Generate.input — leave it at its default (user_message), so the model answers what the user actually typed, framed with the knowledge the rewritten text retrieved:

Python 
from tryll_client._generated.node_params import Placement

generate = GenerateParams(
    system_prompt="You are a helpful aquarium assistant.",
    template=(
        "Use the following information to answer the next question.\n\n"
        "{{#knowledge}}{{#chunks}}- {{text}}\n{{/chunks}}{{/knowledge}}"
    ),
    placement=Placement.BeforeUserAsSystem,
    send=SendAnswer.Streamed,
)

Wire the graph: rewrite → retrieve → generate (with retrieve's not_found_exit falling back to a canned response, as usual).

Transform instead of Generate

If your rewrite is a simple deterministic substitution (e.g. prefixing a fixed context string, or folding in an agent variable) rather than something that needs the model, use a Transform node instead — it renders a Mustache template into its slot with no LLM call. Transform already has send and history_role fixed to None (it never emits or replays), so you only set its template and output_name, then point Retrieve.input at it exactly as above.

docs.title: The node reads the conversation, and may answer it
docs.text:
This is the most common surprise, so expect it rather than debugging it.

A Generate node projects the full turn history, and there is no parameter that turns that off — history_role = None controls whether this node's output is replayed on later turns, not whether the node reads the transcript. So your rewrite node is handed a chat transcript that ends in a user question, which is a very strong cue to answer rather than to rewrite. Small models follow the transcript's shape over the system prompt, and the effect grows as the conversation gets longer: the first couple of turns obey the prompt, and later turns start coming back as replies. They may even pick up the formatting of the assistant turns above them.

Two consequences worth knowing:

  • If you asked for a query, this is a bug. A prompt that says "never answer the question" does not reliably prevent it. Add a worked example of the exact output you want (see Option A), keep max_tokens tight, and inspect what the node actually emitted before blaming retrieval.
  • If you asked for HyDE, this is roughly the behaviour you wanted anyway — which is why an answer-shaped rewrite is the more robust request of the two on a statement-shaped knowledge base. It also resists a related failure: a short keyword rewrite tends to echo the previous turn's topic, while committing to a full sentence forces the model to commit to the current question.

Either way, read the node's output while tuning. With diagnostics enabled the rewrite node's text is in the turn's node trace, and the Dialog Lab inspector shows it per turn — see Compare dialog variants.

docs.title: Hybrid retrieval: add a keyword line
docs.text:
If Retrieve.retrieval_mode is Hybrid, your search text feeds two legs: a dense (embedding) leg and a lexical BM25 leg. A HyDE passage suits the dense leg but gives BM25 a lot of prose to match on, which can pull in off-target chunks.

Ask for a keyword line after the passage, so each leg gets what it wants:

Format — reproduce it exactly:
Passage: <one or two short sentences an encyclopedia would contain>
Keywords: <3 to 6 comma-separated search terms, subject name first>
  • On Dense retrieval the keyword line changes nothing measurable — don't bother.
  • On Hybrid it is worth having, and a bare HyDE passage without it was the weakest variant measured. If you switch a rewrite node to HyDE, switch the keyword line on at the same time or keep the node on Dense.

Small models skip the keyword line

Stating the requirement once is not enough. A 3B model omitted the Keywords: line about half the time, and repeating the requirement — in the opening line, in an explicit format block, as a rule, and again in the closing instruction — only got it to roughly four turns in five. Larger models complied every time. If you need the two-part shape guaranteed, constrain it with a grammar instead of asking: see Constrain output with a grammar, which makes a missing Keywords: line unsampleable rather than unlikely.

docs.title: Why this works: same-turn visibility
docs.text: Even though rewrite never appears on the wire (send = None) and is never replayed on later turns (history_role = None), its slot is fully visible to retrieve and generate within this turn — same-turn visibility is unconditional (see Slots and inter-node value passing). That's what lets you keep the rewrite invisible to the user while still using it internally.

docs.title: Run many agents on a small GPU
docs.text:
A game with several NPC agents can run out of video memory long before it runs out of speed. This page covers the two levers that matter, in the order they are worth pulling: sizing each node's context window, then evicting the agents nobody is talking to.

The figures throughout come from a five-agent murder-mystery demo — four suspects plus a background note-taker, nine language-model contexts in total, on a 16 GB card. Your numbers will differ; the shape of the problem will not.

docs.title: The one fact that makes this tractable
docs.text:
A KV cache is allocated at its full context_size the moment the context is created. It does not grow as the conversation does.

That has three consequences worth internalising before you change anything:

  • The cost is deterministic. It does not depend on how long anyone plays.
  • Short NPC replies do not save memory. Occupancy is irrelevant; the cap is what is allocated.
  • You can measure a sizing change in seconds — create the agents, read VRAM, done. No playtest.

In the demo, agent creation added ~1.6 GB in a single step and a full playtest then added under 100 MB more.

docs.title: Step 1 — size every LLM node
docs.text:
Every node that owns a language-model context takes a context_size in tokens: Generate, the LLM half of GenerateAndSpeak, ToolCall, and ClassifyIntentLLM. Left at 0, ClassifyIntentLLM and ToolCall use a 2048-token node default. Generate and GenerateAndSpeak still fall back to the model variant's context_size, then the server's default_n_ctx — commonly 8192, which is far more than a classifier or tool-call node needs.

The optional context table on those nodes is an advanced structural override (kv_cache_type, veto-only offload_kqv, escape-hatch batch sizes). Leave it unset unless you are tuning a large window; at a right-sized 2048, changing KV dtype rarely saves measurable VRAM.

context_size is structural: it is fixed when the agent is created and cannot be changed with Change agent parameters. Set it when you build the graph.

Bound the prompt, then leave headroom. For a classifier node the budget is computable: framing prompt + label descriptions + history_turns × a turn + the latest player line. A classifier scores one token and generates nothing, so it needs almost no generation reserve. In the demo that came to ~700 tokens worst case, and 2048 was chosen for roughly 3× headroom.

For a Generate node, add the system prompt, whatever retrieval or instruction text the template folds in, and a reserve for the reply itself.

Do not size to the exact budget

When the prompt exceeds the window, the token-budget projection trims the oldest turns. It keeps working, so the failure is silent: a classifier quietly loses the conversation history it needs to resolve "And that one?" or "Yes, do it." — the very inputs that are unclassifiable without it. After tightening a classifier's window, check that intents still fire, not merely that the game still runs.

docs.title: What a context actually costs
docs.text:
Two parts, and the second is easy to forget:

Part Scales with context_size? Notes KV cache Yes, linearly 2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × n_ctx × bytes_per_element Compute buffers and backend allocation No — roughly fixed per context ~145 MB per context in the demo

Two consequences. First, the same window costs very different amounts on different models — attention shape matters more than parameter count. In the demo, a 3B classifier with full attention cost ~499 MB at 8192 while a 4B generator cost ~606 MB, and a sliding-window architecture would cost less again.

Do not assume a sliding-window discount

A model with interleaved local attention might cap most layers at its window size, which would make a large context_size nearly free. Whether the runtime actually does that is a property of the build, not of the architecture on paper. Assuming the discount in the demo under-predicted the saving by 1.78×. Measure one before you plan around it.

Second, once windows are small the fixed per-context overhead dominates. At 2048 tokens the demo's classifier contexts were ~125 MB of KV against ~145 MB of buffers — so shrinking the window further buys little, and the lever becomes context count, not context size.

docs.title: Step 2 — keep only the agents in use resident
docs.text:
Sizing is free. Eviction is not: it trades latency for memory, and you should turn it on deliberately.

With every context resident, switching between agents is nearly free. Evicted, the first message to an agent also pays context allocation and a full prefill — on the order of a second or two — in exchange for the memory back. That is the right trade on a GPU that would otherwise not fit, and the wrong one on a GPU with headroom.

docs.title: Unity
docs.text:
Add a TryllKvResidencyPolicy to any GameObject, register the agents that should participate, and tell it which one the player is using.

using Tryll.Client;

_policy = gameObject.AddComponent<TryllKvResidencyPolicy>();
_policy.Enabled     = playerWantsLowVram;  // drive this from a graphics setting
_policy.HotSetSize  = 2;

foreach (var npc in _npcs)
    _policy.Register(npc.AgentComponent, startsResident: !playerWantsLowVram);

// ...whenever the player's focus moves:
_policy.SetActive(selectedNpc.AgentComponent);

docs.title: Unreal
docs.text: UTryllKvResidencyPolicy is an ActorComponent with the same surface, all Blueprint-callable: Register, SetActiveAgent, Unregister, RestoreAll, plus bEnabled, HotSetSize and PrefillDebounceSeconds as exposed properties.

docs.title: Pair it with deferred allocation
docs.text:
The policy evicts, but most of the saving comes from never allocating in the first place. Create the agents it manages with DeferAllocation:

component.KvCacheInitialization = playerWantsLowVram
    ? TryllKvCacheInitialization.DeferAllocation
    : TryllKvCacheInitialization.AllocateOnly;

This is structural too, so it is fixed at creation. Toggling the setting mid-session still evicts and restores correctly, but only a restart gets the full benefit — worth saying in your options UI if the setting is player-facing.

docs.title: What the defaults are protecting you from
docs.text:
Three behaviours are easy to omit and unpleasant to debug:

  • The prefill debounce. A prefill cannot be cancelled once started, so the only way to avoid paying for agents the player merely scrolled past is not to start. The policy waits (0.35 s by default) for a selection to settle.
  • A hot set larger than one. "Go back to the one I was just using" is the commonest interaction there is. HotSetSize = 1 maximises the saving and punishes exactly that.
  • Idle-only operations. Prefill and evict answer AgentBusy against a running turn. The policy checks first and treats AgentBusy as a retry rather than an error.

Correctness never depends on this

An evicted context is restored automatically before the next send. A badly tuned policy costs time to first token, not behaviour — which is what makes it safe to tune against a real profile.

docs.title: Do not register every agent
docs.text: An agent that runs on a schedule rather than on player attention — a background summariser that fires after every turn, say — should simply not be registered. Evicting it guarantees a restore on its very next turn, which is strictly worse than leaving it resident. Prefill it once during loading instead, with KvCacheInitialization = Prefill.

docs.title: Step 3 — judge the result against the whole GPU
docs.text:
This is the mistake most worth avoiding. Per-process VRAM tells you what your server changed. It does not tell you whether the game fits.

The game process, the editor, and the desktop compositor all draw from the same card. On a developer machine with a browser open, the desktop alone can hold 2 GB before your game starts. Reading only the server's figure once led us to conclude that an 8 GB card was out of reach when, on a clean system, it was not.

Measure both, and size your minimum spec against the whole-GPU peak during play.

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text:
From the demo, as an order of magnitude rather than a promise:

Change Server VRAM Nine contexts at the 8192 default 11.7 GB After sizing (2048 classifiers, 4096 generators) 8.5 GB After eviction, hot set of 2 6.8 GB

Sizing was the larger win and cost nothing in feel. Eviction added a second win of similar magnitude and a 1–3 s cost on the first line to a newly selected agent.

Note also what did not change: a character switch cost ~160 ms before eviction, because every context was already resident. Eviction does not make switching faster — it makes switching cost something, in exchange for memory. If your card has headroom, sizing alone may be the whole answer.

docs.title: Run the Tryll Server
docs.text:
Start a Tryll server so clients can connect to it.

Prerequisites

  • A Windows 10/11 machine (Linux support is evolving but not officially released).
  • Either a pre-built tryll_server.exe from a release, or the source tree and a CMake + Visual Studio 2022 toolchain to build from source.

docs.title: Option A — use a pre-built server
docs.text:
If you have a packaged tryll_server.exe plus its data/ folder:

  1. Unpack the release into a directory, e.g. C:\tryll.
  2. Open data\server-config.json. The defaults are fine for local development; only change what you need. See Server Configuration for every field.
  3. Confirm data\models.json lists at least one model you can use. If not, either add a local entry (see Use Your Own Local Model) or plan to download one after connecting.

  4. Start the server:

    cd C:\tryll
tryll_server.exe

    You should see a log line like [Listener] Listening on 127.0.0.1:9100 (or whichever port you configured). The default network_access: "local" binds loopback (127.0.0.1), which never triggers a Windows Firewall prompt. Set network_access: "local_network" to bind all interfaces instead — the line then reads [Listener] Listening on 0.0.0.0:9100 (private-network peers only).

  5. In a new terminal, verify the port is open:

    netstat -an | findstr 9100

docs.title: Option B — build from source
docs.text:
If you want to hack on the server or your platform does not have a release yet:

  1. Install prerequisites: CMake 3.24+, Visual Studio 2022 with the C++ workload, and Git.

  2. Clone the repository and configure (build presets live in the tryll/ tree, not tryll/server/):

    cd tryll
cmake --preset default

    The default preset uses the Visual Studio 17 2022 generator with TRYLL_CUDA=PREBUILT and TRYLL_VULKAN=PREBUILT — both llama.cpp plugins, no GPU SDK. The committed server-config.json pins backend to vulkan. Prefer CUDA on NVIDIA with --llama-backend auto (or cuda). For a CPU-only build add -DTRYLL_VULKAN=OFF -DTRYLL_CUDA=OFF. The production preset ships the same llama.cpp CUDA+Vulkan payload with CPU ONNX Runtime (no CUDA Toolkit required). For ROCm see the internal developer docs. 3. Build:

    cmake --build --preset debug

  3. Run:

    build\server\Debug\tryll_server.exe

    To point the server at a different config file:

    tryll_server.exe --config path\to\server-config.json

    To listen on a different port without editing the config file:

    tryll_server.exe --port 9200

    Both flags can be combined. --port overrides the port field from the config file. When using ManagedServer (C++ or Python clients) or the Unreal plugin auto-launch, the port is passed automatically — you do not need to edit server-config.json.

    Snapshot file writes (SaveGameMemory / SaveDialog) follow the process saves policy. An unmanaged operator sets saves in server-config.json (or --save-root / --disable-saves / --allow-absolute-save-paths). Auto-launched Unity/Unreal sidecars pass those flags for you. See Server Configuration → Saves.

docs.title: What to edit in server-config.json
docs.text:
The fields you most often want to touch:

  • mode — tryll-dev, client-dev, or (internal) client-prod. Prefer the CLI --mode flag. Debug/Release default tryll-dev; Production accepts only client-dev.
  • network_access — "local" (default) binds loopback (127.0.0.1) and never prompts Windows Firewall; "local_network" binds all interfaces (0.0.0.0) but serves only private/LAN peers, so other machines on your network can connect.
  • storage_root / models_root / logs_dir — process roots. Mode defaults supply them when omitted; the committed config leaves them unset on purpose. Prefer CLI --storage-root, --models-root, --log-dir.
  • Log files — the deployment mode picks the file, not log_mode. Tryll Dev and Client Dev open a new tryll_<timestamp>.log per run; Client Prod rotates a single tryll.log. log_mode is still validated ("production" or "dev").
  • log_level — "info" is a fine default. "trace" turns on the per-turn workflow trace, which logs every node execution — noisy but great for debugging graphs.
  • log_flush_on / log_flush_every_ms — how soon the log file catches up with the running process. Defaults ("warn" + 5000 ms) keep warnings immediate and everything else at most five seconds behind. Set "off" and 0 to leave buffering to the C library.
  • default_canned_responses_path and default_guardrail_patterns_path — server-admin fallback. Point these at files to supply defaults for CannedResponse and RegexGuardrail nodes when the client has not created a string storage. Most client workflows won't need these — use CreateStringStorageRequest (inline or file_path) instead.
  • telemetry — behaviour depends on deployment mode. Client Dev always sends a usage lane (host + hardware + session started). Activity telemetry defaults on and is separately configurable. In Tryll Dev, telemetry is off unless "enabled": true (the shipped file sets it), and "enabled": false or --disable-telemetry turns everything off. See Telemetry.

Every field is documented in Server Configuration.

docs.title: Verify it is working
docs.text:
In another terminal, try connecting with the C++ or Python client:

PythonC++ 
from tryll_client import TryllClient
c = TryllClient.connect("127.0.0.1", 9100)
c.create_session()  # required first (protocol v4)
print(c.list_models())
c.shutdown()

#include <tryll/TryllClient.h>
namespace TC = Tryll::Client;
auto client = TC::TryllClient::Connect("127.0.0.1", 9100);
client.CreateSession({}); // required first (protocol v4)
auto models = client.ListModels();
client.Shutdown();

The server log should show an accept, a ConnectionReady, a CreateSessionRequest, and a ListModelsRequest. (Model management — like every request other than CreateSession — requires a session first; calling list_models() before CreateSession returns SessionNotReady.)

docs.title: Graceful shutdown
docs.text: Ctrl+C in the server console triggers a clean shutdown: the server cancels all active agent turns, closes all sessions, and exits. No client-visible data is kept across restarts — each session starts from scratch.

docs.title: Save and Load Agent State
docs.text:
Add Tryll agents to an existing game-save system without losing their conversation context.

Tryll provides the dialog snapshot; your game still owns the save slots, file format, versioning, validation, and non-Tryll state. For the snapshot API and client-specific encoding examples, first read Export and Import Dialog.

Prerequisites

  • Agents created and idle — no turn running, not paused, and no KV-cache lifecycle operation in flight.
  • A fresh session on load: recreate agents, then import. Do not import into an agent that is mid-turn.
  • Unreal: ExportDialog / ImportDialog are C++ only. The snapshot type is not Blueprint-exposed.

docs.title: Decide what belongs in the save
docs.text:
An exported dialog snapshot contains the completed interactions and the projection state needed to continue the conversation faithfully, including any rolling summary produced by a Summarize node. A snapshot that contains a fold cannot be imported by a pre-Summarize server (DialogUnsupportedComponent). It does not contain:

  • agent variables;
  • the workflow graph or model files;
  • UI transcript rows;
  • quest, world, or progression state;
  • KV-cache bytes;
  • the agent or session ID.

Experimental game memory (protocol v20). Named mutable knowledge bases are a second snapshot: SaveGameMemory(path, save_id) / LoadGameMemory(path, embed_timing, …). Callers supply save_id; the server stamps saved_at_ms. Whichever of dialog or memory is loaded second warns if the save_id values differ. embed_timing is required (Now or Lazy); first-use and eager loads re-embed every record.

Unity: TryllClient.SaveGameMemoryAsync / LoadGameMemoryAsync (embed timing must be Now or Lazy), plus per-store TryllMutableKb.ExportAsync / ImportAsync. Unreal: UTryllSubsystem::RequestSaveGameMemory / RequestLoadGameMemory (same embed-timing rule), plus FTryllMutableKb::Export / Import. Inspect and mutate stores in Window ▸ Tryll ▸ Knowledge in Unity or Window ▸ Tryll ▸ Tryll Knowledge in Unreal (manual Refresh; the window never polls): stores and session save/load on the left, Filter or Query records in the center, write/delete/clear and per-store TMKB export/import on the right — see Inspect and Edit Knowledge Stores. Dialog file APIs are TryllAgent.SaveDialog / LoadDialog and they preserve save_id / saved_at_ms on the TDLG snapshot.

Relative save paths join the process save root, not a per-session client field. An auto-launched Unity/Unreal sidecar passes --allow-absolute-save-paths and, in a player build, --save-root set to persistentDataPath / ProjectSavedDir() (or Project Settings Save Data Folder when you set one). The editor omits --save-root so memory/game.tmkb still lands under the authored storage folder. A standalone server sets saves in server-config.json and ignores any folder the game might wish it had sent; turn saves.enabled off to refuse disk writes. Absolute paths on the four file RPCs work only when the process allows them. See Server Configuration → Saves.

Store those values beside the snapshot in a versioned, game-owned envelope. Use an authored key such as a character ID or workflow asset GUID to identify an agent. Agent and session IDs are runtime handles and change when the game starts again.

For example, a Unity JSON save can store each canonical TDLG snapshot as Base64:

[Serializable]
public sealed class GameSave
{
    public int formatVersion = 1;
    public string scenarioKey;
    public SavedAgent[] agents;
    public QuestState quests;
}

[Serializable]
public sealed class SavedAgent
{
    public string characterKey;   // Stable authored identity, never AgentId
    public string dialogBase64;   // Canonical TDLG bytes
    public SavedVariable[] variables;
    public TranscriptLine[] transcript;
}

The outer schema is yours. Changing it does not require a Tryll protocol change. When a game update changes workflow graphs, bump your envelope version (or migrate) so a strict import fails with a useful message instead of DialogGraphMismatch.

docs.title: Save only at a quiescent point
docs.text:
ExportDialog is strict idle-only. It returns AgentBusy while:

  • a turn is generating or paused;
  • a KV-cache lifecycle operation is running; or
  • another dialog or lifecycle request is in flight.

Lock player input first, wait for every turn to complete, and check lifecycle-idle before starting the export. Your game must track whether a sent turn is still in flight; Unity's agent.IsLifecycleIdle tracks lifecycle requests and pauses, not the turn itself.

Do not cancel a turn merely to make a save unless that is your game's intended behavior. A paused tool call is still an open turn and must be resumed or cancelled before saving.

If you use TryllKvResidencyPolicy, pause its scheduling around the transaction so a debounce cannot start a prefill or eviction while you wait for idle:

policy.SchedulingSuspended = true;   // Unity: still flushes queued sends
try
{
    yield return WaitUntilIdle();
    // export every agent, then write the slot
}
finally
{
    policy.SchedulingSuspended = false;
}

On Unreal, do not call SetActiveAgent during the wait, and finish any in-flight cache operation before export. Register or enable the policy only after restore has imported dialogs and warmed the agents you want resident.

docs.title: Capture each agent
docs.text:
For every persistent agent:

  1. Synchronize its variables from the server if the save needs the authoritative values.
  2. Capture the typed variable values in your own schema.
  3. Export the dialog.
  4. Encode the snapshot as canonical TDLG bytes.
UnityUnrealC++Python 
agent.Variables.SyncFromServerAsync(null, syncError =>
{
    if (!syncError.IsOk)
    {
        FailSave(syncError.Message);
        return;
    }

    var savedVariables = CaptureVariables(agent.Variables);

    agent.ExportDialog((snapshot, exportError) =>
    {
        if (!exportError.IsOk)
        {
            FailSave(exportError.Message);
            return;
        }

        var saved = new SavedAgent
        {
            characterKey = characterKey,
            dialogBase64 = Convert.ToBase64String(snapshot.ToFlatBufferBytes()),
            variables = savedVariables,
            transcript = CaptureTranscript(),
        };
        ContinueSave(saved);
    });
});

Agent->GetVariables().SyncFromServerAsync({}, [Agent, CharacterKey](const FTryllError& SyncError)
{
    if (!SyncError.IsOk()) { FailSave(SyncError.Message); return; }

    Agent->ExportDialog(
        [CharacterKey](const FTryllDialogSnapshot& Snapshot, const FTryllError& Error)
        {
            if (!Error.IsOk()) { FailSave(Error.Message); return; }

            TArray<uint8> Bytes;
            FTryllError EncodeError;
            if (!Snapshot.ToFlatBufferBytes(Bytes, EncodeError))
            {
                FailSave(EncodeError.Message);
                return;
            }

            FSavedAgent Saved;
            Saved.CharacterKey = CharacterKey;
            Saved.DialogBase64 = FBase64::Encode(Bytes);
            Saved.Variables = CaptureVariables();
            ContinueSave(Saved);
        });
});

agent.Variables().SyncFromServer();
auto savedVariables = CaptureVariables(agent.Variables());

auto snapshot = agent.ExportDialog();
auto bytes = Tryll::Client::EncodeFlatBuffer(snapshot);

SavedAgent saved;
saved.characterKey = characterKey;
saved.dialogBase64 = Base64Encode(bytes);
saved.variables = std::move(savedVariables);

from tryll_client.dialog_snapshot import encode_flatbuffer

agent.variables.sync_from_server()
saved = {
    "character_key": character_key,
    "dialog": encode_flatbuffer(agent.export_dialog()),
    "variables": capture_variables(agent.variables),
    "transcript": capture_transcript(),
}

ExportDialog flushes locally staged variable writes before it sends the snapshot request. The explicit synchronization above is still useful when the save must read back the server's authoritative variable mirror.

Export all required agents before writing the file. If any export fails, keep the previous slot untouched.

docs.title: Commit the save atomically
docs.text:
Before replacing a slot:

  1. Confirm every expected stable agent key appears exactly once.
  2. Confirm every dialog blob decodes (FromFlatBufferBytes / DecodeFlatBuffer / decode_flatbuffer).
  3. Serialize the complete envelope to a temporary sibling file.
  4. Replace the previous slot only after the temporary write succeeds.

This prevents a crash, disk error, or failed agent export from destroying the last valid save.

docs.title: Restore in a fresh session
docs.text:
Restore after the session and agents have been recreated:

  1. Read and validate the entire envelope before changing live state.
  2. Recreate each agent with the expected workflow graph and variable declarations.
  3. Match saved records to agents by stable authored key.
  4. Decode and import every dialog with Strict compatibility.
  5. Restore and flush agent variables.
  6. Restore UI, quest, world, and progression state.
  7. Optionally prefill the currently active agents' KV caches, then start any residency policy.

A scene or level reload is a reliable all-or-nothing wrapper: validate the slot first, then load into a new session and abandon that session if any import fails.

UnityUnrealC++Python 
var bytes = Convert.FromBase64String(saved.dialogBase64);
var snapshot = TryllDialogSnapshot.FromFlatBufferBytes(bytes);

agent.ImportDialog(
    snapshot,
    TryllDialogCompatibility.Strict,
    (result, importError) =>
    {
        if (!importError.IsOk)
        {
            FailLoad(importError.Message);
            return;
        }

        RestoreVariables(agent.Variables, saved.variables);
        agent.Variables.FlushIfDirty(flushError =>
        {
            if (!flushError.IsOk)
            {
                FailLoad(flushError.Message);
                return;
            }

            RestoreTranscript(saved.transcript);
            ContinueLoad();
        });
    });

TArray<uint8> Bytes;
FBase64::Decode(Saved.DialogBase64, Bytes);

FTryllDialogSnapshot Snapshot;
FTryllError DecodeError;
if (!FTryllDialogSnapshot::FromFlatBufferBytes(Bytes, Snapshot, DecodeError))
{
    FailLoad(DecodeError.Message);
    return;
}

Agent->ImportDialog(
    Snapshot,
    ETryllDialogCompatibility::Strict,
    [Agent, Saved](const FTryllDialogImportResult& Result, const FTryllError& Error)
    {
        if (!Error.IsOk()) { FailLoad(Error.Message); return; }

        RestoreVariables(Agent->GetVariables(), Saved.Variables);
        Agent->GetVariables().FlushIfDirty(
            [](const FTryllError& FlushError)
            {
                if (!FlushError.IsOk()) FailLoad(FlushError.Message);
                else ContinueLoad();
            });
    });

auto bytes = Base64Decode(saved.dialogBase64);
auto snapshot = Tryll::Client::DecodeFlatBuffer(bytes);
auto result = agent.ImportDialog(snapshot); // Strict by default

RestoreVariables(agent.Variables(), saved.variables);
agent.Variables().Flush();

from tryll_client.dialog_snapshot import decode_flatbuffer

snapshot = decode_flatbuffer(saved["dialog"])
agent.import_dialog(snapshot)  # Strict by default
restore_variables(agent.variables, saved["variables"])
agent.variables.flush_if_dirty()
restore_transcript(saved["transcript"])

Import replaces the agent's whole dialog; it never appends. A failed import is atomic for that agent and leaves its current dialog unchanged.

A multi-agent restore is not one transaction

If three agents import successfully and the fourth fails, Tryll does not roll back the first three. Decode and validate every record up front. For strict all-or-nothing loading, restore into a fresh scene/session and abandon that session if any import fails.

docs.title: Choose compatibility deliberately
docs.text:
Use Strict for normal game loading. It verifies that the saved graph signature matches the recreated agent and returns DialogGraphMismatch (3020) if it does not.

AllowGraphMismatch is a migration tool. It restores compatible interactions, remaps projection windows where possible, and returns warnings. Do not enable it silently for production saves: inspect the warnings and test the changed workflow first.

Version the outer save separately from the Tryll snapshot format. When a game update changes character keys, variable declarations, or workflow graphs, migrate or reject the game save explicitly.

docs.title: Warm only the agents that need it
docs.text:
Dialog import invalidates the reusable LLM prefix and never prefills it. The next SendMessage restores the context automatically, but its first-token latency can be higher.

During a loading screen, call PrefillKvCache for the active character or a small hot set. If a residency policy will manage those agents afterwards, mark a successful restore prefill as already resident so the policy does not repeat it (Unity: policy.MarkResident(component)).

UnityC++Python 
agent.PrefillKvCache((result, error) =>
{
    if (!error.IsOk)
        Debug.LogWarning($"KV prefill failed: {error.Message}");
    else if (policy != null)
        policy.MarkResident(component);
});

auto result = agent.PrefillKvCache();
if (!result.applicable) {
    // Graph has no eligible LLM nodes; nothing to warm.
}

result = agent.prefill_kv_cache()

Avoid prefilling every inactive NPC unless the memory and loading-time cost is intentional. See Manage an Agent's KV Cache and Run many agents on a small GPU.

docs.title: Handle expected failures
docs.text:
Error Meaning Save/load response AgentBusy (3004) Turn, pause, cache operation, or snapshot request is active Keep input locked, wait for idle, and retry with a timeout. DialogSnapshotInvalid (3018) Snapshot data is malformed Reject the save. DialogFormatUnsupported (3019) Snapshot format is not supported by this build Reject or migrate the save. DialogGraphMismatch (3020) Strict import found a different workflow graph Load the matching game version or run an explicit migration. DialogSnapshotTooLarge (3021) Snapshot exceeds the 1 MiB frame cap. Unity/Unreal reject the import on the client so the connection stays up. Do not truncate the encoded blob; start a new dialog or deliberately reduce retained history before a later save. DialogUnsupportedComponent (3022) Snapshot contains a component this build cannot import Reject or migrate the save.

Always bound idle waits and retries. Surface a useful error to the player instead of leaving the save UI spinning indefinitely.

Unity: use TryllAgentCoroutines

The Unity plugin ships coroutine wrappers — TryllAgentCoroutines.ExportDialog, ImportDialog, SyncVariablesFromServer, FlushVariables, and PrefillKvCache — that retry AgentBusy at a polite interval and bound every wait with a wall-clock deadline. On a dropped connection they report Timeout (1003) instead of leaving the coroutine waiting forever.

docs.title: Reference implementation
docs.text:
The Murder Mystery Demo implements this pattern for four suspects and a background note-taker:

  • Assets/Scripts/Save/SaveData.cs — versioned game-owned envelope;
  • Assets/Scripts/Save/SaveService.cs — validation and atomic slot writes;
  • Assets/Scripts/Save/SaveCoordinator.cs — quiescent multi-agent export, ordered strict restore, variable restoration, and hot-set prefill.

The demo stores dialog, variables, disclosure state, UI transcripts, notes, and investigation progress together while keeping the canonical Tryll snapshot opaque. Guard-blocked lines stay in the client transcript (marked out-of-character) and are absent from the server snapshot.
