Python, C++, Unity and Unreal all support it, including the editor palettes, inspectors and Dialog Lab attribute checks.
  • ClassifyIntentLLM writes its decision to a slot. New output_name (empty = node name). The slot holds the winning id on found and not_found_intent on every not_found path, so a Branch can route on it after either exit. not_found_intent also accepts the reserved #uncertain. See Output slot.
  • intents is the only intent list. The comma-separated intents_ids / intents_prompt pair deprecated in v0.8.0 is removed (see Breaking changes).

docs.title: Localization
docs.text:
• Localized prompts use your string tables. Tick Localized on a prompt field and the box becomes a Text ID. Before the agent is created, Unity or Unreal asks your text provider for the text and sends it. See Localize prompts with your localization system.
  • A language change updates live agents. Ticked non-structural prompts (system prompt, template, instruction, acknowledge text) are updated from the next turn, and params you changed at runtime are kept. The update is all or nothing per agent. If a Text ID is missing in the new language, that agent's prompts stay as they were and LocalizedTextFailed (Unity) / OnLocalizedTextFailed (Unreal) fires. ClassifyIntent entry prompts, files already bound and an open voice input still need the agent recreated or the input reopened. See Ship an agent in another language.
  • Unreal: wait for the new text. OnLocalizedTextApplied fires once an agent's new prompts are acknowledged, so a prefill or reset can wait for them. A server rejection of the update now also raises OnLocalizedTextFailed. The Unreal text provider is None by default, so existing projects keep using the Tryll Locale field.

docs.title: Models and catalogs
docs.text:
• Qwen3-TTS 12Hz 1.7B Base (Q4_K_M) is a public catalog voice. It clones its voice from a reference clip, so the profile's reference_voice is required. It speaks zh, en, de, it, pt, es, ja, ko, fr and ru through lang, and it runs on the CPU, Vulkan and CUDA backends without ONNX Runtime. Delivery modes switch reference clips. See TTS models.
  • SenseVoice Multilingual and Streaming Paraformer zh-en are now public speech-to-text entries.
  • LFM2.5 1.2B Thinking (Q4_K_M) joins the catalog. It always opens with a <think> block, so it is not a good host for an immersion guard.
  • New Model Benchmarks section. Model cards and per-trait leaderboards for catalog models: the immersion guard (General and World classifiers), prefill and generation speed for a 1K and a 4K prompt, and VRAM at an 8K context. Treat the results as provisional.

docs.title: Diagnostics and Agent Log
docs.text:
• Prefill and generation speed per node. Language-model nodes add engine.llama_perf to turn diagnostics, with prompt and generation time and token counts for the node's context. See Turn Diagnostics JSON.
  • Agent Log export. Export writes the journal to one JSON file in Unity and Unreal. The file has a header describing the server, the capture and the agents, then the events with their payloads, then a turn index. The inspectors show the event's raw JSON. The file can contain player input, prompts and tool arguments, so treat it like a bug report. See Use the Agent Log and Agent Log format.

docs.title: Unreal
docs.text:
• Play → Standalone Game starts its own server. A standalone game used to skip auto-launch silently and then fail every connect attempt. It now launches the bundled server on a free port, separate from the editor's server, and the server exits 60 s after the game closes. See Auto-launch the server.
  • Saved assets survive node parameter changes. Workflow and agent assets saved by an older plugin load correctly after a node field is removed, renamed or given a new default. A saved ClassifyIntentLLM CSV intent pair is converted into intents on load.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• New Use Cases section. Each page starts from what the player experiences and lists the building blocks that produce it, with links to the how-to guides: Talking NPC step by step, Ambient world, Voice control, In-game assistant, and AI director, an idea we have not built yet.
  • New reference pages: Voice Profile, TryllVoiceProfile, Classify Attributes (LLM) and Agent Log format. TTS models gains a per-family table of what a delivery mode can change.

docs.title: Breaking changes and behavior changes
docs.text:
• The schema changed — rebuild every client. The agent voice, ClassifyAttributesLLM, the ClassifyIntentLLM changes and LoRA adapters all change shape. Upgrade the server and every client together (Unity, Unreal, Python, C++). An older server would ignore adaptation and quietly run the base model, so mismatched peers fail at connect: the client rejects the server's protocol version with 5004 ProtocolVersionMismatch. See Wire Protocol.
  • One voice per agent. Speak and GenerateAndSpeak lose tts_model_name, speaker_id, speed, tts_lang, tts_voice, tts_voice_description, tts_delivery_instruction and emit_visemes. They keep only their text routing and chunking (min_sentence_chars, first_chunk_max_chars). A graph with a speaking node and no voice fails with 3025 AgentVoiceRequired. An agent created without a voice cannot be given one later. ChangeAgentParam can no longer change any voice field. Write down your TTS values before you upgrade the plugin, then follow Migrate to the agent voice.
  • tts_model_name is required. An empty name no longer means "the first TTS voice in the catalog", and a missing TTS model fails with 3023 InvalidVoiceProfile instead of 3003 GraphCompilationFailed.
  • Fixed-language voices reject lang. A non-empty lang on Pocket TTS, Orpheus or Maya1 fails with 3023 instead of being ignored. Leave it empty.
  • The audio format is announced once per turn. A turn with two speaking nodes no longer sends a second format frame or restarts the viseme clock. Code that reset playback on each format announcement now sees one per turn.
  • ClassifyIntentLLM CSV intents removed. intents_ids / intents_prompt are gone, and intents (id + prompt pairs) must hold 2–26 entries. Unreal assets convert a saved CSV pair on load. If the two lists had different lengths, the missing entries are left empty and a warning is logged. Other assets that still carry a CSV pair must move it to intents before upgrading. The diagnostics key parameters.intents_ids is unchanged.
  • LoRA adapters are structural. adaptation is fixed at agent creation. Changing it on a live agent returns 3006 ParamNotMutable.
  • Unreal Play → Standalone Game launches a server. A standalone run that used to have no server now starts its own on a free port.

docs.title: New error codes
docs.text:
• 3023 InvalidVoiceProfile — a voice profile field fails validation, names an unknown model, or uses a field the model cannot use.
  • 3024 UnknownDeliveryMode — SetAgentDeliveryMode named a mode the voice does not define. The current mode stays.
  • 3025 AgentVoiceRequired — a speaking graph has no voice, or a voice call was made on an agent created without one.

See Error Codes for the full list.

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
What can you build with Tryll, and which pieces do you need for it? Each page in this section starts from something a player experiences and walks through the building blocks that produce it. The pages link to the How-to Guides for the exact steps, so read a use case first to choose your design, then follow the links to build it.

All of these run on the player's own PC, inside your Unity or Unreal game.

docs.title: The building blocks
docs.text:
Every use case combines the same few blocks:

Block What it does for your game Speech-to-text (STT) Turns the player's voice into text. Small language model (SLM) Reads the conversation and writes the reply. Text-to-speech (TTS) Speaks the reply in a character's voice. Retrieval (RAG) Looks up lore, history or game facts and hands the relevant ones to the model. Classification Reads the player's line and turns it into a value your game can use, such as "accusing", "flirting" or "rude". Tool calls Lets the model ask your game to do something, such as open a door or attack. Your code decides and runs it. Graph Connects the blocks. An agent is a graph of nodes, edited visually in Unity or Unreal.

docs.title: The use cases
docs.text: Use case The player experiences Main blocks Talking NPC A character you speak with: a basic NPC that talks and stays in its role, plus add-ons for knowledge, mechanics, emotion, actions and memory. STT, SLM, TTS, then retrieval, classification, tool calls, memory Ambient world Background characters who chat among themselves, and a narrator, radio or newspaper that reports what happened in the game. SLM, TTS, game events, background priority Voice control Commanding the game or your squad by voice. Characters may answer with prewritten lines. STT, SLM, tool calls In-game assistant A helper that knows the game, remembers what you did, looks things up and acts for you. STT, SLM, TTS, retrieval, tool calls AI director (idea) A model that plans quests or directs the story, while your game systems carry out the plan. We have not built this yet; the page shows the research and the blocks you would use. SLM, grammar-constrained output, tool calls

docs.title: AI Director (Idea)
docs.text:
This is an idea, not a feature

We have not built an AI director, and we have not measured how well small on-device models do this job. This page describes the idea, what published research says about it, and which Tryll building blocks you would use to try it. Every block it needs exists today.

So far, every use case has the model talking. An AI director has the model deciding: which quest to offer next, how a rival faction responds to the player, what a village does tomorrow, when to raise the tension. Think of a dungeon master who watches the game and plans what happens next.

docs.title: The model plans, the game executes
docs.text:
A language model is good at reading a messy situation and proposing a sensible next move. It is bad at keeping exact rules, counts and world state consistent over a long game. Research on LLM game masters finds exactly this split: models write engaging stories but struggle to run consistent, verifiable game mechanics (RPGBench), and they cannot reliably check their own plans (Kambhampati et al.).

So divide the work:

  • High level, the model: pick goals and write a plan. "The bandits raid the mill at dawn, because the player killed their scout and the guard is away."
  • Low level, your game: carry out the plan with the systems you already have: pathfinding, combat AI, crafting recipes, schedules. These are exact and tested.

The best-known example of this loop is Voyager: in Minecraft, the model proposes the next task and writes the steps, the game's own API executes them, and the results go back to the model for the next round. Generative Agents uses the same split for characters: the model writes each character's plan for the day, and the game moves them around.

flowchart LR
    State["Game state<br/>snapshot"] --> Plan["Model writes<br/>a plan (JSON)"]
    Plan --> Check["Game validates<br/>the plan"]
    Check -->|invalid| Plan
    Check -->|valid| Run["Game systems<br/>execute it"]
    Run --> Events["Outcomes<br/>become events"]
    Events --> State

docs.title: How you would build it with Tryll
docs.text:
1. Give it the current state, every time. Your game sends a short, up-to-date summary of the world with each planning request: who is where, what the player did, what the factions want. Do not rely on the model to remember the world across many turns. Run the director stateless, or with a summary at most.
  2. Give it your design. Put your designers' material in a knowledge base: quest templates, faction goals, story beats that are allowed to happen. The model then chooses and adapts authored content instead of inventing the world. Drama Llama works this way: authors write story fragments with conditions, and the model decides when they fire.
  3. Force a plan your game can read. Add a grammar to the generation node, so the output is always a JSON plan in your schema. Grammar-constrained decoding produces reliable structured output without fine-tuning (Geng et al.). See Constrained output. Alternatively, let the director call tools such as spawn_patrol(...) or offer_quest(...); giving an LLM game master game-specific functions improved both its storytelling and its consistency with the game state (Song et al.).
  4. Validate before you run. The grammar guarantees the plan's shape, never that it makes sense. Your game checks every plan: does this character exist, is this recipe real, can this patrol reach the mill? If not, send the errors back and ask for a new plan, or fall back to a scripted choice. This "the model proposes, something exact checks" structure is the core recommendation of Kambhampati et al., and LLM+P takes it further by letting a classical planner do the planning.
  5. Plan in stages. Ask for the big picture first (this act's three main beats), then the details of each beat in separate calls. A recent world-to-quest pipeline found that each stage conditioned on the structured output of the previous one reduced drift and invented facts (Borawski et al.).
  6. Keep it off the player's path. A director thinks between moments, not during them. Create it with the Background workload so its work yields to the characters the player is talking to. See Ambient world.

An illustrative plan schema, the kind of output a grammar would enforce:

{
  "goal": "raid_mill",
  "faction": "red_bandits",
  "reason": "scout killed by player; mill guard reassigned",
  "steps": [
    {"action": "gather", "units": 6, "at": "bandit_camp", "time": "night"},
    {"action": "move",   "to": "old_mill", "time": "dawn"},
    {"action": "attack", "target": "old_mill"}
  ]
}

docs.title: Risks to plan for
docs.text:
• Invalid plans. Models name places, items and characters that do not exist. Validation in step 4 is not optional.
  • Drift over a long game. In a benchmark of long interactive stories, the best model tested kept its narrative commitments in only 42% of runs after 20 turns (NCP-Bench). Your game, not the model, must hold the canonical state, and send it fresh every time.
  • Latency. Plan, check and retry loops take several model calls. That is fine for a director that plans the next hour of play, and wrong for anything that must react within a second.
  • Small models are untested here. The research above uses large cloud models. Whether a 4B to 14B model on the player's GPU plans well enough is an open question. Start small to find out.

docs.title: A small first experiment
docs.text:
Do not start with a full story director. Pick one narrow decision with a clear fallback:

  • Choose the next side quest from ten authored templates and fill in its parameters (giver, target, reward) from the current game state.
  • Plan a villager's day as a list of activities and places that your schedule system then runs.
  • Pick a faction's response to the player's last major action from a short menu of authored responses.

Each is one grammar-constrained call, easy to validate and easy to replace with a scripted choice when the plan is rejected.

docs.text:

  • Wang et al., 2023. Describe, Explain, Plan and Select (DEPS)
  • Liu et al., 2023. LLM+P: Empowering Large Language Models with Optimal Planning Proficiency

docs.title: Ambient World
docs.text:
Not every character waits for the player to speak. Townsfolk gossip at the market, two guards argue at the gate, a radio host reports last night's raid, a newspaper prints the player's latest scandal. This page covers the agents that talk on their own: the player hears or reads them but does not converse with them.

There are two kinds:

  • Background characters: short lines and overheard conversations that make a place feel alive.
  • Narrators: a radio, a newspaper, a chronicler or an in-world announcer that turns what happened in the game into a story.

Both follow the same pattern as the Talking NPC: your game owns the events, the agent owns the words. Your game decides what happened and when it is worth mentioning. The agent decides how to say it.

flowchart LR
    Ev["Game events<br/>(raid, trade, rumour)"] --> Game["Your game picks<br/>what to report"]
    Game -->|SendMessage| Agent["Ambient agent"]
    Agent --> Out["Spoken line, radio segment,<br/>newspaper text"]

docs.title: Getting game events into the model
docs.text:
The model only knows what you send it. Three ways to pass events, usually combined:

  • Describe the event in the message. Send a short factual line as the agent's input, such as The player stole bread from the baker. Two guards saw it. The agent's prompt tells it to react to the event in character.
  • Put standing facts in variables. Facts that change slowly, such as the town's mood, the season or the player's reputation, go in agent variables and are rendered into the prompt template with {{var.reputation}}. Your game updates them; it does not have to repeat them in every message.
  • Seed recent history. To give an agent a few recent events as context without asking it to answer each one, append them to its history while it is idle. See Seed and edit dialog history.

Decide whether the agent should remember. A gossiping villager who reacts to one event at a time works best stateless: every call starts fresh, so old events never leak into new lines. A radio host running a whole evening's show should keep its history, so it can say "as I told you earlier", with a Summarize node to keep that history short.

docs.title: Background characters
docs.text:
Barks. Short reactive lines ("Hey, watch it!", "Lovely weather today"). Three options, from most to least controlled:

  • Prewritten lines. A CannedResponse node picks a line from a list, and a Speak node voices it. No language model is involved.
  • Generated, but from a fixed set. A grammar on the generation node limits the output to an allowed list, so the model chooses the fitting bark but cannot invent new ones. See Constrain output with a grammar.
  • Free generation. The model writes a fresh line for the situation. Best for ambient chatter, where variety matters more than control.

Overheard conversations. Two background characters talking to each other are two agents, and your game passes the lines between them: A's reply becomes B's input, and so on. Your game controls the whole exchange: who starts, what the topic is (a recent event works well) and when it stops. Cap it at a few lines; long AI-to-AI conversations drift.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Game
    participant A as Guard A
    participant B as Guard B
    Game->>A: "Topic: the player was seen near the vault."
    A-->>Game: line 1 (spoken)
    Game->>B: line 1
    B-->>Game: line 2 (spoken)
    Game->>A: line 2
    A-->>Game: line 3 (spoken), game ends the exchange

Each speaking character has its own voice profile, so the guards do not sound alike.

docs.title: Narrators: radio, newspaper, chronicler
docs.text:
A narrator is one agent with a strong style and a stream of events.

  1. Collect events. Your game logs what happens: quests finished, fights won, prices rising, the player's notable choices.
  2. Pick and batch. At the right moment (the radio's next segment, the morning edition, the end of a chapter) your game selects the events worth reporting and sends them to the narrator in one message.
  3. Write in style. The narrator's prompt sets the voice: a tabloid headline writer, a breathless sports commentator, a dry royal chronicler. One example paragraph in that style steers a small model better than any description.
  4. Deliver. For a newspaper or a journal, display the text. For a radio or an announcer, use GenerateAndSpeak with a narrator voice.

Keep the facts in your game's hands. If the newspaper must state the exact bounty or the score, pass it as a variable and let Tryll insert it into the text, as described in Substitute agent variables in output. The model then cannot get the number wrong.

A narrator can also sit inside a conversation. One turn can produce a narrator line and a character line, each tagged with the node that wrote it, so your UI can show them differently. See Send multiple answers in one turn.

docs.title: Keeping the world from slowing the player down
docs.text:
Ambient agents compete with the conversation the player is actually having, and with your game's rendering, for the same GPU. Tryll has two controls for this.

  • Background priority. Create ambient agents with the Background workload. Nobody is waiting on their output, so the server paces them and gives way to the agent the player is talking to. The workload is a scheduling hint only: it changes when the work runs, never what is generated.
  • Inference throttle. When your game needs the GPU back, for example during a heavy fight or a level load, it can tell the server to yield. Background work slows first; visible streaming text slows last. See Inference throttle and agent workload.
UnityPython 
// Set before the agent is created; it is fixed for the agent's lifetime.
agentComponent.Workload = TryllWorkload.Background;

from tryll_client import AgentWorkload

narrator = client.create_agent(graph, workload=AgentWorkload.Background)

Ambient agents are also cheap in memory when they share a model. A model loads once and every agent that uses it shares the weights; each agent adds only its own working cache. Give ambient agents small context sizes, since their prompts are short. See Run many agents on a small GPU.

docs.title: Ideas
docs.text:
Idea Kind Input from the game Output Market gossip Background Recent player actions, town mood Overheard lines between two villagers Guard barks Background Player is sneaking, running, armed One spoken line from a fixed set War radio Narrator Battles won and lost, territory changes Spoken news segment Town newspaper Narrator The player's notable deeds and scandals Headline and short article Captain's log Narrator Mission events Written journal entry Case notes Narrator Each finished interrogation Running investigation summary

docs.title: In-Game Assistant
docs.text:
A helper that lives in the game: a ship's computer, a familiar on your shoulder, a guild clerk, a tutorial companion. The player asks it things ("what does this rune do?", "where did I leave the cart?", "what did the mayor promise me?") and it answers from what it knows about the game and about this playthrough. It can also do things for the player.

Building blocks: speech-to-text, a small language model, text-to-speech, retrieval and tool calls. It is a Talking NPC whose main job is knowledge instead of drama.

docs.title: Two kinds of knowledge
docs.text:
An assistant answers from two very different sources, and each needs its own tool.

Game knowledge Playthrough history Examples Item stats, crafting recipes, lore, quest hints, controls Where the player went, what they bought, who they promised what Changes Only when you patch the game Every minute of play Lives in A knowledge base you ship with the game Your game's own records, or a knowledge base written during play Read with Retrieval Tool calls, or retrieval from a writable knowledge base

docs.title: Game knowledge: retrieval
docs.text:
Ship your game's reference material as a knowledge base and put a Retrieve node in front of the answer. Each question pulls the few matching entries into the prompt. If nothing matches, the assistant says it does not know, instead of guessing.

Two things matter for an assistant in particular:

  • No spoilers. Tag entries with the chapter or quest they belong to, and filter on the player's progress, kept in an agent variable. The assistant cannot reveal what it cannot retrieve.
  • Vague questions. Players ask "how do I beat him?". A query-rewriting step turns the question, together with the recent conversation, into a proper search.

docs.title: Playthrough history: two options
docs.text:
Option A: query your game's records with tool calls. Your game already tracks what happened: inventory, quest log, visited places, combat log. Give the assistant a tool such as query_log(event_type, place, character). When the player asks "where did I last see the orc?", the model calls the tool, the turn pauses, your game runs the query and returns the result, and the assistant answers from it.

flowchart LR
    Q["'Where did I last<br/>see the orc?'"] --> TC["ToolCall:<br/>query_log(...)"]
    TC -->|turn pauses| Game["Your game<br/>runs the query"]
    Game -->|result| G["GenerateAndSpeak:<br/>'In the north mine,<br/>an hour ago.'"]

This keeps the facts exact, because they come straight from game state. Choose the model with care: this is the hardest of our tool-call suites. On our game-log suite (two tools, four filters, and players who never name every detail), NVIDIA Orchestrator 8B, Ministral 3 14B and Qwen 3.5 4B pass 19 of 20 cases, while Llama 3.1 8B passes 12.

Option B: a memory the assistant writes and reads. Tryll can keep a writable knowledge base for the session. Your game, or the agent itself, writes notes into it during play ("The mayor promised 200 gold for the wolf pelts"), and a Retrieve node finds the relevant ones when the player asks. The WriteToMemory node lets the agent record facts from the conversation without any game code. The whole memory is saved and loaded with the player's save game.

Option B suits loose, conversational facts that your game does not track in a table. Option A suits anything your game already stores precisely. Many assistants use both.

docs.title: Acting for the player
docs.text: The same tool-call mechanism lets the assistant act: mark a location on the map, sort the inventory, set a waypoint, pause the game and open the right menu. As always, the model only asks; your game checks and performs the action. For anything the player might regret, such as selling an item, have your game ask for confirmation first.

docs.title: Putting it together
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    In["Player question"] --> TC["ToolCall<br/>(query_log, set_waypoint, ...)"]
    TC -->|tool_called| Game["Your game:<br/>query or act"]
    Game --> R["Retrieve game knowledge<br/>(filtered by progress)"]
    TC -->|no_tool_called| R
    R --> C["Transform:<br/>facts + question"]
    C --> G["GenerateAndSpeak"]

Keep the assistant inside the fiction where your game has one. A ship's computer that answers "as an AI language model..." breaks it. The immersion guard from the Talking NPC page applies here too.

In the demo: AquariumExpert (an assistant that answers from a knowledge base, with query rewriting and an "I don't know" path), Mother (an experimental ship computer that reports status and reads and writes the ship's log through tools and a writable knowledge base) and Nessa (an experimental character who records what the player tells her with WriteToMemory).

docs.title: Talking NPC
docs.text:
A character the player can speak with: it listens, answers in its own voice, knows its world, takes part in your game's mechanics, shows emotion, acts and remembers.

You do not build all of that at once. Every talking character starts from the same basic NPC: it holds a conversation, by text or voice, and stays in its role. On top of that, the advanced NPC features are add-ons. Each one is independent of the others, so pick the ones your game needs, in any order.

Part Feature What it adds Building blocks Basic NPC Natural dialogue Free conversation, no dialogue tree A small language model Basic NPC Voice in and out The player speaks; the character answers aloud Speech-to-text, text-to-speech Basic NPC Roleplay guardrails The character stays in its world A pattern check and two classifiers Advanced NPC Knowledge and lore Answers from your world's facts Retrieval (RAG) Advanced NPC Talking is the gameplay Dating, interrogation, trading, negotiation Classification, pause, branching Advanced NPC Emotions Mood in the words and in the voice Instructions, voice delivery modes Advanced NPC Actions and tools The conversation changes the game Tool calls Advanced NPC Memory and summarization The character remembers, across saves too Summaries, writable memory, save snapshots

One principle runs through every feature: your game owns the rules, the agent owns the words. The model never decides a price, a relationship score or whether a door opens. It reads the player, and it speaks. Your game code holds the state and makes the decisions.

docs.title: Basic NPC
docs.text: The three things every talking character needs. With these alone you can ship a character the player talks to freely.

docs.title: Natural dialogue
docs.text:
The player experiences: a character who understands plain language and answers in character, for as long as they keep talking. There is no dialogue tree and no list of lines to pick from.

Building block: a small language model.

The smallest working graph is one node. For a voiced character it is GenerateAndSpeak, which writes the reply and speaks it (see Voice in and out); for a text character it is Generate.

What makes the character feel right is mostly the prompt: the role, the backstory and the way the character speaks. Our NPC prompt study found two rules that matter most: include at least one line of the character's own dialogue, and never put a speaker label such as Kira: in front of it, because models copy the label into the reply.

The same prompt can change with your game. A template such as {{var.player_title}} reads an agent variable your game sets, so a quest giver greets a newcomer and a hero differently without a second graph.

In the demo: TavernBartender (a text NPC) and QuestGiver (one character, two attitudes, driven only by game variables).

Build it: Design an NPC prompt · Build a chat agent with a graph · Use Mustache templates · Agent variables

docs.title: Voice in and out
docs.text:
The player experiences: they speak to the character and it answers out loud, in its own voice, with almost no wait.

Building blocks: speech-to-text (STT), text-to-speech (TTS). Both run on the player's device, and the lighter models run on the CPU.

GenerateAndSpeak starts speaking the first sentence while later sentences are still being generated, so the character starts talking almost at once. The voice belongs to the agent, set through its voice profile: pick a TTS model and a voice, or clone one from a short recording. You do not record every line.

Voice input sits outside the graph. Your game streams microphone audio to Tryll, gets the transcript back, and sends the final phrase to the agent as if the player had typed it. You choose push-to-talk or hands-free.

flowchart LR
    Mic["Player's voice"] -->|STT| Text["Transcript"]
    Text --> GAS["GenerateAndSpeak"]
    GAS -->|TTS| Audio["NPC speaks"]

Languages depend on the models you choose; see speech-to-text and voice input and the TTS models. For a face that moves with the voice, add lip sync.

In the demo: VoiceCharacter (the full voice loop).

Build it: Add voice output · Use voice input · Clone a voice · Add lip sync

docs.title: Roleplay guardrails
docs.text:
The player experiences: a character who stays in its world, however hard they push. "Ignore your instructions", "what model are you?" or "tell me about smartphones" in a medieval village get an in-character answer.

Building blocks: a pattern check and two classifiers, in front of the reply.

Players will test your character. An immersion guard catches those lines before they reach the reply model. The recommended guard has three stages, cheapest first:

  1. Pattern check. A RegexGuardrail catches the well-known phrasings at almost no cost.
  2. General check. A classifier catches lines aimed at the software rather than the character: jailbreaks, questions about the AI, requests to change the rules.
  3. World check. A second classifier catches lines that do not belong in your world, such as modern technology in a fantasy setting.
flowchart LR
    In["Player line"] --> P["Pattern check"]
    P -->|caught| D["In-character deflection"]
    P -->|ok| G["General check"]
    G -->|caught| D
    G -->|ok| W["World check"]
    W -->|caught| D
    W -->|ok| R["Reply"]

A caught line gets a prewritten, in-character deflection from a CannedResponse and never reaches the reply model. Your game can also remove it from the conversation history, so it does not echo in later turns.

In the demo: Death on Set (every suspect has the three-stage guard in front of its reply).

Build it: Build an immersion guard · Use canned responses and guardrails

docs.title: Advanced NPC
docs.text: Add-ons to the basic NPC. Each one works without the others; combine the ones your game needs.

docs.title: Knowledge and lore
docs.text:
The player experiences: the character knows the world's history, the town's gossip and its own past, stays consistent about them, and says so when it does not know.

Building block: retrieval (RAG).

You could paste all your lore into the prompt, but a long prompt is slow, and small models lose track of facts buried in it. Instead, keep the lore in a knowledge base and add a Retrieve node in front of the answer. Each turn, it finds the few passages that match what the player said and hands only those to the model.

flowchart LR
    In["Player line"] --> R["Retrieve"]
    R -->|found| C["Transform: lore + question"]
    R -->|not_found| D["CannedResponse: 'I don't know about that'"]
    C --> G["GenerateAndSpeak"]

Three things make retrieval work in a game:

  • Separate world lore from character history. Use one shared knowledge base for the world and one per character, so a blacksmith does not know the queen's secrets.
  • Gate what the character is allowed to say. Each passage can carry metadata, and a filter can compare it with a game variable. For example, a filter that keeps passages whose secret_level is at most the player's trust variable reveals more as trust grows, without changing the graph.
  • Handle the miss. When nothing matches, route to a short in-character answer instead of letting the model invent lore.

If players ask vague follow-ups ("what about him?"), a query-rewriting step turns the line into a proper search before retrieval.

In the demo: AquariumExpert (retrieval, the miss path and query rewriting) and Death on Set in the murder-mystery project (world lore plus per-suspect history, with secrets unlocked as the investigation progresses).

Build it: Retrieval-augmented generation · Create a simple RAG assistant · Query rewriting for RAG · Drive prompts and retrieval from game state

docs.title: Talking is the gameplay
docs.text:
The player experiences: what they say is the gameplay. Flattery works on one character and annoys another; an accusation backed by evidence breaks a suspect; a good argument lowers a price.

Building blocks: classification, pausing the turn, branching, game state.

A mechanic needs numbers and decisions, and those belong in your game code. The agent's job is to turn the player's free-form line into values your mechanic can read, and then to voice whatever your mechanic decided. That makes a loop:

  1. Classify. Judge the player's line along the dimensions your mechanic cares about. ClassifyAttributesLLM scores up to 16 dimensions in one batched call, each as a choice, a yes/no or a 0–1 score.
  2. Let the game decide. Your game receives the results as an event, updates its own state (affection, suspicion, the current price) and decides what happens.
  3. Pass the decision back. Put a Pause node after the classifier. While the turn is paused, your game can set agent variables and node parameters, and the rest of the same turn sees the new values. Then it resumes, either along the graph or straight to a node it names.
  4. Branch. If the character has distinct modes (friendly, suspicious, hostile), a Branch node or the resume target picks the path.
  5. Speak. The answering node reads the state through its template, such as {{var.affection}} or {{var.mood}}, and phrases the reply to fit.
flowchart LR
    In["Player line"] --> CL["ClassifyAttributesLLM"]
    CL --> P["Pause"]
    P -. "game updates state,<br/>picks the path" .-> P
    P --> B["Branch on mode"]
    B -->|friendly| T1["Transform: friendly tone"]
    B -->|hostile| T2["Transform: hostile tone"]
    T1 --> G["GenerateAndSpeak"]
    T2 --> G

What to classify and what the game owns depends on the mechanic:

Mechanic Classify the player's line Your game owns Dating charm, respect, humour, pushiness affection, relationship stage, what the character will agree to Interrogation accusation, evidence presented, pressure, sympathy suspicion, which secrets are unlocked Trading which item, offer, insult to the goods prices, stock, whether the deal closes Negotiation concession, threat, appeal, counteroffer each side's limits, the current offer

When a number must be exact, such as a price, do not ask the model to say it. Let the model write a placeholder, and Tryll replaces it with your game's value before the player hears it. See Keep merchant prices deterministic.

Simpler options

If you only need one label per turn, such as the player's intent, ClassifyIntentLLM picks it from a short menu, and IntentToInstruction turns the label into a tone instruction for the reply without any game code.

In the demo: Death on Set (interrogation: intents shape the suspect's answers, and the game unlocks per-suspect secrets as the case progresses), QuestGiver (the same character behaves differently for a newcomer and a hero, driven only by game variables), IntentGuard (intent becomes a tone directive) and StationMerchantHaggle (an experimental price-haggling loop).

Build it: Build an intent-driven NPC · Classify intent without a knowledge base · Pause and resume a turn · Branch on a slot · Agent variables · Keep merchant prices deterministic

docs.title: Emotions
docs.text:
The player experiences: the character's mood changes with what happens, and they can hear it in both what the character says and how it sounds.

Building blocks: your game's emotion system, instructions in the prompt, voice delivery modes.

The emotional state is another piece of game state, so your game owns it, just like a mechanic. It can change because of a classifier's results or because of anything else in the game: the player broke a promise, the character was hurt, night fell. Tryll then carries the mood into two places.

What the character says. Pass the mood into the reply prompt:

  • as an agent variable in a Transform template, for example The innkeeper is {{var.mood}} right now.;
  • or as an instruction, set by your game through an Instruction node, or chosen from a table by IntentToInstruction.

An adjective alone is a weak signal for a small model. A single example line spoken in that mood works much better, because models imitate an example far more reliably than they follow a description. Keep one short example line per mood and inject the one that matches.

How the character sounds. A voice profile can define delivery modes, one per mood. For voices cloned from a recording, each mode has its own reference clip, such as mack_calm.wav and mack_angry.wav, and the mood of the clip carries into the speech. Your game switches mode through the client API, for example SetDeliveryModeAsync("angry", 0.8f) in Unity. The change applies from the next sentence, even in the middle of a reply. Only your game code switches modes; the model cannot.

Voice Emotion control Pocket TTS, Qwen3-TTS, Chatterbox A reference clip per mood Maya1 A spoken-style instruction per mood, such as "whisper" or "sarcastic", with intensity Supertonic 3, Orpheus No emotion control; a mode can only change speed

On Unreal, the MetaHuman lip-sync plugin can also take the mood, so the face matches the voice.

In the demo: EmotionalVoiceCharacter (one voice with eight moods, each from its own clip; the mood is switched from the editor rather than by game logic).

Build it: Add emotions to a voice · Design a voice clip with Qwen3-TTS · Voice profile reference · Use Mustache templates · Add lip sync to a MetaHuman

docs.title: Actions and tools
docs.text:
The player experiences: the conversation has consequences. The guard opens the gate, the merchant hands over the item, the bandit draws a sword, the healer heals.

Building block: tool calls.

You give the agent a list of actions, each with a name, a description and optional arguments, through a ToolCall node. When the conversation calls for an action, the model picks one. Tryll sends the action's name and arguments to your game, and your game decides whether to do it and does it. The server never runs anything itself.

Two patterns cover most cases:

  • Fire and forget. The NPC attacks, follows or leaves. Your game plays the action and the conversation moves on.
  • Wait for the result. The NPC asks the game something before answering, such as the price of an item or whether a door is locked. The turn pauses, your game returns the result, and the reply uses it.
flowchart LR
    In["Player: 'Open the gate!'"] --> TC["ToolCall"]
    TC -->|tool_called| Game["Game: open_gate()"]
    Game --> G["GenerateAndSpeak: 'Fine, go through.'"]
    TC -->|no_tool_called| G

Choose the model by the job. In our tool-call comparison, on an NPC reaction suite (attack, trade, follow, leave, stay quiet), Nemotron Orchestrator 8B scored 20 of 20 and Qwen 3.5 4B scored 16, while Llama 3.2 1B scored 2. Keep the action list short and the descriptions clear: the descriptions are the prompt the model actually reads.

In the demo: StationMerchant (the merchant asks the game for a price and waits for it) and Mother (an experimental ship computer that reads and writes the ship's log through tools).

Build it: Tool calling · Define and handle tool calls · Design a tool-call prompt · Compare tool-call models · Test tool calls in the editor

docs.title: Memory and summarization
docs.text:
The player experiences: the character remembers. It does not lose the thread of a long conversation, it brings back what the player told it hours ago, and it still knows after the game is saved and loaded.

Building blocks: a rolling summary, a writable memory, save snapshots.

Memory works at three time scales.

Within a conversation. Every model has a fixed context window, and when the conversation outgrows it, the oldest turns drop out of the prompt. Add a Summarize node and the older turns are folded into a rolling summary instead, so the conversation can go on at a fixed token cost without the character forgetting how it started.

Facts that last. To keep specific facts, such as "the player likes cats" or "the player killed Atticus Pünd", write them into a memory the character can search. A WriteToMemory node stores a line in a named knowledge base, one per character if you like, and a Retrieve node on the same store, placed before the reply, brings the matching facts back when they become relevant. Writable memory is experimental in this release.

flowchart LR
    In["Player line"] --> R["Retrieve: character's memory"]
    R --> G["GenerateAndSpeak"]
    G --> W["WriteToMemory"]

To pull out structured facts, such as the clues a suspect mentioned, let a second agent read the exchange and answer through a grammar, so the result is always data your game can store.

Across saves. Your game owns the save file, and Tryll gives it what to put there: a snapshot of each agent's conversation, and a snapshot of every memory store. Load them back into a new session and the characters continue where they left off.

In the demo: TavernBartender (a long conversation kept coherent with a rolling summary) and Death on Set (a note-taker agent writes up each interview into the detective's case notes).

Build it: Keep long conversations coherent · Inspect and edit knowledge stores · Constrain output with a grammar · Export and import dialog · Save and load agent state

docs.title: All together
docs.text:
The Death on Set murder mystery in the Unity demos combines most of these features in one graph per suspect:

flowchart LR
    In["Player line"] --> Guard["Immersion guard<br/>(regex + 2 classifiers)"]
    Guard -->|caught| Deflect["CannedResponse → Speak"]
    Guard -->|ok| CI["ClassifyIntentLLM"]
    CI -->|intent| I2I["IntentToInstruction"]
    CI -->|none| RW["Retrieve world lore"]
    RW --> RC["Retrieve suspect history<br/>(gated by game state)"]
    I2I --> Comp["Transform"]
    RC --> Comp
    Comp --> GAS["GenerateAndSpeak<br/>(per-suspect voice)"]
    GAS --> Sum["Summarize"]

Four suspects share one loaded model, each with its own voice. The game tracks what the player has discovered and widens each suspect's retrieval filter as secrets unlock. A fifth agent, the note-taker, quietly writes up each interview; see Ambient world for agents the player does not talk to.

docs.title: Voice Control
docs.text:
The player speaks, and the game does it. Order a squad to flank, cast a spell by saying its name, tell a companion to wait by the door, steer a ship, open a menu. Unlike a Talking NPC, the point here is not conversation. It is turning free-form speech into a command your game can run.

Building blocks: speech-to-text, a small language model, and either tool calls or a grammar. Text-to-speech is optional.

flowchart LR
    Mic["'Bravo, get behind<br/>the red truck'"] -->|STT| Text["Transcript"]
    Text --> SLM["SLM: understand"]
    SLM --> Cmd["move(unit=bravo,<br/>target=red_truck)"]
    Cmd --> Game["Your game checks<br/>and runs it"]
    Game --> Ack["'Moving!'<br/>(prewritten line)"]

The model's only job is understanding. Players do not say commands the same way twice ("Bravo, cover behind that truck", "get Bravo to the red truck", "Bravo, truck, now"), and a small model maps all of them to the same command. Your game does everything else: it checks the command makes sense, runs it, and plays the reply.

The characters' replies do not need a language model at all. A soldier answering "Moving!" can use your game's usual recorded lines, or a CannedResponse node picking from a list. Add text-to-speech only if you want generated replies.

docs.title: Two ways to get a command
docs.text:
Tool calls Grammar What the model writes A call to one of your tools, with typed arguments, such as move(unit, target) One line that must match a pattern, such as <action> <object> Best for Commands with different shapes and arguments One flat vocabulary of actions and objects How it fails The model can call no tool when it should; that path is routed, not an error The output always fits the pattern, but can be the wrong command Node ToolCall Generate with a grammar Read Define and handle tool calls Constrain output with a grammar

Tool calls fit most games. Each command is a tool with a clear description and only the arguments it really needs. When the player says "get Bravo behind the red truck", your game receives the tool name and its arguments as JSON.

A grammar fits a fixed vocabulary, such as open door, take key, go north. The grammar only allows lines in that form, so the output is always machine-readable. The grammar can be changed at runtime, so your game can rebuild it from what is on screen right now: only the units that exist, only the doors in this room.

Either way, the model guarantees the form of the command, never that it is the right one. Your game must still check it: is there a red truck, is Bravo alive, can Bravo reach it? When the answer is no, have the character say so ("Can't see a red truck, sir"), the same way a human squadmate would.

docs.title: Make it hear your words
docs.text:
Voice control fails first in speech recognition, not in the model. Game words are hard for it: unit call signs, invented place names, spell names.

  • Hotwords. Give the speech recognizer a list of your game's words, and it will prefer them: "Aeltharion" instead of "Al Therion", "frostbolt" instead of "frost bolt". See Bias voice input with hotwords. Not every speech model supports this: Parakeet and Zipformer do; Whisper, SenseVoice and Paraformer do not.
  • Push-to-talk. For commands, a key to hold while speaking is more reliable than always listening. The player decides what is a command and what is chatter with friends.
  • Short words. One-word commands such as "Fire!" are easy to clip. Keep a little silence padding around each recorded phrase. See Use voice input.

docs.title: Keep each command independent
docs.text: A command agent usually should not remember earlier commands. Make it stateless: every phrase is understood on its own, and an old order can never leak into a new one. If a command depends on what the player sees, such as "attack that one", pass the current situation with each phrase, for example the selected target, as an agent variable rendered into the prompt.

docs.title: Choosing a model
docs.text:
Command parsing is one of the easier jobs for a small model. In our tool-call comparison, on a suite that maps player speech to heist-game commands:

Model Commands passed NVIDIA Orchestrator 8B 20 / 20 Ministral 3 14B 20 / 20 Bonsai 8B (1-bit) 20 / 20 Qwen 3.5 4B 18 / 20 Llama 3.1 8B 17 / 20 Llama 3.2 1B 14 / 20

Bonsai 8B in its 1-bit form scores 20 of 20 while needing about 1.9 GB of video memory, which leaves the rest of the GPU to your game.

In the demo: CommandParser (a stateless agent that turns any phrase into one of 16 <action> <object> commands with a grammar, on Llama 3.2 3B).

docs.title: typedef AnswerTextCallback
docs.text:
Callback type for streaming text chunks. 

using Tryll::Client::AgentProxy::AnswerTextCallback = std::function<
       void(std::string_view nodeName, std::string_view text, bool isDelta, bool isFinal)>;

Invoked on the reader thread for each AnswerText frame received from the server. Must return quickly and must not call any blocking TryllClient or AgentProxy methods.

Parameters: * nodeName — name of the workflow node that produced this text (multi-sender attribution; e.g. distinguishing two Generate nodes voicing different characters in the same turn). * text — streamed text chunk. * isDelta — true when text is an incremental token/chunk; false when it is the accumulated response so far. * isFinal — true for the last chunk before TurnComplete.

docs.title: typedef NodeEventCallback
docs.text:
Generic NodeEvent callback. 

using Tryll::Client::AgentProxy::NodeEventCallback = 
std::function<void(std::string_view nodeName,
                   std::string_view eventType,
                   const std::vector<NodeEventKeyValue>& kvPairs)>;

Invoked on the reader thread when a NodeEvent arrives whose event_type is unrecognised or whose typed callback is not set. If a typed callback (e.g. ToolCallCallback, IntentClassifiedCallback) is registered for the incoming event_type, this callback is NOT fired for that event.

Parameters: * nodeName — name of the emitting workflow node. * eventType — event discriminator. * kvPairs — ordered string→string payload.

using Tryll::Client::AgentProxy::PausedCallback = 
std::function<void(std::string_view nodeName, std::string_view pendingExit)>;

Invoked on the reader thread for each NodeEvent with event_type="paused" — fired by the executor when it pauses the turn between nodes (see PauseNode, pausing ToolCallDisposition values).

Parameters: * nodeName — the node that just exited and triggered the pause. * pendingExit — the exit route that will be taken on a plain (non-jump) Resume.

Must return quickly and must not call any blocking methods.

docs.title: typedef TtsAudioCallback
docs.text:
Callback type for streaming TTS PCM chunks. 

using Tryll::Client::AgentProxy::TtsAudioCallback = 
std::function<void(std::string_view nodeName, std::span<const int16_t> pcm)>;

Fired for each int16 LE PCM chunk synthesized by a GenerateAndSpeak/Speak node. End-of-stream is signalled by the existing turn-complete future returned from SendMessage — there is no per-chunk final flag.

Parameters: * nodeName — name of the producing node (multi-sender attribution). * pcm — the PCM chunk.

Must return quickly and must not call any blocking methods.

docs.title: typedef TtsAudioFormatCallback
docs.text:
Callback type for the TTS audio format announcement. 

using Tryll::Client::AgentProxy::TtsAudioFormatCallback = 
std::function<void(std::string_view nodeName, uint32_t sampleRate, uint16_t channels, uint16_t bitsPerSample)>;

Fired once per GenerateAndSpeak/Speak turn, before the first TtsAudioFrame.

Parameters: * nodeName — name of the producing node (multi-sender attribution). * sampleRate — PCM sample rate (e.g. 22050). * channels — channel count (always 1 for current models). * bitsPerSample — bit depth (always 16).

docs.title: typedef TtsVisemesCallback
docs.text:
Callback type for streaming TTS viseme frames. 

using Tryll::Client::AgentProxy::TtsVisemesCallback = 
std::function<void(std::string_view nodeName, std::span<const VisemeEvent> events)>;

Fired after each synthesized sentence when the agent's voice has emit_visemes set (any speaking node). The frame trails that sentence's audio frames (timing needs the final sample count). The contract is that events for a sample range arrive before that range plays under normal client buffering.

Parameters: * nodeName — name of the producing node (multi-sender attribution). * events — the viseme events in this frame (span valid only for the duration of the callback).

Must return quickly and must not call any blocking methods. Same threading as SetOnTtsAudio (dispatch thread).

Invoked on the reader thread once per turn, immediately after TurnComplete arrives. Covers client-initiated turns (via SendText).

Parameters: * status — turn outcome (::Tryll::TurnStatus). * debugInfoJson — JSON diagnostics string; non-empty only when the agent was created with enableDiagnostics=true. * tokensGenerated — total tokens sampled across all generation nodes.

Must return quickly and must not call any blocking methods.

docs.title: function ChangeParamsAsync
docs.text:
Apply typed node parameters to a named workflow node asynchronously. 

std::future< void > Tryll::Client::AgentProxy::ChangeParamsAsync (
    std::string_view nodeName,
    NodeParamsVariant params
)

The supplied params must match the concrete type of the target node (type mismatch → InvalidParamValue 3007 from the server). The mutation diff-loop on the server vetoes structural fields and invokes OnXxxChanged callbacks for fields that have changed.

The C++ client does not cache a baseline copy of authored params: callers must own the typed params they last sent (or authored at CreateAgent) and start each mutation from that local copy. Structural fields must match the create-time values or the server returns ParamNotMutable.

Typical clone-set-send idiom: 

GenerateParamsT p = myBaseline;   // caller-owned copy of authored params
p.system_prompt    = "New system prompt";
agent.ChangeParams("gen", std::move(p));

Parameters:

  • nodeName Instance name of the target node (as declared in the graph).
  • params Whole authored typed params for the node.

Returns:

Future completing on Ack. Throws TryllError on server-reported errors (UnknownNode 3005, ParamNotMutable 3006, InvalidParamValue 3007, or AgentBusy 3004).

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
Obtained via Tryll::Client::AgentProxy::Variables. Reads are synchronous, served from the local mirror — only the client writes variables in v1, so no server round-trip is needed to read one back. Writes are validated locally (unknown name / type mismatch throws Tryll::Client::TryllError immediately, no wire traffic) and staged; the proxy flushes any staged writes as one batched UpdateAgentVariablesRequest automatically, immediately before the next agent interaction (SendText / Resume / ChangeParams — not Cancel). Staged writes are coalesced per name (last value wins for scalars; a minimal add/remove delta, or a whole-set assign, whichever is smaller, for sets) so rapid repeated writes never grow the batch unboundedly.

Flushed writes are non-blocking. The batch is retained in-flight until the server acknowledges it: on a transient AgentBusy the batch is re-staged behind any newer writes and retried on the next interaction; on a hard rejection (rare, since the mirror pre-validates unknown-name/type-mismatch locally) the affected names are re-synced from the server so the mirror never stays silently diverged. Either way the error surfaces through the agent's usual Tryll::Client::AgentProxy::SetOnError callback, the same path SendText errors use.

docs.title: function SyncFromServer
docs.text:
void Tryll::Client::AgentVariables::SyncFromServer (
    std::vector< std::string > names={},
    std::chrono::milliseconds timeout=std::chrono::seconds{10}
)

Debug/verification round-trip: fetch current values from the server and merge them into the local mirror (does not touch pending/staged writes). Normal reads never need this — only the client writes variables in v1, so the mirror is authoritative; use this only to double-check server state. names empty means every declared variable. Blocks until the response arrives or timeout elapses.

Exception:

  • TryllError On server error, disconnect, or timeout.

auto session = Tryll::Client::TryllClient::RunAndConnect(opts);

docs.title: function AddGenerateAndSpeak
docs.text:
GraphDescriptionNodeMethods & Tryll::Client::GraphDescriptionNodeMethods::AddGenerateAndSpeak (
    std::string name,
    ::Tryll::NodeParams::GenerateAndSpeakParamsT params
)

Add a GenerateAndSpeak node. LLM-driven text generation + streaming TTS synthesis in a single fused node. Streams LLM tokens, segments them into sentences, synthesizes each sentence on a dedicated TTS strand, and emits PCM frames via OnTtsAudio callbacks. The voice (model, speaker, delivery mode, visemes) belongs to the agent: CreateAgentRequest.voice. Agent creation fails without one (3025).

Add a Retrieve node. RAG retrieval node. Embeds the HumanMessage, searches an embedded storage, and attaches a KnowledgeComponent to the current interaction.

docs.title: function AddSpeak
docs.text:
GraphDescriptionNodeMethods & Tryll::Client::GraphDescriptionNodeMethods::AddSpeak (
    std::string name,
    ::Tryll::NodeParams::SpeakParamsT params
)

Add a Speak node. Standalone TTS-only node. Voices its input-resolved slot (any upstream node's output — Generate, CannedResponse, etc. — or user_message itself), segments it into sentences, and synthesizes each on a dedicated TTS strand, emitting PCM frames via OnTtsAudio callbacks. Unlike GenerateAndSpeak it runs no LLM inference, so it can voice canned/scripted lines or any upstream-produced answer without paying for a generation pass. The voice belongs to the agent (CreateAgentRequest.voice); agent creation fails without one (3025).

docs.title: function AddSummarize
docs.text:
GraphDescriptionNodeMethods & Tryll::Client::GraphDescriptionNodeMethods::AddSummarize (
    std::string name,
    ::Tryll::NodeParams::SummarizeParamsT params
)

Add a Summarize node. Rolling conversation summary. Every time the history since the last fold crosses a trigger, this node compresses the older interactions (everything outside keep_recent_turns) into a SummaryComponent. Generate-class projection then renders that summary at the end of its system message and replays history only from covered_through + 1, so a long dialogue stays coherent at a fixed token cost instead of being trimmed away. Place it last in the graph, after the node that produced the player-facing reply.

Add a Transform node. Model-free input-composition node. Renders a Mustache template over user_message and the current turn's slots into its own slot; performs no inference and never emits on the wire (send = None, history_role = none, fixed). Typical use: query rewriting, fan-out composition feeding a downstream Retrieve/Generate input.

docs.title: function Stop
docs.text:
Release this handle without killing the server. 

void Tryll::Client::ManagedServer::Stop (
    std::chrono::milliseconds timeout=std::chrono::seconds{8}
)

Does not terminate the process. A managed server launched with idleShutdownTimeoutSeconds > 0 self-exits once no session is using it; this just drops our OS handle. Idempotent — safe to call more than once. Use Terminate for an immediate hard kill (e.g. the spawn succeeded but the handshake/connect afterward failed, so no session was ever created and nothing else can be relying on this process).

Parameters:

  • timeout Unused; kept for source compatibility.

docs.title: function Terminate
docs.text:
Immediately hard-kill the child process. 

void Tryll::Client::ManagedServer::Terminate (
    std::chrono::milliseconds timeout=std::chrono::seconds{8}
)

Sends a termination signal and waits up to timeout for the process to exit; force-killed if it does not exit in time. Idempotent — safe to call more than once, including after Stop. Intended for failure paths where the caller knows this process is theirs and nothing else can depend on it (e.g. spawn succeeded but connect/handshake failed) — do not call this after a successful handshake, since another consumer could be relying on the server staying up until its own idle timeout.

Parameters:

  • timeout How long to wait for graceful exit before force-killing.

docs.title: variable idleShutdownTimeoutSeconds
docs.text:
int Tryll::Client::ManagedServerOptions::idleShutdownTimeoutSeconds;

Seconds of idle (zero sessions, no in-flight downloads) after which the launched server self-exits. Passed as --idle-shutdown-timeout <N> on the command line when non-zero. Default 60: an auto-launched server is disposable — this manager's Stop()/destructor no longer kill the process (see Stop()), so the server must be told to exit on its own once nothing is using it, or it leaks until the machine reboots. Pass 0 only when the caller has its own explicit reap strategy (e.g. the QA harness, which always calls a hard kill on teardown).

docs.title: function CreateAgent [1/2]
docs.text:
Blocking convenience wrapper over CreateAgentAsync . 

AgentProxy Tryll::Client::TryllClient::CreateAgent (
    const GraphDescription & graph,
    bool enableDiagnostics=false,
    std::optional< std::chrono::milliseconds > timeout=std::nullopt,
    bool maintainDialogueHistory=true,
    std::vector< AgentVariableDecl > variables={}
)

Parameters:

  • graph Fully-built graph description.
  • enableDiagnostics When true, the server serialises per-node execution data into TurnComplete.debug_info for every turn. Off by default; enable for QA/eval pipelines.
  • timeout Maximum time to wait for CreateAgentResponse. Defaults to 30 seconds.
  • maintainDialogueHistory When true (default), the agent keeps its full dialogue history. When false, the history is discarded after each turn — a stateless agent, useful for technical/classification agents that should not store or project prior turns.
  • variables The agent's complete variable declaration. See CreateAgentAsync. Empty by default.

Returns:

AgentProxy bound to the new server-side agent.

Exception:

  • TryllError On validation failures, server-reported errors (e.g. GraphCompilationFailed when the graph references a model that has not been acquired), or timeout.

std::future< AgentProxy > Tryll::Client::TryllClient::CreateAgentAsync (
    const GraphDescription & graph,
    bool enableDiagnostics=false,
    bool maintainDialogueHistory=true,
    std::vector< AgentVariableDecl > variables={}
)

Parameters:

  • graph Fully-built graph description.
  • enableDiagnostics When true, the server serialises per-node execution data into TurnComplete.debug_info for every turn. Off by default for zero overhead in production; enable for QA/eval pipelines.
  • maintainDialogueHistory See CreateAgent.
  • variables The agent's complete variable declaration — every variable it will ever have, with its initial value (the value's active alternative fixes the type for the agent's lifetime). Post-create writes to an undeclared name are rejected locally by AgentProxy::Variables without a wire round-trip. Empty by default.

Note:

The returned future completes when creation succeeds or fails definitively. A graph that references a model not yet acquired (see DownloadModel) fails fast with GraphCompilationFailed.

Returns:

Future yielding an AgentProxy bound to the new agent. Calling future::get() propagates any TryllError raised during validation or creation.

EmbeddedStorageInfo Tryll::Client::TryllClient::CreateEmbeddedStringStorage (
    std::string_view name,
    std::string_view configPath,
    std::string_view embeddingModel={},
    std::optional< std::chrono::milliseconds > timeout=std::nullopt
)

Path A: the server loads records and (optionally) an on-disk HNSW index described by a *.json config referencing a *.kb.json records file.

Parameters:

  • name Session-unique storage name.
  • configPath Server-side *.json path.
  • embeddingModel Optional catalog embedding-model name for cross-check; when non-empty must match the config's embedding_model.
  • timeout Maximum time to wait for the response; embedding large corpora is slow.

Returns:

EmbeddedStorageInfo with name, record count, and dimension.

Exception:

  • TryllError On server-reported errors (including InvalidStringStorageData when embeddingModel mismatches the config) or timeout.

docs.title: function CreateSession
docs.text:
Create the logical session for this connection (mandatory, one-shot). 

void Tryll::Client::TryllClient::CreateSession (
    const SessionConfig & cfg
)

Must be called exactly once after Connect and before CreateAgent or any model-management/storage/voice call — those are rejected with SessionNotReady until the session exists. A second call is rejected by the server with SessionAlreadyExists. On success the server-allocated session id becomes available via GetSessionId.

docs.text:
Send a dev-only debug command to the server and report the outcome. 

DebugCommandResult Tryll::Client::TryllClient::SendDebugCommand (
    std::string_view command,
    std::string_view payload={},
    std::chrono::milliseconds timeout=std::chrono::seconds{5}
)

The server handles this only in non-Production builds with debug_commands.enabled. command is a verb (e.g. "crash"); for crash, payload is the mode token (nullderef / abort / throw / throw_posted / stackoverflow / fastfail; empty defaults to nullderef).

docs.title: function SetSessionLocale
docs.text:
Change the session language without tearing the session down. 

void Tryll::Client::TryllClient::SetSessionLocale (
    std::string_view locale,
    std::chrono::milliseconds timeout=std::chrono::seconds{30}
)

Same BCP-47 grammar as SessionConfig::locale; an empty string clears the locale, restoring pre-locale behaviour everywhere.

Applies to every agent, existing and future, from its next turn: TTS language and the locale template keys are read per turn, not captured. A new voice input picks up the new STT language hint; one already open keeps its recognizer. Storage paths re-resolve on the next load, but content already bound to a node (a Retrieve KB, canned lines) does NOT swap - those params are structural. Use this for the voice + template half of a language change; switching authored content still means recreating agents.

Not turn-atomic: a turn already running may render its prompt under the old locale and synthesize under the new one. Send it between turns if that matters.

Exception:

  • TryllError On a malformed tag (InvalidLocale, 2004) or timeout.

docs.text:
A per-model hint. Sparse: list only the models you have an opinion about; anything absent takes every field's default.

placement is a hint, never a command: a host that cannot honour it downgrades and reports what it did — read LoadModelResponse rather than assuming.

hotwords is not downgradable. Hotword biasing needs beam-search decoding, which a recognizer fixes when it is constructed, so it selects which recognizer this session is served. HotwordBias_On costs a few percent of decode time and changes that model's transcripts whether or not a lexicon is supplied; HotwordBias_Off makes CreateVoiceInput reject a hotwordsStoragePath with HotwordBiasDisabled (4106) instead of accepting it and biasing nothing. Left at HotwordBias_Default, the model's catalog entry decides.

Optional, advisory hint: the engines this session expects to touch, as (role, engine) pairs. Leaving it empty is legal and unremarkable — a model's engine comes from the server's catalog, so a load works whether or not this named the engine it needs.

What it buys is timing: the server initialises the named engines' backends at CreateSession instead of at first use, which is worth doing when that cost is large (an ORT CUDA cold start was measured in tens of seconds). A harness that wants determinism about which engines a run touched can also state it here; the editors derive it from their model manifest and expose no engine control.

Only an out-of-range ordinal is rejected (InvalidEngineSet, 2005). A duplicate pair is logged and ignored.

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
Move-only handle to a server-side VoiceInput session.

Obtained via TryllClient::CreateVoiceInput or CreateVoiceInputAsync.

Lifetime guarantee: the destructor issues an implicit CancelUtterance (if active) followed by DestroyVoiceInput so the server-side ISttSession is always cleaned up. Move the handle to extend its lifetime.

Thread-safety: this handle is NOT internally synchronized. All public methods — including SendAudioBuffer — must be called from the same thread, or the caller must provide external synchronization. Moving or destroying the handle must likewise be serialized with any concurrent method calls.

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
Declares Tryll::Client::TryllClient, the primary client class, and Tryll::Client::ConnectedSession, the recommended one-call entry point for local-server deployments. Model-catalog entries are returned as ::Tryll::ModelInfoT (FlatBuffers gen-object-api type).

Recommended flow (local server, automatic lifecycle):

Tryll::Client::ManagedServerOptions opts;
opts.exe  = "path/to/tryll_server.exe";
opts.port = 9100;
auto session = Tryll::Client::TryllClient::RunAndConnect(opts);
// An empty config is the normal case: each model's engine comes from the
// server's catalog. Name engines only to pre-warm them (see SessionConfig).
session.GetClient().CreateSession({});
auto agent = session.GetClient().CreateAgent(graph);
agent.SendText("hi");
agent.Destroy();
// session destructor: shuts down client, then stops the server

Advanced / remote-server flow (no server management):

auto client = Tryll::Client::TryllClient::Connect("127.0.0.1", 9100);
client.CreateSession({});
auto agent = client.CreateAgent(graph);
agent.SendText("hi");
agent.Destroy();
client.Shutdown();

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
All failures surfaced by Tryll::Client::TryllClient and Tryll::Client::AgentProxy — server-reported errors, protocol decode failures, and connection-level problems — are raised as Tryll::Client::TryllError. Server-reported errors carry a numeric code that matches the ranges defined in server/common/include/tryll/ErrorCodes.h; client-side errors (timeouts, closed socket) carry code 0.

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text:
Plain C++ handle for a server-side agent. Created by UTryllSubsystem after a successful CreateAgentResponse.

Ownership: typically held as TSharedPtr<FTryllAgent> by UTryllAgentComponent. Lifetime: deterministic — the owning component releases the shared_ptr; this triggers PushDestroyAgent via UTryllSubsystem::RequestDestroyAgent().

All callbacks are invoked on the game thread (from UTryllSubsystem::Tick).

docs.title: function ChangeParams
docs.text:
void FTryllAgent::ChangeParams (
    const FString & NodeName,
    UTryllNodeParamsBase * Params,
    TFunction< void(const FTryllError &)> OnComplete=nullptr
)

Apply typed node parameters to a workflow node at runtime. The agent must not be processing a turn. Completion is invoked on the game thread via the OnComplete callback.

Clone-set-send idiom (C++): auto* P = UTryllNodeParamsFactory::CloneParams(AgentComp->GetNodeParamsBaseline("gen"), this); Cast<UTryllGenerateParams>(P)->SystemPrompt = TEXT("New prompt"); Agent->ChangeParams(TEXT("gen"), P);

Ticked Localized fields are resolved through the project's text provider on a copy before send (Params is not modified). An empty Text ID, no provider, or an unknown ID fails with InvalidParamValue and nothing is sent. To send your own text for such a field, untick its b<Field>Localized flag first.

void FTryllAgent::HandleNodeEvent (
    const FTryllDecodedNodeEvent & Event,
    bool bSessionListenerBound
)

Agent-scope half of NodeEvent dispatch. The caller has already broadcast session-level delegates. Records tool calls, fires the per-agent callbacks, then (for a pause) runs RegisterTool auto-resume.

Parameters:

  • bSessionListenerBound true when a session-scope listener for this event's kind is bound: OnPaused for a pause, any of OnToolCall / OnToolCallWithId / OnToolCallDetailed for a tool call (subsystem Blueprint delegates, or in PIE a direct editor listener / registered listener probe). Used only to decide whether a pause is resumable. Agent-scope listeners are counted here as well.

void FTryllAgent::Resume (
    const FString & ResumeNode=FString{},
    TFunction< void(const FTryllError &)> OnComplete=nullptr
)

Resume a turn that is currently paused (see the Pause node / typed OnNodeEvent event_type="paused" wiring on UTryllSubsystem). ResumeNode empty continues via the paused node's pending exit route; non-empty jumps to that node by name. Completion is invoked on the game thread: nullopt-equivalent (Error.IsOk()) on success, AgentNotPaused (3012) if the agent is not currently paused, or UnknownNode (3005) if ResumeNode does not name a node in the graph.

void FTryllAgent::RetryPausedToolBatch ()

Re-attempt the retained paused tool-call batch: handlers that already produced a result on a previous attempt are skipped (not re-run — no duplicate side effects), remaining handlers run, and a fresh Resume is sent. No-op if there is no retained batch (HasPausedToolBatch() is false). Use after OnToolHandlerError reports a failed handler or a rejected/disconnected resume.

docs.title: function SetOnTtsAudio
docs.text:
void FTryllAgent::SetOnTtsAudio (
    TFunction< void(const FString &NodeName, TArrayView< const int16 > Pcm)> Callback
)

Streaming TTS audio callback. Fires for each TtsAudioFrame within a turn. NodeName is the producing node's name (multi-sender attribution). The view references the FTryllConnEvent storage and is valid only for the duration of the callback. End-of-stream is signalled by OnTurnComplete — TtsAudioFrame intentionally carries no is_final field.

    TFunction< void(const FString &NodeName, uint32 SampleRate, uint16 Channels, uint16 BitsPerSample)> Callback
)

TTS audio format callback. Fires once per turn, before any OnTtsAudio. Parameters: (NodeName, SampleRate, Channels, BitsPerSample). NodeName is the producing node's name (multi-sender attribution — mirrors OnAnswerText). Only mono int16 PCM is currently emitted by the server.

docs.title: function SetOnTtsVisemes
docs.text:
void FTryllAgent::SetOnTtsVisemes (
    TFunction< void(const FString &NodeName, TArrayView< const FTryllVisemeEvent > Events)> Callback
)

Viseme track callback. Fires once per synthesized sentence when the agent's voice has emit_visemes (FTryllVoiceProfileData::bEmitVisemes) on, after that sentence's audio. Offsets are turn-absolute samples at the rate from OnTtsAudioFormat; frames of a turn continue from one another. The view is valid only for the duration of the callback.

docs.title: function SetVoice
docs.text:
void FTryllAgent::SetVoice (
    const FTryllVoiceProfileData & Voice,
    TFunction< void(const FTryllError &)> OnComplete=nullptr
)

Replace the agent's voice (protocol v27 SetAgentVoice). Idle-only: AgentBusy (3004) while a turn runs, unless it is paused before resume. A profile the model cannot use fails with InvalidVoiceProfile (3023) and the old voice stays. The active delivery mode survives when the new profile defines a mode of the same name; otherwise the new profile's default mode applies. On success GetVoice() returns the new profile.

docs.text:
Fluent C++ builder for FTryllGraphDescription. Typed AddXxx methods are declared in TryllGraphBuilder.Nodes.h (generated). Not a USTRUCT — for programmatic C++ use only.

Example: UTryllGenerateParams* P = UTryllNodeParamsFactory::MakeGenerateParams(this); P->ModelName = TEXT("qwen2.5-0.5b-instruct"); P->SystemPrompt = TEXT("You are helpful.");

// Protocol v2: wiring lives on each node's params (e.g. P->DefaultExit). FTryllGraphDescription Graph = FTryllGraphBuilder() .AddGenerate(TEXT("gen"), P) // P->DefaultExit defaults to "" = END .SetStartNode(TEXT("gen")) .Build();

docs.title: Detailed Description
docs.text: Live agents created with ticked Text IDs. On a language change each agent is refreshed from its current params baseline (so runtime ChangeParams survive): ticked non-structural fields are re-resolved on a clone and only nodes whose text changed are sent. One failed field sends nothing for that agent. An AgentBusy reply marks the agent dirty; the refresh is redone when its turn ends. Applied fires once the latest refresh of an agent is fully acknowledged, or at once when no text changed. A refresh started later makes the replies of an earlier one stale.

docs.title: function Spawn
docs.text:
bool FTryllManagedServerProcess::Spawn (
    const FString & ExePath,
    int32 Port,
    int32 IdleShutdownTimeoutSeconds,
    double ReadinessTimeoutSeconds,
    const FString & LlamaCppBackend,
    FString & OutError,
    bool & bOutPortConflict
)

Spawns ExePath with "--port Port --idle-shutdown-timeout Seconds --llama-backend LlamaCppBackend" and waits up to ReadinessTimeoutSeconds for its TCP port to start accepting.

Returns true when the launch should proceed to connecting — either the port is already accepting, OR the readiness wait elapsed but the process is still alive (a cold start still warming up). In the latter case the server is deliberately left running, not killed: killing an almost-ready server discards the warmup and forces a cold re-spawn — the root cause of "first launch hangs, relaunch works". The caller connects anyway and the connection worker retries until the server is ready.

Returns false only for a genuine launch failure: the process could not be spawned, or it exited on its own before the port opened. OutError is then populated with a clear reason, and bOutPortConflict is set to true iff the process exited with Tryll::ServerExitPortInUse (3), so callers can special-case a bind collision (retry on a different port).

Defaults to LlamaCpp, not Mock: Mock is the enum's zero value and a production server refuses it.

docs.title: variable Languages

BCP-47 primary language subtags this model declares, cached from the catalog.

The one piece of catalog metadata cached here rather than read live. Everything else can wait for a ListModels round trip, but the settings language dropdown and the model-picker warnings have to work with no server running - an editor that can only validate languages while connected would be worse than no validation at all. Written by the Model Manager from the live FTryllModelInfo at the moment the model is registered.

Empty means undeclared, not "supports nothing".
